title: Effects of Cognitive-Behavioral Treatment in Children With Affective Dysregulation (ADOPT-Treatment): A Randomized Controlled Trial
journal: J Am Acad Child Adolesc Psychiatry
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Affective dysregulation (AD) in childhood is characterized by heightened reactivity to emotional stimuli and impairments across multiple domains. Evidence on the efficacy of psychosocial interventions specifically tailored to AD is scarce.

METHOD: In this multicenter randomized controlled trial, 159 children aged 8-12 years with AD were randomized to either a modular cognitive-behavioral intervention (THOPAS; 24 sessions) or treatment as usual (TAU). Primary outcome was clinician-rated AD symptom severity (blinded and composite), and secondary outcomes were functional impairment, co-occurring conditions, emotion regulation, and parenting. Assessments were conducted at baseline, post-intervention, and 32-week follow-up. The analyses followed modified intention-to-treat and per-protocol principles.

RESULTS: No between-group differences emerged for the primary outcome, and only isolated effects were found for secondary outcomes. Both THOPAS and TAU showed small-to-moderate improvements over time. Exploratory subgroup analyses suggested that children with higher baseline symptom severity may have benefited more from THOPAS. Feasibility indicators suggested high therapist fidelity, strong parental engagement, high satisfaction, and high safety for THOPAS.

CONCLUSION: The trial found no overall superiority of THOPAS over high-quality TAU. While THOPAS was feasible and well-received, the study was not powered to detect small effects. Future research should incorporate both standardized and individualized outcome measures, refine baseline severity thresholds, and examine the long-term stability of treatment effects.

CLINICAL TRIAL REGISTRATION INFORMATION: Efficacy of a Personalized Modular Outpatient Treatment of Affective Dysregulation and Coexisting Conditions in Children (ADOPT Treatment); https://drks.de/search/en/trial/DRKS00013317.

title: Longitudinal patterns of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder medication use and subsequent incident substance use among US youth
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Understanding potential substance use risks or protection associated with ADHD medication use over time among US youth with ADHD has clinical and public health importance. Using longitudinal nationally representative data and accounting for pre-existing differences in youth can shed light on these associations.

METHODS: This study used longitudinal prospective data from the Population Assessment of Tobacco and Health Study (2013/14-2023). Analyses included youth ages 12-17 with a parent-reported history of an ADHD diagnosis by a doctor, nurse, or health professional (n = 4,700 observations; n = 2,140 unique individuals). Using propensity score weighting to account for pre-exposure differences, the effect of ADHD medication initiation compared to no ADHD medication use and the effect of ADHD medication discontinuation compared to continuation on five incident substance use outcomes (alcohol, nicotine/tobacco, e-cigarettes, cannabis, other drugs) 1 year later were examined.

RESULTS: Among youth with parent-reported ADHD, those who initiated ADHD medication did not differ from youth who did not use ADHD medication in subsequent incident substance use risk (adjusted odds ratios ranged from 0.94 to 1.36). Similarly, those who discontinued ADHD medication did not differ from youth who continued ADHD medication in subsequent risk for incident substance use (adjusted odds ratios ranged from 0.98 to 1.02).

CONCLUSIONS: These results add to the evidence that ADHD medication use initiation and medication discontinuation patterns are not related to an increased risk for incident substance use among US youth. This study highlights the importance of considering baseline differences between youth when considering the effect of ADHD medication on future substance use risk.

title: Functional brain connectivity in patients with anorexia nervosa before and after short-term weight restoration
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Resting-state functional connectivity (RSFC) studies have consistently identified widespread alterations in the brain's functional network architecture in anorexia nervosa (AN), but it remains unclear whether they are reversible with weight restoration. Furthermore, it is not clear whether there are associations between RSFC and neuroendocrine changes, such as leptin suppression in the underweight state of AN and its increase during short-term weight restoration.

METHODS: We first analyzed RSFC data cross-sectionally in young female patients with AN (n = 117) and healthy control participants (n = 117) using network-based statistic (NBS) and graph theory metrics and subsequently explored relationships with plasma leptin as a marker of undernutrition. A subset of patients (n = 73) was reassessed longitudinally after short-term weight restoration [mean body mass index (BMI) increase: 28.0%] to test for changes in identified alterations.

RESULTS: NBS revealed increased RSFC in cingulo-occipito-cerebellar circuitry in underweight patients with AN (p = .0018), which decreased over the inpatient weight restoration interval (p < .001). This change correlated negatively with plasma leptin concentrations (p = .042), and plasma leptin appeared to partially mediate the association between BMI increase and RSFC decrease (p = .039), suggesting a possible region-specific modulatory effect. Underweight patients with AN also showed higher characteristic path length (p = .035), indicating reduced integration between brain regions, and higher assortativity (p = .013), indicating stronger coupling among similarly connected regions. Longitudinally, characteristic path length decreased during weight restoration (p = .004), whereas findings for assortativity were suggestive of no change.

CONCLUSIONS: The results provide novel longitudinal evidence that functional connectome alterations in AN partially normalize during short-term weight restoration. Speculatively, taking previous results in long-term recovered individuals into consideration, higher assortativity might reflect potential vulnerability for AN. Our finding of a tentative association between the normalization of plasma leptin concentrations and RSFC suggests the possibility that leptin may modulate changes in specific patterns of functional connectivity, offering a potential neurobiological target for novel pharmacotherapies.

title: Does early childhood education and care for infants and toddlers cause behavior problems up to age 8?
abstract:
BACKGROUND: The causal effect of attending Early Childhood Education and Care (ECEC) for infants and toddlers on child behavior problems is contested. Yet, most previous research is correlational. Findings from previous research are mixed, but with some evidence of harmful effects on children's behavior. Some correlational studies also suggest that ECEC may be most harmful for children from socioeconomically advantaged families.

METHODS: We estimate the effect of age of entry into ECEC on externalizing behavior problems at ages 3, 5, and 8 years in a large sample (n = 66,394) from The Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Cohort study (MoBa). We use two quasi-experimental methods, Two-way fixed-effects models and instrumental variable models, that exploit variations in how early families enrolled their children in ECEC due to a national scale-up of publicly funded centers.

RESULTS: In this high-powered, rigorous approach to testing the causal impact of age of entry into ECEC, we find no evidence that entry around age 1 relative to later affects behavior problems either during preschool years (at ages 3 or 5) or after school entry (at age 8 years). We also find no evidence that these effects vary by parental education or family income.

CONCLUSIONS: We find no evidence suggesting that early entry into ECEC has harmful consequences for children's behavior regulation during the preschool years or after school entry. We argue that our null results may be due to ECEC pedagogy in Norway that emphasizes young children's well-being and playful learning experiences.

title: Measurement invariance of the affective reactivity index across five countries
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: Irritability is a globally relevant dimension of youth psychopathology, yet cross-national comparisons require evidence that assessment tools function equivalently across countries and languages. We examined the reliability, factor structure, and measurement invariance of the Affective Reactivity Index (ARI) across samples from Brazil, China, Japan, Spain, and the United States (US).

METHOD: Community samples (N = 6,195; ages 6-18 years) completed parent- or youth-report ARI versions. Single-factor confirmatory factor analyses evaluated model fit and internal consistency. Multi-group CFA tested measurement invariance. Differences in observed total scores between samples and pooled age and sex associations were examined using linear regression.

RESULTS: Internal consistency was acceptable to good across country samples and informants. A single-factor structure was broadly supported. For parent report, measurement invariance was well supported across China and Japan using the original three-category format and also supported across China, Japan, and the US after dichotomization of all items, due to lack of endorsement of the highest category of Item 4 in the US sample. For youth report, threshold and loading invariance were supported, but scalar invariance was not. Parent-reported irritability was higher in the Chinese and Japanese samples than in the U.S. sample, whereas youth-reported irritability was highest in the Brazilian sample. Parents reported higher irritability in boys and younger youth; youth self-report showed no significant age or sex effects.

CONCLUSION: The ARI showed broadly comparable measurement properties across the participating samples, with stronger evidence for parent report than youth report. However, parent-report comparisons involving the US were based on a dichotomized response format, and full intercept invariance was not established for youth report. Observed score differences should therefore be interpreted cautiously, and as differences between participating samples rather than population-level cross-national differences.

title: Behavioural parent training for disruptive behaviour in children with autism: moderators and mediators of the effects of a randomized controlled trial
abstract: Behavioural parent training is a well-established intervention for children with autism and disruptive behaviour. In a recent randomized controlled trial on parent training for children with autism and disruptive behaviour, we found positive effects of face-to-face (but not blended) parent training on children's noncompliance and irritability, and on parenting sense of competence and overreactive parenting. However, effect sizes were medium, which may indicate room for improvement. Here, we investigated two potential avenues to achieve such improvement: (1) by getting a better understanding of the mechanisms of change of the intervention (i.e., mediation effects); (2) by identifying whether there are subgroups for whom the intervention works better or worse (i.e., moderation effects). We tested whether parenting sense of competence, parenting stress and parenting style mediated the effects of parent training on our primary outcome measures child noncompliance and irritability. In addition, we examined if parenting sense of competence, parenting stress, parenting style, parental attitudes or parental psychopathology moderated treatment success. We found that an improvement in parenting sense of competence was associated with the effect of face-to-face parent training on children's noncompliance, but not on irritability, while changes in parenting stress or parenting style were not related to treatment effects. We did not find any moderating effects on the effects of parent training. We conclude that, based on these results, more focus on increasing parents' feelings of competence as a parent might be a way forward to increase the effectiveness of behavioural parent training for children with autism and disruptive behaviour.

title: Brain health in children born extremely preterm: a multidimensional perspective
abstract: Gestational age and developmental stage of the brain at birth are major determinants of child health, and long-term consequences of preterm birth and altered brain maturation are inadequately understood simply through brain injury, survival rates, or diagnostic labels. In this Review, we conceptualise brain health in children born extremely preterm (before 28 weeks' gestation) as a developmental condition shaped by maturational timing, biological vulnerability, neonatal intensive care exposure, sensory and relational experiences, family circumstances, and social environments. We integrate evidence from research on early brain development and consciousness, long-term multidomain neurodevelopmental outcomes, neonatal intensive care practice, relational caregiving, early developmental interventions, and ethical, psychological, and social dimensions of care. Across these domains, extremely preterm birth emerges not as a single event but as a neuroplastic system that adapts to biological and environmental risks and protective factors that shape neurodevelopmental resilience and vulnerabilities and establish developmental trajectories. We argue that care for the infant born extremely preterm is optimised through a brain-health framework where care becomes a longitudinal, ethical process that integrates family support, minimises harmful exposures, promotes adaptive development, and fosters participation, wellbeing, and quality of life.

title: Satisfaction, Regret, and Harm After Hormone Therapy in Youth From a Multidisciplinary Gender Clinic
abstract:
Key Points Question What degrees of satisfaction, regret, and harm are reported by transgender and gender-diverse participants who initiated testosterone or estrogen therapy (ie, hormone therapy [HT]) as youth, and are these experiences associated with demographic or clinical characteristics? Findings In this cohort study of 372 participants who received care at a single multidisciplinary clinic, satisfaction with HT was high and regret and harm were rare. Decisional regret was slightly higher among youths not currently receiving HT and those identifying on the nonbinary spectrum, but it remained low in absolute terms. Meaning Results provide support for existing standards of care rather than broad restrictions on youths’ access to HT.

Importance Concerns about regret and harm have led to restrictions on transgender and gender-diverse youths’ access to testosterone or estrogen therapy (ie, hormone therapy [HT]), while empirical data on decisional regret among those initiating HT as youth remain limited. Objectives To examine satisfaction, regret, and perceived harm among individuals who initiated HT as youth and to identify demographic and clinical characteristics associated with regret or harm and current HT status (receiving vs not). Design, Setting, and Participants This cohort study evaluates self-report surveys collected from October 2023 to October 2025 among former patients who initiated HT as youth at a single multidisciplinary gender clinic in the US. Data analysis was conducted from December 2025 to August 2026. Exposure Initiation of estrogen or testosterone. Main Outcomes and Measures Decision Regret Scale (DRS) total score (range, 0-100; higher scores indicate greater regret); item-level satisfaction, regret, and perceived harm; and current HT status. Associations with demographic and clinical characteristics were examined using nonparametric, Welch t , Fisher exact, or Pearson χ 2 tests as appropriate, with parametric sensitivity analyses for the DRS total score. Results Of the 376 participants who initiated HT as youth (112 [29.8%] initiating estrogen and 264 [70.2%] initiating testosterone; current age, 14-28 years; mean [SD] age, 20.9 [2.9] years; time since HT initiation: range, 1.2 months to 10.7 years; mean [SD], 4.9 [2.5] years), 4 were missing DRS scores, all of whom were currently receiving HT. Among the 372 respondents with DRS scores, overall decisional regret was very low (mean [SD] DRS score, 4.3 [14.7]; median [IQR], 0 [0-0]); 360 participants (96.8%) endorsed that receiving HT was the right decision, 10 (2.7%) reported regret, and 7 (1.9%) reported perceived harm. DRS scores were higher among participants not currently receiving HT vs currently receiving HT and among those identifying on the nonbinary vs binary spectrum; parametric sensitivity analyses estimated mean differences of 15.95 points (95% CI, 8.50-23.39) and 6.07 points (95% CI, 2.15-9.99), respectively. Participants not currently receiving HT (65 participants [17.3%]) were more likely than those currently receiving HT (311 [82.7%]) to have received testosterone (odds ratio, 3.58; 95% CI, 1.65-7.78; P = .001) and identify on the nonbinary spectrum (odds ratio, 8.88; 95% CI, 4.76-16.58; P < .001), were older (mean difference, 1.04 years; 95% CI, 0.45-1.64 years; P = .001), and had longer time since initiating HT (mean difference, 1.00 year; 95% CI, 0.48-1.53 years; P < .001). Neither regret or harm nor current HT status was associated with age at HT initiation or prepubertal gender diversity. Conclusions and Relevance The findings of this cohort study complement the literature documenting mental health benefits of HT, providing further support for existing standards of care for transgender and gender-diverse youth.

This cohort study examines satisfaction, regret, and perceived harm among individuals who initiated hormone therapy as youth and identifies demographic and clinical characteristics associated with regret or harm and current hormone therapy status.

Introduction Current estimates suggest that approximately 3.3% of 13- to 17-year-olds in the US identify as transgender or gender diverse (TGD). However, only a small proportion receive hormone therapy (HT; ie, testosterone, estrogen), with insurance-based analyses indicating rates below 0.1% of the general youth population. More than a dozen short-term follow-up studies and several large cross-sectional and retrospective studies have consistently found improvements in mental health and quality of life among TGD youth receiving HT. Prior research from our clinic found significant reductions in body dissatisfaction, depression, and anxiety and improvement in psychosocial functioning in 2 cohorts of youth 1 year after initiating HT and/or puberty suppression. This previous research indirectly suggests that TGD youth may be satisfied with HT. However, concerns about potential regret and harm have intensified, leading to widespread efforts to prevent minors from accessing HT despite standards of care continuing to support its use. While more limited in scope, several initial studies have demonstrated very low levels of regret among youth, consistent with low regret levels documented among TGD adults. One of the first major longitudinal studies of youth receiving HT reported that no participants expressed regret regarding puberty suppression or HT an average of 6 years after starting treatment. Three other clinic-based studies of youth have documented regret rates between 0% and 2%. These findings are also consistent with a community-based sample of youth who socially transitioned in childhood and later accessed HT. While the rate of regret was slightly higher in this sample (5 of 119 respondents [4.2%]), nearly all respondents (115 of 119 [96.6%]) reported satisfaction with treatment. Preliminary research also suggests that rates of treatment discontinuation are low for those initiating HT as youth. van der Loos et al reported that only 16 of 720 participants (2.2%) who started puberty suppression as adolescents were no longer receiving HT at median (IQR) follow-up of 3.5 (1.5-6.6) years later for youth assigned female and 2.3 (1.2-4.8) years later for youth assigned male. In another clinic-based sample with median follow-up of 2.7 years, 57 of 1050 participants (5.4%) initiating HT as youth discontinued HT for at least 3 months, although 20 subsequently restarted and 210 were lost to follow-up. In a third sample using a US military insurance database, the 4-year continuation rate for those starting HT as minors was somewhat lower (74%), but it was still higher than for those who started HT as adults (64%). Most studies examining reasons for stopping treatment have been conducted with adults, and findings suggest that stopping treatment is influenced by a range of internal and external factors and thus is not synonymous with regret. Given recent increases in external barriers to accessing HT, rates of stopping treatment are likely increasing. The present study seeks to strengthen the research base regarding TGD youths’ experiences with HT, considering the substantial shifts in access to HT and concerns about the well-being of youth receiving this care. Building on our previous work, our first aim was to examine the degree of perceived satisfaction, regret, and harm among youth who initiated HT, including those who were currently receiving HT as well as those who were not. Our second aim was to examine whether demographic and clinical factors were associated with (1) youths’ reports of regret or harm and/or (2) current HT status (receiving vs not). Methods Participants and Procedure Participants in this cohort study included former patients who were seen by a US multidisciplinary program for TGD youth and received HT. The process for initiating HT was guided by the World Professional Association for Transgender Health’s standards of care, version 7 (the current version at the time), and the Endocrine Society’s guidelines, which included a semistructured assessment with patients and their parent(s) or guardian(s) conducted by a mental health professional in the program. This assessment visit was designed specifically for patients potentially interested in initiating medical treatment. For patients younger than 18 years, consent for HT was required from all parent(s) or guardian(s) with legal medical decision-making rights in addition to patient assent. Regardless of whether they subsequently initiated medical treatment, patients and parents who participated in the assessment were also approached to provide assent or consent for the clinical information from their medical record to be used for research purposes as part of a study approved by the institutional review board at University of Texas Southwestern Medical Center. Consent from a parent or guardian was required for research participants who were minors (aged <18 years) at the time of assent. Starting October 2023, patients and parents who provided initial assent or consent were reapproached to complete a yearly online research survey as part of a newly funded National Institutes of Health study. Participants could complete the survey from 1 month before to 6 months after the yearly anniversary of their initial assessment. The present study uses data collected from October 2023 to October 2025. Recruitment materials encouraged former patients to participate even if they never started treatment, stopped treatment, and/or were no longer receiving care. While all participants completed an assessment with the program, a minority started HT before or after being seen by the program (eg, transferred care after moving). Participants were compensated $45 to $65; changes in compensation aligned with adding new measures. We followed the Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology ( STROBE ) reporting guidelines. Data analysis was conducted from December 2025 to August 2026. Measures For treatments started prior to the participants’ last visit with the program, start dates documented in medical records were used. Self-report was used for any additional start and stop dates and participants’ current gender and sexual orientation identities. Participants’ assigned sex, race, and ethnicity were obtained from medical records when self-report was not available. Prepubertal onset of gender diversity was assessed by 3 yes vs no items completed by the clinician indicating the presence of gender nonconformity, physical dysphoria, and/or a stated gender identity different than assigned sex prior to puberty onset. Patients’ self-reported age at which they first identified with the gender identity reported at the initial assessment (hereafter termed age at first identification ) was also obtained from the assessment note. Participants completed the Decision Regret Scale (DRS), a 5-item measure with 5 response options prompting respondents to “reflect on your decision to start estrogen/testosterone therapy.” Total scores range from 0 to 100; higher scores indicate higher levels of decisional regret. For participants with multiple versions of the survey, the most recent version was used. However, all participants who agreed or strongly agreed that they experienced regret or harm on any version of the survey were included in analyses examining the subgroup of participants who reported regret or harm. Starting in October 2024, if a participant reported that they agreed or strongly agreed that they experienced regret or harm, they were prompted to describe their experiences in an open-ended text box. Statistical Analysis To characterize the sample, we compared patients who consented vs those who were not reached or who declined participation by age at initial assessment and assigned sex and ethnicity (Hispanic or Latino vs not Hispanic or Latino). Among those who consented, we also tested for differences between those who completed vs did not complete the survey by the same characteristics, prepubertal onset of gender diversity, and age at first identification. To characterize each participant’s perception of satisfaction, regret, and harm, we examined total scores on the DRS and responses on individual items reflecting the participant’s perceptions of whether they made the right decision, experienced regret, and were harmed by the treatment. We also examined whether assigned sex, current gender identity (dichotomized into binary vs nonbinary spectrum, excluding cisgender), prepubertal onset of gender diversity, age at first identification, age at HT initiation, current age, and time since initiating HT were associated with (1) DRS scores, (2) whether participants ever reported regret or harm, and (3) HT status (receiving vs not). Qualitative responses were grouped into themes based on consensus between coauthors. Given DRS scores showed substantial positive skew (4.7), kurtosis (23.9), and a pronounced floor effect (median [IQR], 0 [0-0]), nonparametric analyses were selected as a conservative primary approach. Spearman rank-order correlations examined associations between DRS scores and continuous variables, and Mann-Whitney U tests compared DRS score distributions across dichotomized variables, with effect sizes ( r ) computed from the standardized test statistic. Parametric analyses using Pearson correlations and Welch t test were also conducted as sensitivity analyses. Demographic and clinical characteristics were compared by regret or harm and current HT status using Welch t tests or Mann-Whitney U tests for markedly nonnormal continuous variables and Fisher exact or Pearson χ 2 tests for categorical variables, as appropriate. Effect estimates and 95% CIs were reported when applicable. Results Participants who consented to the initial study did not differ in age at initial assessment, assigned sex, or ethnicity from those who did not (eg, declined, not reached). However, among those who initially consented, those assigned male and those who experienced physical dysphoria prior to puberty were less likely to complete the current survey. No other differences were found between these groups. Figure 1 provides a flowchart of participant inclusion. Table 1 and Table 2 provide information on participant demographic and clinical characteristics separated by current HT status and ever experiencing regret or harm from receiving HT. title: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder Accommodations, Behavior Therapy, and Stimulant Medication: A Randomized Clinical Trial
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Although widely deployed, little is known about the efficacy of academic accommodations for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), alone or in combination of behavior therapy and stimulant medication.

OBJECTIVE: To evaluate the efficacy of academic accommodations alone and in combination with behavioral interventions and stimulant medication.

DESIGN, SETTING, AND PARTICIPANTS: This was a crossover randomized clinical trial with participants introduced to all conditions. Children with ADHD were enrolled in kindergarten through sixth grade. Academic accommodations were changed daily in a randomized order. Stimulant medication and placebo alternated weekly. The general classroom and enhanced behavior classroom intervention alternated every 2 weeks. The study was conducted in summer treatment program classrooms. For the present study, behavior was evaluated in (1) a classroom period where participants completed independent assignments and (2) a classroom period where participants were taught a lesson, completed small group cooperative tasks related to the lesson, and then took a quiz. Study data were analyzed from March to July 2026.

INTERVENTIONS: The single and combined effects of academic accommodations, behavior therapy, and stimulant medication (methylphenidate, 0.3 mg/kg) were evaluated. Academic accommodations were extended time on tasks, frequent breaks during tasks, a low-distraction workspace, and the ability to stand at the desk, compared with a condition without an accommodation. A general classroom setting was compared with a classroom setting with enhanced behavior intervention.

MAIN OUTCOMES AND MEASURES: Main outcomes were classroom rule violations during each of the two, 1-hour class periods, the number of seatwork items completed correctly (ie, academic productivity), and the quiz score.

RESULTS: Of 306 children screened, 280 were enrolled in the study. A total of 255 children (mean [SD] age, 8.8 [1.6] months; 201 male [79%]) started the intervention, and 235 (84%) completed the study. Compared with placebo, stimulant medication increased effects related to seatwork productivity by 22% (ie, the rate ratio [RR] for this condition indicated that receiving medication compared with placebo multiplied the expected count of problems completed per minute by 1.22; 95% CI, 1.19-1.25), and quiz scores were significantly improved by 3.9 points (95% CI, 3.10-4.70 points). Medication and behavioral therapy significantly reduced classroom rule-breaking behavior by 37% (RR, 0.63; 95% CI, 0.60-0.67) and 61% (RR, 0.39; 95% CI, 0.37-0.42), respectively. There was no evidence that any of the academic accommodations significantly improved behavior or academic outcomes. No interactions were significant.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Results of this crossover randomized clinical trial question whether school-based academic accommodations for children with ADHD should continue to be emphasized as accommodations were ineffective when used alone or in combination with other ADHD treatments. Results support the continued use of behavioral and pharmacological treatment for ADHD.

TRIAL REGISTRATION: ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT05469386.

title: Comparative efficacy and tolerability of pharmacological interventions for the acute treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder across the lifespan: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pharmacological treatment is recommended for obsessive-compulsive disorder. Several options are available, yet little is known on comparative effects of individual medications. We aimed to elucidate the efficacy and tolerability of pharmacotherapy for people with obsessive-compulsive disorder, across the lifespan.

METHODS: We did a systematic review and network meta-analysis comparing short-term pharmacological interventions for obsessive-compulsive disorder. We searched multiple databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, PsycInfo, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, for literature on licensed or recommended pharmacological treatments for obsessive-compulsive disorder, without age restrictions, from database inception up to March 11, 2026. We included double-blind, randomised controlled trials with outcomes between 8 and 16 weeks. Two reviewers independently and in duplicate extracted outcomes, with a quality check done by a third reviewer. Primary outcomes were efficacy, defined as change from baseline score, and tolerability, defined as the proportion of participants discontinuing treatment due to adverse events. Separately for children and adolescents (aged 0-17 years) and adults (aged ≥18 years), we calculated standardised mean differences (SMDs) and odds ratios (ORs) with random-effects pairwise and network meta-analysis. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the Confidence in Network Meta-Analysis (CINeMA) framework. People with lived experience of obsessive-compulsive disorder were involved in the entire review process, including protocol development, writing, and interpretation of the findings. The study was preregistered in Open Science Framework (identifier 4V3GS).

FINDINGS: We included 52 randomised controlled trials with 7316 participants. Nine trials were included for children and adolescents (N=822; median age 12·5 years [IQR 11·6-13·2]; 352 [55%] male and 285 [45%] female among 637 participants with reported sex distribution). 43 trials were included for adults (N=6494; median age 36·4 years [35·0-37·9]; 3105 [49%] male and 3200 [51%] female among 6305 participants with reported sex distribution). Data on ethnicity were reported in 15 (29%) of 52 randomised controlled trials, using inconsistent definitions. In children and adolescents, clomipramine was more efficacious than placebo (SMD -1·19, 95% CI -1·73 to -0·64, CINeMA low), as were sertraline (-0·52, -0·80 to -0·02, low), fluoxetine (-0·43, -0·76 to -0·10, low), and fluvoxamine (-0·39, -0·71 to -0·07, low). Clomipramine was more efficacious than fluoxetine (SMD -0·75, 95% CI -1·39 to -0·11; very low), fluvoxamine (-0·79, -1·43 to -0·16; very low), paroxetine (-0·87, -1·51 to -0·22; very low), and sertraline (-0·87, -1·51 to -0·22; very low). Only sertraline was less tolerable than placebo (OR 4·51, 95% CI 1·36 to 14·96; low). In adults, clomipramine (SMD -0·71, 95% CI -0·88 to -0·54; high), fluvoxamine (-0·63, -0·83 to -0·43; high), paroxetine (-0·51, -0·73 to -0·29; moderate), sertraline (-0·49, -0·70 to -0·28; moderate), escitalopram (-0·43, -0·85 to -0·02; moderate), and fluoxetine (-0·37, -0·6 to -0·08; moderate) were more efficacious than placebo, and clomipramine was more efficacious than fluoxetine (-0·34, -0·65 to -0·04; low). Clomipramine (OR 4·65, 95% CI 3·27 to 6·60; moderate), fluvoxamine (2·73, 1·77 to 4·20; moderate), fluoxetine (2·52, 1·27 to 4·98; moderate), sertraline (2·23, 1·49 to 3·34; moderate), and paroxetine (1·99, 1·36 to 2·93; moderate) were less tolerable than placebo. Clomipramine was less tolerable than all active comparators (OR range 1·70 to 3·50; moderate) except fluoxetine (moderate) and venlafaxine (low).

INTERPRETATION: Clomipramine showed the largest estimated efficacy for obsessive-compulsive disorder but had a lower tolerability than SSRIs. The evidence of its superiority over individual SSRIs was more pronounced in children and adolescents. Our findings suggest that the trade-off between efficacy and tolerability should be discussed within an individualised, shared, decision-making framework.

FUNDING: None.

title: Intervening on Therapy-Interfering Behavior
abstract: Therapy-interfering behavior (TIB), although commonly encountered in clinical practice, often goes unaddressed. But if behaviors preventing treatment engagement are not addressed, patients may struggle to achieve their treatment goals, remain at a high chronic risk for suicide, and drop out of treatment. Therefore, to truly help our patients approach their stated goals and target suicide risk, it is critical to address TIB. In this second column of a 2-part series, we discuss common contexts in which TIBs emerge, how to explore the function of TIBs, and methods for addressing them.

title: Deaths due to elderly suicide in Turkey: a retrospective study
abstract:
Background Understanding the dynamics of elderly suicides is of great importance for the development of effective prevention strategies. This study aims to identify the characteristics of elderly suicides and to assess the impact of the pandemic on these incidents. Methods In this study, we retrospectively analysed the suicides of adults aged 65 years and over who died by suicide in Turkey between 01/01/2014 and 31/12/2023 using the data of the Turkish Statistical Institute. Results A total of 4066 elderly suicides were identified. 75% of elderly suicide deaths occurred in males. Suicide rates were significantly higher among individuals aged ≥ 75 compared with those aged 65–69 (RR = 1.40, 95% CI: 1.30–1.50) and 70–74 (RR = 1.36, 95% CI: 1.26–1.47). Elderly males had a 3.83-fold higher suicide rate than females (RR = 3.83, 95% CI: 3.56–4.11). Population-adjusted Poisson regression showed that suicide rates increased significantly during the pandemic period compared to the pre-pandemic period (IRR = 1.10, 95% CI: 1.02–1.18). This increase was significant among males (IRR = 1.11, 95% CI: 1.02–1.22) but not females (IRR = 1.02, 95% CI: 0.88–1.19). In the post-pandemic period, suicide rates declined marginally in both males (IRR = 0.91) and females (IRR = 0.84). Hanging was the most common method of suicide overall, whereas suicides involving firearms and those attributed to financial difficulties occurred predominantly among males. Conclusion Elderly suicide rates in Turkey were consistently higher among males and individuals aged ≥ 75 years. Higher population-adjusted suicide rates were observed during the COVID-19 period, particularly among elderly males, followed by a decline in the post-pandemic period. These findings highlight the importance of age- and sex-specific suicide prevention strategies and strengthening mental health and social support services for elderly adults. Background The elderly population is increasing every year and suicide remains an important public health problem in this very vulnerable population. Although elderly suicides declined before the pandemic, they still cause thousands of preventable deaths each year [ 1 ]. Elderly people remain at the top of the risk of death from suicide worldwide [ 2 ]. Compared to young people, elderly people are less likely to attempt suicide but more likely to die [ 3 ]. With ageing, losses in health, social roles, and relationships may lead to serious psychological distress [ 4 ] The rise of nuclear families has increased loneliness and social isolation among the elderly [ 5 ]. Among adults who commit suicide, it is estimated that the elderly are nine times more likely to live alone than other age groups [ 6 ]. Lack of social interaction, isolation and loneliness are the most important risk factors for suicidal behaviour in the elderly [ 7 ]. Especially depression, physical illnesses, previous suicide attempts, substance abuse, loneliness, marital status, financial stress, history of psychiatric disease or suicide in first-degree relatives and low social support are the factors that most frequently increase suicidal tendencies in elderly adults [ 1 , 8 ]. As the global elderly population grows, elderly suicide cases are expected to rise [ 9 ]. COVID-19, declared as an epidemic by World Health Organization (WHO) on 11 March 2020, was first seen in Turkey in March 2020. As most COVID-19 deaths occurred in those over 65, strict curfews and isolation were imposed on the elderly. These strategies have deepened social isolation and the decline in quality of life, which are among the risk factors for suicide in the elderly [ 10 ]. In addition, common psychiatric diseases and disorders, which are important risk factors for suicide, may be seen in individuals due to reasons such as quarantine practices during pandemic periods, fear of infection, insufficient information, and support [ 11 ]. In our study, we aimed to determine the suicide characteristics of adults over 65 years old who died due to suicide in the 10-year period between 2014 and 2023 and the change in suicide characteristics over the years by using the data of the Turkish Statistical Institute. Materials and methods This retrospective study examined suicides among adults aged 65 and older in Turkey between 2014 and 2023. Data were retrieved from the Turkish Statistical Institute’s (TSI) publicly available online reports. As the study used anonymised, retrospective TSI data, informed consent was not required. The study was approved by Abant Izzet Baysal University Clinical Research Ethics Committee (September 09, 2024 date and 2024/236 desicion no). Our research adhered to the ethical criteria outlined in the Helsinki Declaration of 1964, as revised in 2013. The evaluation focused on several aspects, including gender, the crude suicide rate, changes in suicide rates over the years, the impact of the pandemic, methods of suicide, and factors associated with suicide. Suicide deaths were identified from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TSI) national mortality database, which is compiled from official death registration records completed by law enforcement authorities and coded according to the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10). Deaths classified as intentional self-harm (ICD-10 codes X60–X84) were included in the present study. Information on suicide methods and reported reasons for suicide was obtained directly from the annual “Death and Cause of Death Statistics” published by TSI. Suicide methods (e.g., hanging, firearm, jumping from height, chemical intoxication, drowning, sharp instruments, and other methods) and reported reasons (e.g., illness, family conflict, economic difficulties, emotional relationship problems, educational failure, and unknown) were analysed using the predefined administrative categories provided by TSI without modification. The reported reason for suicide was recorded by the Turkish Statistical Institute (TSI) using information obtained from official death investigation records completed by law enforcement authorities. Each suicide death was assigned to a single predefined administrative category in the TSI database. The present study analysed these classifications as provided and did not independently verify or reclassify the reported reasons for suicide. The study period was categorised into three phases based on major changes in public health measures implemented in Turkey rather than the WHO declaration of the end of the Public Health Emergency of International Concern. The pre-pandemic period spanned from 2014 to 2019. The pandemic period included 2020–2021, corresponding to the years during which strict public health measures, including lockdowns, age-specific curfews, and social distancing restrictions, were implemented nationwide. The post-pandemic period was defined as 2022–2023 because most COVID-19-related restrictions had been lifted in Turkey by early 2022, allowing a return to routine social and healthcare activities. Statistical analysis R 4.4.0 version (R Core Team (2024). _R: A Language and Environment for Statistical Computing_. R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria. < https://www.R-project.org/ >) was used for data analysis of the study. The primary outcome variable was the annual number of suicide deaths among elderly adults (≥ 65 years). The corresponding annual elderly population obtained from the Turkish Statistical Institute (TSI) was used as the population at risk. Independent variables included calendar year, age group (65–69, 70–74, and ≥ 75 years), sex (male/female), pandemic period (pre-pandemic, pandemic, and post-pandemic), suicide method, and reported reason for suicide. Categorical variables were summarised as frequencies and percentages and compared using Pearson’s chi-square test. Homogeneity of proportions was evaluated using the proportion test. Pairwise comparisons of suicide rates between age groups, sexes, suicide methods, and reported reasons were performed using z-tests for rates. Rate ratios (RRs) and corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated. The Cochran–Armitage trend test was performed across three ordered elderly age categories: 65–69, 70–74, and ≥ 75 years, to assess whether suicide rates increased linearly with advancing age. In addition, to determine whether a temporal trend existed before the COVID-19 pandemic, a separate Cochran–Armitage trend test was performed for annual elderly suicide rates during the pre-pandemic period (2014–2019). Two complementary Poisson regression analyses were conducted. First, a period-based Poisson regression model was fitted to evaluate the association between the COVID-19 period and elderly suicide rates. In this model, the pandemic period (2020–2021) and post-pandemic period (2022–2023) were entered as categorical independent variables, with the pre-pandemic period (2014–2019) serving as the reference category. Separate models were fitted for the total elderly population, males, and females. Second, a segmented Poisson regression (interrupted time-series) analysis was performed to distinguish underlying temporal trends from changes associated with the COVID-19 pandemic. Calendar year was entered as a continuous variable, together with variables representing the immediate level change at the onset of the pandemic and the change in trend during the post-pandemic period. For all Poisson regression models, the logarithm of the annual elderly population was included as an offset term to account for differences in population size. Incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were estimated. Model adequacy was evaluated using the Pearson dispersion statistic and the Cameron–Trivedi dispersion test. No evidence of overdispersion was detected; therefore, Poisson regression was considered appropriate. All statistical tests were two-sided, and a p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Of the 35,777 suicides in Turkey the 10-year period (between 01/01/2014 and 31/12/2023) of the study, 1,296 (3.5%) were in the 65–69 age group, 942 (2.63%) in the 70–74 age group and 1,828 (5.1%) in the ≥ 75 age group. Among elderly suicide deaths, 75.1% were male (n:3,055) and 24.9% were female (n:1,011). The crude suicide rate of the elderly was significantly higher than the suicide rate of general population between 2014 and 2021 ( p < 0.001) (Table 1 ). In addition, the crude suicide rate was significantly higher in all years only in the ≥ 75 age group compared to the suicide rate of general population ( p < 0.001) (Table 1 ). The highest suicide rate for females was in the ≥ 75 age group in 2015, while for males was in the ≥ 75 age group in 2020. Suicide rates in the ≥ 75 age group were significantly higher than those in the 65–69 and 70–74 age groups (RR = 1.40 and RR = 1.36, respectively; both p < 0.001). The Cochran–Armitage trend test, performed across three ordered elderly age categories — 65–69, 70–74, and ≥ 75 years — showed a significant positive age-gradient in suicide rates in most study years. In the pooled analysis for 2014–2023, the trend was highly significant (Z = 9.46, p < 0.001), indicating that suicide rates increased progressively with advancing age (Table 2 ). Poisson regression analysis adjusted for population size demonstrated that suicide rates among the elderly increased significantly during the pandemic period compared to the pre-pandemic period (IRR = 1.10, 95% CI: 1.02–1.18, p = 0.018). A significant reduction was observed in the post-pandemic period (IRR = 0.90, 95% CI: 0.83–0.97, p = 0.008) (Table 3 ). An interrupted Poisson regression analysis was performed to evaluate whether the observed increase during the pandemic reflected a continuation of an existing temporal trend. No significant temporal trend was observed during the pre-pandemic period (IRR = 0.98, 95% CI: 0.96–1.01, p = 0.144). However, a significant level increase in elderly suicide rates was detected during the pandemic period (IRR = 1.31, 95% CI: 1.15–1.50, p < 0.001), followed by a significant declining trend during the post-pandemic period (IRR = 0.93, 95% CI: 0.88–0.97, p = 0.002) (Table 3 ). The Cochran–Armitage trend test also showed that there was no significant linear trend in suicide rates among elderly adults during the pre-pandemic period (2014–2019) (Z = − 1.46, p = 0.144). Sex-stratified analyses revealed that the pandemic-related increase was significant among elderly males (IRR = 1.11, 95% CI: 1.02–1.22, p = 0.014), whereas no significant increase was observed among females (IRR = 1.02, 95% CI: 0.88–1.19, p = 0.772). During the post-pandemic period, suicide rates declined marginally in both males (IRR = 0.91, p = 0.042) and females (IRR = 0.84, p = 0.036) (Table 3 ). A statistically significant association was observed between gender and method of suicide ( p < 0.001). Among firearm-related suicides, 97.9% occurred in males, and males similarly accounted for 87.0% of suicides involving sharp or piercing instruments (Table 4 ). A statistically significant association was observed between gender and the reason for suicide ( p < 0.001). Illness was the most frequently reported known cause of suicide across all elderly age and sex groups; however, the database does not distinguish between physical and psychiatric illnesses. Among suicides attributed to financial difficulties and marital discord, 94.0% and 92.3%, respectively, occurred in males (Table 4 ). The distribution of suicide methods differed significantly across age groups ( p < 0.05) (Table 4 ). Across all age groups, hanging was the most frequently used suicide method. The proportional distribution of reported suicide reasons also differed significantly across age groups ( p < 0.001) (Table 4 ). Among suicides attributed to financial difficulties, 57.3% occurred in individuals aged 65–69 years, whereas 45.5% of illness-related suicides occurred in those aged ≥ 75 years. Among the elderly population, the suicide rate of males was 3.83 times higher than that of females (RR: 3.83, p < 0.001) (Table 5 ). The rates of suicide by hanging, firearm, jumping from height, chemical intoxication and sharp-piercing instrument were higher in elderly males than females (Table 5 ). However, the firearm-related estimate should be interpreted cautiously because the relatively small number of female cases may have resulted in an inflated rate ratio.
