title: Dialogical therapy plus treatment as usual versus treatment as usual in adults with distressing and persistent auditory hallucinations in the UK (Talking with Voices-II): a randomised controlled trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Existing treatments for auditory hallucinations (hereafter voice hearing) among people with serious mental health problems (SMHPs; diagnoses include schizophrenia spectrum disorders, bipolar disorders, and personality disorders) show only modest clinical benefits, produce inconsistent long-term outcomes, and seldom prioritise personal recovery as a primary treatment goal. We aimed to investigate the effectiveness of Talking with Voices (TwV), a lived-experience informed intervention in which therapists engage in direct dialogue with voices, in improving both personal recovery and clinical outcomes for individuals experiencing persistent and distressing voice hearing.

METHODS: Talking with Voices-II was a rater-blinded, parallel-arm, multisite, randomised controlled trial to test the efficacy and underlying mechanisms of TwV therapy compared with treatment as usual (TAU) in community-based National Health Service mental health services across four UK sites. Participants with SMHPs who experienced distressing voices were randomly assigned (1:1), using random-sized blocks, stratified by site and presence of schizophrenia diagnosis, to receive either TwV plus TAU or TAU alone. Therapy was provided in up to 26 sessions over 8 months, and assessments were conducted at baseline, 8 months, and 14 months by assessors masked to treatment allocation. The primary outcome was the Questionnaire about the Process of Recovery score at 8 months, a self-reported measure of personal recovery in psychosis. Secondary outcomes were voice-related measures, self-beliefs, dissociation, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms. The primary analysis followed the intention-to-treat principle, and moderation and mediation were prespecified in the statistical analysis plan. The mediation analysis was carried out using the mediate command, utilising bootstrapping to obtain percentile CIs. The trial was prospectively registered with ISRCTN, ISRCTN15897915, and all research and clinical procedures were co-led by individuals with lived experience of psychosis.

FINDINGS: Between Sept 1, 2023, and June 30, 2025, we screened 1316 participants, of whom 309 consented, completed baseline assessments, and were randomly assigned to either TwV plus TAU (n=156) or TAU alone (n=153). The mean age of participants was 41·1 years (SD 13·1). 159 (52%) participants were men, 145 (47%) were women, and four (1%) were another gender, and one preferred not to say; 222 (72%) participants were White. At 8 months, personal recovery was significantly better in the TwV group than in the TAU group (adjusted difference 6·97 [95% CI 5·00-8·95]; p<0·0001; standardised effect size [SES] 0·63). Significant differences favouring TwV were found for 12 (80%) of 15 of secondary outcomes, unadjusted for multiple testing, including all voice-related measures, negative self-beliefs, and PTSD outcomes, with SES ranging from 0·18 to 0·86. There were no effects on dissociation-related measures or positive self-beliefs (SES ranging from <0·01 to 0·16). An effect was still evident on personal recovery at 14 months, although reduced (adjusted difference 3·55 [0·96-6·14]; p=0·0073; SES=0·32). 55 serious adverse events occurred in 36 participants in the TwV group, and 60 serious adverse events occurred in 45 participants in the TAU group, none of which were deemed definitely related to the therapy or research procedures.

INTERPRETATION: TwV significantly improves personal recovery, showing efficacy for individuals with SMHPs who experience distressing voices. Further research comparing TwV with an active control and evaluating its implementation in routine care settings is warranted.

FUNDING: National Institute for Health and Care Research.

title: Prolonged exposure, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing therapy, and cognitive restructuring versus waiting-list for individuals with PTSD and psychosis (RE.PROCESS): A multicenter, four-arm, assessor-masked, superiority randomized controlled trial
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Evidence indicates the potential efficacy of trauma-focused therapies for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in psychosis. This is the first randomized controlled trial to evaluate the superiority of Prolonged Exposure (PE), Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing therapy (EMDR), and Cognitive Restructuring (CR) plus treatment as usual, compared to a waiting-list (WL) plus treatment as usual control group.

METHODS: We conducted a multicenter, assessor-masked, randomized controlled trial in patients with a lifetime schizophrenia spectrum psychotic disorder and PTSD. Participants ( N  = 162) were randomized (1:1:1:1) to PE, EMDR, CR, or WL and followed up until 6 months post-randomization. Therapy conditions had a maximum of 16 twice-weekly sessions. Primary outcome was researcher-rated PTSD symptom severity (Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5; CAPS-5).

RESULTS: PE, EMDR, and CR significantly reduced PTSD severity compared to WL over time from baseline to 6-month follow-up. At 6-months, adjusted differences and between-group effect sizes on the CAPS-5 were -9.76 (95% CI -16.13,-3.38;  p = 0.0029) with  d = -0.90 (95% CI -1.36,-0.44) for PE, -11.74 (95% CI -18.04,-5.44;  p = 0.0003) with  d = -1.04 (95% CI -1.50,-0.58) for EMDR, and -12.72 (95% CI -18.89,-6.55;  p = 0.0001) with  d = -1.00 (95% CI -1.46,-0.54) for CR. Significant therapy effects were also found for secondary PTSD (-related) outcomes, but not for psychosis.

CONCLUSIONS: In comparison to WL, PE, EMDR, and CR were effective in reducing PTSD symptoms in individuals with PTSD and psychosis, with large effects. Replication in larger samples is needed, although these results support expanding access to trauma therapies in this underserved population.

title: Conceptualization and Management of Suicide Risk in Individuals with a History of Traumatic Brain Injury
journal: Phys Med Rehabil Clin N Am
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is associated with greater functional impairment, psychiatric symptoms, and suicide risk. Routine suicide prevention efforts are essential for TBI care. Screening supports risk assessment and guides steps such as safety planning and lethal means counseling. Risk management should be adjusted for TBI sequelae by using direct language, visual aids, relating questions to TBI symptoms, and obtaining collateral information. Research on suicide interventions specific to TBI remains limited, with few targeted trials and primarily small, non-generalizable samples, underscoring the need for rigorous evaluation of interventions for this population.

title: Staff Experiences Delivering Hospital Outreach Post-Suicidal Engagement (HOPE) in a Regional Context: A Qualitative Study
abstract:
ABSTRACT Suicide rates remain disproportionately high in regional Australia, where geographical, workforce and service‐system constraints can limit access to post‐suicidal care. This study explored staff experiences of delivering the Hospital Outreach Post‐Suicidal Engagement (HOPE) program across three regional hospital sites in Victoria, Australia. Semi‐structured individual interviews and one focus group were conducted with 16 HOPE staff, including nurses, peer workers, psychosocial support staff and allied health professionals. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, with reporting guided by the COnsolidated criteria for REporting Qualitative research (COREQ) checklist. Four themes were identified: regional influences on HOPE service delivery; adaptations to individual consumer needs; workforce capacity and teamwork; and HOPE's integration with the broader healthcare system. Staff valued HOPE's multidisciplinary and person‐centred approach but identified barriers associated with geographical distance, infrastructure, workforce capacity and fragmented service pathways. The findings demonstrate how regional context shapes the delivery of post‐suicidal care and highlight the importance of adequately resourced, flexible and integrated service models. These findings have implications for multidisciplinary HOPE practice, workforce planning and continuity of post‐suicidal care across regional communities.

1 Introduction Suicide remains a major public health concern globally and in Australia, where 3214 suicide deaths were recorded in 2023, representing a rate of 11.8 per 100 000 people (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2026 ). Suicide rates are higher in many regional, rural and remote communities than in metropolitan areas (Australian Institute of Health and Welfare 2026 ). In this study, the term ‘regional’ is used to describe non‐metropolitan locations (Department of Health 2026 ). People living in regional communities may experience reduced access to mental health services, longer travel distances, workforce shortages, stigma, social isolation and increased availability of lethal means (Casant and Helbich 2022 ; Houston 2024 ; Kavanagh et al. 2023 ). These challenges can affect both the immediate crisis responses and continuity of care following a suicidal crisis. Addressing suicide therefore requires approaches that respond to the psychological, social and structural factors influencing a person's wellbeing (Modderman, Veresova, McAleer, et al. 2026b ). A previous suicide attempt is one of the strongest predictors of future suicidal behaviour (Beghi et al. 2013 ), highlighting the importance of post‐suicidal care. Evidence suggests that effective post‐suicidal care services are integrated with broader health and community service systems, commence engagement as early as possible, and provide flexible, assertive and clinically supported follow‐up that is informed by the perspectives of people with lived experience. Although lived‐experience involvement is increasingly recognised as important in suicide prevention and post‐crisis support, research examining how it is actively incorporated into these services remains limited (Martin et al. 2023 ; Purdon et al. 2025 ). Despite the importance of post‐suicidal care, less is known about how these services are experienced by staff in regional settings. Regional service delivery may be shaped by geographical distance, local workforce capacity, infrastructure, referral pathways and the availability of complementary services. Therefore, further research is needed to understand the contextual and organisational factors that enable or constrain the delivery of post‐suicidal care in regional communities. 2 Background The Hospital Outreach Post‐Suicidal Engagement (HOPE) program was established in Victoria, Australia, with funding from the Victorian Government as part of the Suicide Prevention Framework 2016–2025 (Department of Health 2016 ). HOPE is a community‐based post‐suicidal care service that provides intensive, short‐term support for up to 12 weeks following a suicidal crisis. Multidisciplinary HOPE teams include mental health professionals and peer support workers with lived experience. They work collaboratively with consumers to deliver flexible, tailored, person‐centred support (Better Place Australia 2025 ). The HOPE model is designed to address the complex and interconnected needs that may follow a suicidal crisis. Support may include psychological and psychiatric care, housing assistance, financial counselling, substance‐use services, family‐violence support, employment assistance and cultural services (Better Place Australia 2025 ). HOPE has been widely implemented across Victoria, and a growing body of research has examined its outcomes (Kehoe et al. 2023 ; Williamson et al. 2021 ; Wright et al. 2021 ; Innes et al. 2026 ). Studies involving adults have reported reductions in suicidal ideation and psychological distress, as well as improvements in coping self‐efficacy, hopeful thinking and overall wellbeing (Kehoe et al. 2023 ; Williamson et al. 2021 ; Wright et al. 2021 ; Innes et al. 2026 ). Young people who have accessed HOPE have also reported reduced suicide risk and increased quality of life (Meyer et al. 2024 ), while parents have described the program positively (Webb et al. 2025 ). HOPE engagement has additionally been associated with reduced reliance on emergency departments and other hospital services (Wright et al. 2021 ). Existing research indicates that the characteristics and practices of HOPE staff are central to the delivery of the program (Kehoe et al. 2023 ; Williamson et al. 2021 ; Wright et al. 2021 ; Innes et al. 2026 ). However, previous research has focused primarily on consumer, carer and service outcomes, with limited attention to staff experiences of delivering HOPE. In addition, existing evaluations have largely been conducted in metropolitan settings (Kehoe et al. 2023 ; Williamson et al. 2021 ; Wright et al. 2021 ; Innes et al. 2026 ). These findings may not fully reflect the geographical, workforce, infrastructure and service‐system conditions that shape post‐suicidal care in regional communities. Consequently, little is known about how regional context and organisational conditions shape the delivery of HOPE. This study aimed to explore staff experiences of delivering the HOPE program across three regional hospital sites in Victoria, Australia. Specifically, it examined how geographical, organisational, workforce and service‐system factors shaped the delivery of responsive, person‐centred and continuous post‐suicidal care. The study also explored how collaboration between HOPE teams and other health and community services enabled or constrained care delivery in regional settings. The research question was: What are the experiences of staff delivering the HOPE program in regional settings? 3 Methods 3.1 Study Design A qualitative descriptive design was used to explore staff experiences of delivering the HOPE program across three regional hospital sites in Victoria, Australia. This design was appropriate because the study aimed to produce a clear, practise‐oriented account of staff experiences and of the organisational, geographical, workforce and service‐system conditions that shaped care delivery. Such an account can inform service planning by showing how these conditions affect the delivery of post‐suicidal care in practice. Qualitative description also supported analysis that remained close to participants' language, while recognising that the findings reflect interpretation within the social, organisational and temporal context in which the data were generated (Kim et al. 2017 ; Furidha 2023 ). Reporting was guided by the COnsolidated criteria for REporting Qualitative research (COREQ) checklist (Tong et al. 2007 ). Ethics approval was granted by the La Trobe University Human Ethics Committee (HEC 25032). 3.2 Participant Selection and Recruitment Staff members working in the HOPE program at the three participating regional hospital sites were eligible to participate. A total population sampling approach was used, whereby all eligible staff across the three sites were invited to participate rather than a purposive subset. Site managers distributed an email invitation and participant information sheet to all eligible staff. Site managers' role was limited to distributing the study information; participation was voluntary, and staff were not required to inform their manager whether they participated. Because the invitations were distributed by site managers, the researchers could not determine the total number of eligible staff who received the invitation or declined participation. None of the authors hold managerial or supervisory responsibility for participants, and participation or non‐participation had no effect on participants' employment or relationship with the HOPE program. Participants received a gift card in acknowledgement of their time and contribution; this was explained in the participant information sheet. A demographic questionnaire collected information about participants' characteristics, including their employment site. Employment site was not reported because the small number of participants at each site meant that combining site with professional role and other characteristics could increase the risk of identification. 3.3 Procedure Interested staff provided informed consent through an online survey and supplied an email address for study contact. Following consent, the second author contacted participants to arrange a mutually convenient time for data collection. Participants could choose between attending a pre‐scheduled focus group or completing an individual interview. Offering both formats was a pragmatic decision intended to support accessibility and convenience for staff working across geographically dispersed sites. The formats were used to elicit staff accounts, rather than to generate different types of data or to compare the formats. The same core topics were explored in both. Staff who did not attend the focus group were offered an individual interview to minimise exclusion because of scheduling or availability. All sessions were conducted online using Microsoft Teams. The second author coordinated and scheduled the sessions directly with participants. All authors were involved in individual interviews and/or facilitated the focus group. With participants' consent, all sessions were audio‐recorded and transcribed for analysis. 3.4 Data Collection Data were generated through 12 semi‐structured individual interviews and one focus group involving four participants. All sessions were conducted online using Microsoft Teams. The second author coordinated the sessions and scheduled them directly with participants after consent had been obtained. All authors were involved in individual interviews and/or facilitated the focus group. With participants' consent, all sessions were audio‐recorded and transcribed for analysis. 3.5 Interview and Focus Group Schedule The interview and focus group topic guide was developed by the research team to address the study aim and research question. It was informed by the researchers' experience in suicide prevention and rural health systems (Modderman and Sanders 2026 ; Modderman, Veresova, Canosa, et al. 2026 ; Modderman, Veresova, McAleer, et al. 2026a ) and HOPE service delivery (Better Place Australia 2025 ; Kehoe et al. 2023 ; Williamson et al. 2021 ; Wright et al. 2021 ; Innes et al. 2026 ). It consisted of open‐ended questions exploring five broad areas: challenges, enablers, collaboration, suggested improvements to the HOPE model, and additional resources or strategies that could strengthen care delivery. Follow‐up prompts were used where appropriate to clarify participants' responses and encourage further examples. The same core topics were explored in the individual interviews and focus group, while allowing the discussion to develop according to participants' experiences. The full topic guide is provided in Supplementary File 1 . 3.6 Data Analysis Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, informed by Braun and Clarke's six‐phase approach (Braun and Clarke 2006 , 2014 ). This approach was selected because it supports the development of interpretive themes from patterns of meaning across qualitative data while recognising the active role of researchers in producing the analysis. Themes were therefore understood as interpretive outputs developed through engagement between the researchers, the dataset and the study context, rather than as categories existing independently within the data (Braun and Clarke 2021 ). The six phases involved familiarisation with the data, generating initial codes, searching for themes, reviewing themes, defining and naming themes and producing the analytic account (Braun and Clarke 2006 , 2014 ). The first three authors familiarised themselves with the interview and focus group transcripts and recordings. They independently coded an initial subset of the transcripts, including material from both the individual interviews and the focus group. Coding was primarily inductive, grounded in participants' accounts, while being informed by the researchers' existing knowledge of regional health service delivery and post‐suicidal care (Modderman and Sanders 2026 ; Modderman, Veresova, Canosa, et al. 2026 ; Modderman, Veresova, McAleer, et al. 2026a ). The researchers compared and discussed their interpretations, and codes were revised, combined, separated or discarded as the analysis developed. They then coded the remaining transcripts and continued to discuss emerging codes and potential themes during research meetings with all authors. These discussions supported reflexive consideration of similarities, differences and alternative interpretations; they were not undertaken to establish statistical inter‐coder reliability. Codes were subsequently grouped into potential themes, which were reviewed against the coded extracts and the dataset as a whole. Themes were refined, defined and named before being organised into a coherent analytic account. The final themes were developed across the combined interview and focus group dataset and were supported with illustrative participant quotations (Braun and Clarke 2006 ). NVivo software (Lumivero 2025 ) was used to store the transcripts, organise codes and facilitate retrieval of coded data. All authors contributed to discussion of the developing thematic interpretation. 3.7 Reflexivity and Positionality The research team included six women and one man with backgrounds in psychology, social work, nursing and physiotherapy, as well as experience in suicide prevention and qualitative health research. The researchers recognised that their professional training, practice experience and perspective on regional health service delivery could influence the research questions

title: Comparative efficacy and acceptability of antidepressants in the long-term treatment of major depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Major depressive disorder carries high risks of relapse and chronicity, necessitating treatments that achieve and maintain response (sustained response). This study aimed to compare antidepressants on their ability to achieve sustained response, and on acceptability, by synthesising data from randomised controlled trials.

METHODS: For this systematic review and network meta-analysis, we searched the Cochrane Register, AMED, CINAHL, Embase, LILACS, MEDLINE, MEDLINE In-Progress, PsycINFO, the UK National Research Register, and regulatory agency websites from inception to March 27, 2026. We included double-blind randomised controlled trials that compared any of 21 antidepressants head-to-head or with placebo for long-term treatment (>12 weeks) of adult unipolar major depressive disorder. We included enrichment, non-enrichment, continuation, and continuation-extension designs, and extracted study-level data. We could not derive the sex or gender distribution of participants other than female and did not extract data on race or ethnicity. Primary outcomes were efficacy (sustained response rate) and acceptability (all-cause discontinuation). We synthesised data in random-effects pairwise and network meta-analyses to estimate pooled odds ratios (ORs), using fluoxetine as a reference in the ranked forest plots. The primary analysis included head-to-head continuation and continuation-extension design studies. Enrichment design studies were incorporated in the analysis using a chain-of-evidence approach. Risk-of-bias assessment was done using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool. No people with lived experience were involved in the design, conduct, or interpretation of this study.

FINDINGS: From 54 231 records, 115 studies (30 428 participants; mean age 45·3 years [SD 8·5], 20 066 [66%] female) were included. In head-to-head continuation and continuation-extension design studies (35 studies; n=9888), sustained response differed across antidepressants. Escitalopram (OR 1·62, 95% CI 1·21-2·18), duloxetine (OR 1·57, 1·08-2·26), and agomelatine (OR 1·40, 1·06-1·85) showed higher sustained response rates than fluoxetine. Bupropion and reboxetine showed lower sustained response rates against four other antidepressants in the league table of pairwise comparisons. Escitalopram (OR 0·60, 0·43-0·83) and duloxetine (OR 0·64, 0·44-0·95) demonstrated lower all-cause discontinuation compared with fluoxetine, while reboxetine and milnacipran showed higher all-cause discontinuation against six and four other antidepressants, respectively, in the league table of pairwise comparisons. Sensitivity analyses incorporating enrichment-design studies corroborated these results. However, the certainty of evidence of the network meta-analysis results and the risk of bias in the included studies (19 [54%] of 35 had high risk of bias) might limit the reliability of the current findings.

INTERPRETATION: Antidepressants can differ in their efficacy for achieving sustained response and in their acceptability. These findings can inform the shared decision making for patients, prescribers, and carers in real-world practice. However, more head-to-head comparative studies are needed to provide reliable information about long-term effects of all licensed antidepressants.

FUNDING: None.

title: Rethinking University Mental Health for the AI Era: From Crisis Response to Core Mission
abstract:
IMPORTANCE: Universities have become frontline mental health care settings for adolescents and young adults, a group with rapidly rising rates of common psychiatric disorders. Conventional campus counseling services cannot meet this demand. Students are increasingly turning to unregulated generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools. There is an urgent need for an evidence-informed architecture that integrates digital tools and AI into university mental health systems safely, equitably, and at scale.

OBJECTIVE: To synthesize epidemiologic and clinical trial data on student mental health and digital interventions and integrate these findings with experience in institutional governance to propose an integrated, data-driven, stepped-care model for student mental health, implemented and governed at the university level, that begins with universal prevention, tracks need, and uses precision treatment selection to monitor and match students in need with the least-intensive effective level of care.

EVIDENCE REVIEW: We draw on findings from the World Mental Health International College Student (WMH-ICS) initiative, national surveys of student mental health and service use, randomized clinical trials of student internet-delivered digital interventions, implementation studies of digital navigators and task sharing, and emerging evaluations of AI-supported mental health systems.

FINDINGS: WMH-ICS studies find that 37% to 58% of first-year students worldwide meet 12-month criteria for a DSM-5 disorder, with low treatment rates and substantial impairment in academic performance. This unmet need exceeds the capacity of traditional short-term, face-to-face counseling services, even with expanded staffing and telehealth contracts. Hybrid stepped-care models combining universal prevention with light-touch human support (eg, digital navigators) and low-intensity digital interventions offer a more scalable approach that can expand reach, optimize use of clinicians' limited time, and improve outcomes. Building on these strands, we outline a 2-step system anchored in prematriculation life skills training and a guided first-year cohort model, embedded within a broader digital ecosystem that includes measurement, precision treatment algorithms, and explicit AI governance.

CONCLUSIONS AND RELEVANCE: Reframing student mental health as core to the mission of universities justifies investment in digitally enabled care. With appropriate guardrails, AI can be integrated as a regulated component of this ecosystem, extending the reach of effective interventions while maintaining safety, equity, and institutional accountability.

title: Clinical Risk Factors for Suicide in Persons With Epilepsy: A Nationwide Population-Based Case-Control Study
abstract:
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Individuals with epilepsy face an elevated risk of suicide, but risk factors for suicide remain incompletely understood. We conducted a nationwide case-control study in Sweden to investigate clinical characteristics associated with suicide risk in persons with epilepsy.

METHODS: Persons with epilepsy were identified through Swedish nationwide registers, with epilepsy diagnoses validated through medical record review. Cases were individuals who died by suicide between 2006 and 2011, validated through autopsy reports, and controls were derived from the source population using similar validation procedures. Characteristics included epilepsy type, etiology, tonic-clonic seizure (TCS) frequency, antiseizure medication (ASM) treatment, living conditions, and psychiatric comorbidity. Odds ratios (ORs) with 95% CIs were estimated using conditional logistic regression.

RESULTS: The study included 111 suicide cases and 1,147 controls. Suicide cases had a mean age at epilepsy onset of 20 years, and 35% were female. Alcohol abuse (OR 11.81, 95% CI 6.25-22.30) and other substance abuse (OR 10.71, 95% CI 4.52-25.38) showed stronger associations than depression (OR 2.94, 95% CI 1.56-5.53) and anxiety disorders (OR 2.93, 95% CI 1.57-5.44). Living alone was associated with increased risk (OR 2.59, 95% CI 1.58-4.26). Recent TCS showed a dose-response relationship, with the highest risk among individuals experiencing 4-10 TCS in the preceding year (OR 5.01, 95% CI 2.2-11.3). Structural and unknown epilepsy etiologies were associated with elevated risk (OR 3.07, 95% CI 1.0-9.5 and OR 8.80, 95% CI 2.9-27.1, respectively). ASM treatment was associated with lower suicide risk (monotherapy OR 0.51, 95% CI 0.27-0.95; polytherapy OR 0.21, 95% CI 0.1-0.5), and nonadherence was associated with higher risk (OR 3.02, 95% CI 1.8-5.1).

DISCUSSION: This study identified a distinct risk profile for suicide in persons with epilepsy, highlighting alcohol and substance abuse, living alone, seizure burden, nonadherence, and structural or unknown etiologies as key risk factors. The stronger associations for substance abuse may reflect characteristics specific to epilepsy populations and the focus on completed suicide. Screening for substance abuse and improved seizure control may contribute to suicide prevention. Major limitations include the modest number of cases and incomplete information on prior suicidal behavior.

title: Reward reactivity in non-suicidal self-injury in adolescents: protocol for a longitudinal study
abstract:
Background The high incidence and serious consequences of non-suicidal self-injurious (NSSI) behaviors in adolescents warrants the attention of medical professionals, sociologists, and educators. Evidences of enhanced reward reactivity have been observed in adolescents with NSSI as well as those with suicidal risks. It is hypothesized that elevated reward reactivity toward general rewards may increase the risk of suicide. To test the hypothesis, a cohort study has been designed to systematically evaluate the reward reactivity in combination with other risk factors commonly reported in NSSI adolescents, with follow-up for at least 24 months. Methods This protocol is for a longitudinal cohort study that aims to enroll adolescents with NSSI and healthy controls at the Affiliated Kangning Hospital of Ningbo University. The primary outcome will be time to first documented suicide attempt during the 24-month follow-up, while psychological well-being and related clinical measures will be assessed as secondary outcomes. Clinical information, pathopsychological assessments and brief cognitive assessment will be collected at the baseline. Reward reactivity will primarily be tested in behavioral tasks under functional magnetic resonance imaging, accompanied with the assessment of the traits of reinforcement. Discussion This study proposes a highly integrative, multimodal investigation of the neurobiological and systemic inflammatory pathways underlying NSSI in Chinese adolescents with MDD, with a central focus on reward circuit dysfunction. Trial registration This study is registered in https://www.chictr.org.cn under protocol registration number ID: ChiCTR2500107121. It was registered on August 4, 2025. Recruitment started in September, 2023. The version of this protocol is v1.0.

Background Non-suicidal self-injury behaviors, previously known as deliberate self-mutilation, deliberate self-harm (DSH), or self-injurious behaviors [ 1 ], is globally increasing in recent decades. Half a century ago, literature about self-mutilation was usually related with certain genetic and developmental disorders [ 2 ]. During 1972 and 1973, incidence observed base on the Accident and Emergency Departments of hospitals was 0.17% in male and 0.66% in female aged 15–20 years in the City of Bristol, UK, 91% of which was taken the forms of drug overdose [ 3 ]. A review in 1983 [ 4 ] claimed that self-harm behaviors occurring in late adolescence were seen ‘among violent and antisocial youth in institutional settings’. However, when Klonsky and colleges [ 5 ] drew attention to the nonclinical population in 2003, they reported 4% percent of the participants with a history of DSH in a military recruiting sample of young people in the USA. This was one of the earliest surveys that raised NSSI as a prevalent problem. Meanwhile, a survey of a community sample in Quebec reported the prevalence of DSH as high as 13.9% in the year of 2002 [ 6 ]. Demographic surveys since then reported similar prevalence worldwide, around 17% to 21% in community samples in Finland [ 7 ], Belgium [ 8 ], and Israel [ 9 ]. In China, one of the earliest demographic studies about deliberate self-harm was carried out in 2006 in Hong Kong, which reported 13.4% and 19.7% prevalence rates in the male and female students of 9–12 years old, respectively [ 10 ]. Another study in mainland China [ 11 ] reported the rates of 22.7% and 22.6% in the male and female middle school students in 2011. Meanwhile, a most recent survey reported lifetime prevalence of NSSI among adolescents is as high as 28.7% [ 12 ]. The wide spread phenomenon of NSSI behaviors in adolescents warrants the attention of medical professionals, sociologists, and educators. NSSI as a medical term was established in the fifth version of the Statistical and Diagnostic Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) in the section of Emerging measures and models. NSSI is defined as the deliberate, self-inflicted destruction of body tissue without suicidal intent and for purposes not socially sanctioned, includes behaviors such as cutting, burning, biting and scratching skin [ 13 ]. It is usually co-morbid with depressive disorders. However, a recent survey in a community sample in China [ 14 ] found 32.1% of the adolescents who had self-injurious history were not depressive. Moreover, this cohort seemed to show more resilient features than their non-NSSI counterparts. On the other hand, NSSI associates closely with suicidal risks. Suicidal ideation and attempt were found in 42.2% and 13.8% adolescents with frequent NSSI behaviors, 8.0 and 12.2 times higher compared with those without these behaviors [ 15 ]. Few longitudinal researches about the developmental outcomes have been conducted. One of these studies in Sweden found two thirds of the adolescents stopped the self-injurious behaviors when reaching young adulthood. However, these young people still had elevated level of stress, anxiety and emotional dysregulation, though milder than those with prolonged NSSI behaviors [ 16 ]. Therefore, NSSI seems to be a developmental problem in emotionally unstable adolescents with significant elevated risks of suicide. NSSI adolescents and suicidal patients may differ from “purely” depressed ones in reward activity. Low reactivity to reward feedback was observed in depressed adolescents [ 17 , 18 ]. However, NSSI adolescents had increased putamen reactivity to monetary rewards [ 19 ], while suicidal young people had also relatively increased electroencephalogram(EEG) reactivity to rewards [ 20 ]. Similar to substance addiction, brain reactivity to visual cue was increased in NSSI subjects [ 21 ]. Painful stimuli evoked greater response in self-injurious subjects in several valence- related brain areas, and correlation between blood oxygen level dependent(BOLD) signal and relief was greater in NSSI patients in areas associated with reward/pain and addiction including thalamus, dorsal striatum and anterior precuneus [ 22 ]. The phenomenon of diverging reward reactivity in distressful adolescents suggests its potential application in behavioral prediction and intervention development. It is not clear whether the up-regulated reward reactivity is genetically determined or could be affected by the environment. Large twin surveys suggested that the correlation between NSSI and suicidal ideation could mostly be explained by overlapping genetic influences [ 23 , 24 ], while trauma experience may confer direct risk among females [ 24 ]. Several DNA methylation sites had been reported in NSSI adolescents with childhood adversity, such as the Glucocorticoid receptor gene [ 25 ] and catecholamine- O- methyl- transferase(COMT) [ 26 ]. Hence we propose the hypothesis that enhanced reactivity toward general rewards and rewarding pain may increase the risk of suicide in self-injurious patients. Both genetic and environmental factors could contribute to the altered reward reactivity. To test the hypothesis and hopefully to develop predictive models for suicidal risk, we will build a cohort with clinical NSSI adolescents. Reward reactivity is assessed with task-state fMRI. The reinforcement traits, the severity of addictive feature, the presence of game disorder and the anhedonic feelings are also evaluated with self-rating scales, in order to give a full profile of the reward system. Pathological manifestation as well as environment assessment is carried out for detailed risk assessment. This is the first longitudinal fMRI study to examine reward reactivity as a prospective predictor of suicide attempts in Chinese adolescents with NSSI. By integrating multimodal assessments within a specialized cohort and biobank, this study addresses a critical gap in the literature and provides a foundation for future risk stratification and intervention research. Methods Research design This is a prospective longitudinal study. Trained researchers will evaluate participants’ physical/psychological functioning during the study and at 6-/12-/18-/24-month follow-ups post-baseline. Baseline assessments collected demographics, emotional status, self-harm/suicidal behaviors, personality traits, cognitive function, multimodal MRI data, and biospecimens. Remote follow-ups via WeChat/telephone will document volunteers’ health status. We have no additional intervention measures and treatment plan is entirely dependent on the patient’s corresponding clinician. Moreover, we excluded patients who had used MECT, and all participants could withdraw from the project at any time. Objectives The main objective of the study is to test the hypothesis whether elevated reward reactivity toward general rewards predicts time to first documented suicide attempt during the 24-month follow-up. The secondary objective is to establish a specialized cohort and follow-up platform for adolescents with a history of NSSI patients, as well as creating a NSSI-specific disease information database and bio-sample dataset that includes clinical diagnosis and treatment information, environmental and psychological depictions, imaging data, basic biochemical examinations, and specimens such as blood, urine, and feces that warrant further studies. Study setting The study is conducted at the Affiliated Kangning Hospital of Ningbo University. The detailed workflow is illustrated in Fig. 1 . Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria for adolescents with self-harming behaviors Aged between 11 and 18. Meet the diagnostic criteria for non-suicidal self-injury in DSM-5: engagement in NSSI on 5 or more days in the past year; the expectation that NSSI will solve an interpersonal problem, provide relief from unpleasant thoughts and/or emotions, or induce a positive emotional state; the experience of one or more of the following: interpersonal problems or negative thoughts or emotions immediately prior to NSSI, preoccupation with NSSI that is difficult to manage. frequent thoughts about NSSI; 4. the NSSI is not socially sanctioned or restricted to minor self-injurious behaviors; 5. the presence of NSSI-related clinically significant distress or interference across different domains of functioning (e.g., work, relationships). 6. the NSSI does not occur only in the context of psychosis, delirium, or substance use/withdrawal and is not better accounted for by another psychiatric disorder or medical condition. Voluntarily participating in the study, informed consent with the themselves and the legal guardian. Inclusion criteria for healthy adolescents as a control group We will recruit a group of healthy controls who will have the same follow-up time points as the patients. This group will undergo diagnostic tests, questionnaires, and task-based psychological tests, MRI structural and functional examinations, and biochemical tests such as blood tests. We anticipate recruiting at least 100 participants for this control group by placing advertisements on the WeChat platform. Aged between 11 and 18. No history of mental or emotional disorders. No history of consciousness disturbances lasting more than five minutes. Voluntarily participating in the study, informed consent with the themselves and the legal guardian. Exclusion criteria Meets the criteria for psychotic disorders, such as schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. History of any psychotic episodes with symptoms of delusion or hallucination. Meets the criteria for bipolar 1 disorder. Meets the criteria for autism spectrum disorder. History of organic brain disease, or cranial injury that has led to a loss of consciousness for more than 5 min. History of chronic medical conditions that may impact psychological well-being, including thyroid-related diseases and any other endocrine disorders, any kinds of autoimmune diseases, chronic infections with tubercle bacillus, and brain tumors, etc. Conditions not suitable for functional magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) examination, including metal brace wearing, tattoo in the head and neck areas, claustrophobia, etc. Measurements Biochemical tests Venous blood samples are collected from all participants after an 8-hour overnight fast to assess routine biochemical profiles, including hepatic and renal function, glucose and lipid metabolism, electrolytes, complete blood count, and high-sensitivity C-reactive protein. Psychological function Self-reported general status inventory The self-reported general status inventory evaluates adolescents’ psychological states across four domains: risk-taking propensity, emotional volatility, recreational habits, and academic stress during the past six months. A final binary question assesses history of non-suicidal self-injury behaviors. The scale uses mixed response formats including categorical comparison, time-based frequency selection, and graded stress evaluation, with temporal anchors ranging from recent month to half-year recall. Sleep assessment The sleep assessment questionnaire evaluates sleep patterns during holidays and school periods, incorporating key elements from the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), including measures of sleep duration, sleep quality, and habitual sleep efficiency [ 27 ]. Each section contains 10 questions, including sleep onset and offset times, frequency assessments of sleep difficulties and related symptoms. WHO-5 The WHO-5 depression assessment tool evaluates emotional states and sleep recovery over the past two weeks [ 28 ]. Children’s depression inventory (CDI) The CDI, adapted from Beck’s Depression Inventory (BDI) for adults by Kovacs [ 29 , 30 ], is a self-rating scale specifically designed to assess depressive symptoms in children and adolescents aged 7 to 17. It assesses affective, cognitive, and social functioning. Ottawa self-injury inventory(OSI) The OSI is a widely used assessment tool that includes evaluations of the methods, locations, motivations, frequency, and emotional management aspects of self-harm behaviors [ 31 ]. It not only includes assessments of NSSI behaviors but also covers emotional management, self- harm related events, and potential addictive characteristics. Beck scale for suicide ideation (BSS) The BSS is a tool developed by Aaron T. Beck that is designed to assess the degree of suicidal ideation in individuals by evaluating their suicidal desire, plans, actions, and motivations related to suicide [ 32 ]. title: Trends and seasonal patterns in suicide and traffic accident mortality among youth in Hungary, 2000-2024: a nationwide population-based study
abstract:
Background External causes of death represent the leading causes of mortality among adolescents and young adults. This study aimed to investigate long-term, seasonal patterns, and regional disparities in mortality from external causes among individuals aged 15–24 years in Hungary between 2000 and 2024, including comparisons between the pre-pandemic (2000–2019) and pandemic (2020–2024) periods. Methods Nationwide data on monthly and annual mortality from external causes (ICD-10: V01–Y89) were obtained from the Dissemination Database of the Hungarian Central Statistical Office for 2000–2024. Analyses focused on the two leading causes of external mortality in this age group: suicide and self-harm (X60–X84, Y87.0) and traffic accidents (V01–V99). Mortality rates were calculated using corresponding population data stratified by sex, age group, and region. Annual and seasonal trends were analysed using negative binomial regression models with population offsets. Results are presented as incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). Results Between 2000 and 2024, 7,209 deaths from external causes were recorded among individuals aged 15–24 years (79% males). Significant declining trends were observed in overall external-cause mortality (IRR = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.96–0.97; p < 0.001), suicide (IRR = 0.98; 95% CI: 0.97–0.98; p < 0.001), and traffic accident mortality (IRR = 0.95; 95% CI: 0.94–0.95; p < 0.001). Seasonal variation was significant for overall external-cause mortality, with a peak in July ( p < 0.001), and for suicide and traffic accident mortality, peaking in May ( p < 0.001) and August ( p < 0.001), respectively. Regional disparities were pronounced, with the highest mortality rates consistently observed in the Southern Great Plain region. Mortality patterns during the COVID-19 period did not substantially deviate from pre-pandemic trends. Conclusions Although mortality from external causes among Hungarian youth declined significantly over the past 25 years, substantial gender and regional inequalities persist. The marked summer peak in traffic accident mortality and the elevated risk in specific regions highlight the need for targeted, seasonally sensitive prevention strategies. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12887-026-07419-9 .

Background Hungary has long ranked among the countries with the highest mortality rates within the European Union [ 1 ]. Although cardiovascular diseases and cancers account for the majority of deaths in the total population, the pattern of mortality among adolescents and young adults differs substantially [ 2 ]. According to mortality data from the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (HCSO), external causes of death account for approximately 60% of deaths among individuals aged 15–24 years and traffic accidents and suicide together constitute nearly three-quarters of external-cause deaths in this age group [ 2 ]. External causes of death constitute a heterogeneous group of events, including unintentional injuries, intentional self-harm (suicide), assault, and injuries of undetermined intent, as classified by the International Classification of Diseases, 10th Revision (ICD-10) [ 3 ]. Among young people, these deaths are particularly tragic because they occur at the beginning of the life course and are largely preventable. Beyond the immediate loss of life, they generate profound social, psychological, and economic consequences for families and communities. Understanding their temporal and spatial distribution is therefore of major public health importance. Suicide remains a significant public health concern worldwide and has consistently ranked among the leading causes of death in young people [ 4 , 5 ]. Hungary historically exhibited one of the highest suicide rates in Europe, although a long-term decline has been observed over recent decades [ 6 , 7 ]. Traffic accidents similarly represent a major source of premature mortality among youth [ 8 ], particularly among young males, who are more likely to engage in high-risk behaviours [ 9 ]. In the Hungarian population aged 15–24 years, suicide and traffic accidents constitute the two leading causes of external-cause mortality and together account for the majority of deaths from external causes [ 2 ]. Examining these causes in parallel may therefore provide a more comprehensive understanding of preventable mortality patterns among Hungarian youth. Previous Hungarian studies have primarily focused on overall suicide trends or adult populations. Mortality patterns among children under 15 years have recently been analysed in detail, highlighting the predominance of traffic-related deaths in that younger age group [ 10 ]. To our knowledge, no study has yet extended a similarly comprehensive analysis to the 15–24-year age group, despite the distinct developmental, behavioural, and social characteristics of this life stage. Consequently, comprehensive investigations of long-term trends, seasonal variation, and regional disparities specifically in the 15–24-year age group remain limited. Moreover, little is known about how these patterns evolved during the COVID-19 pandemic period in Hungary. Given that the majority of deaths among individuals aged 15–24 years are attributable to external causes, a detailed examination of their annual trends, seasonal fluctuations, and territorial distribution is essential. The present nationwide population-based study, therefore, aimed to investigate mortality from all external causes, with particular emphasis on suicide and traffic accidents, among Hungarian youth between 2000 and 2024. In addition, we compared patterns observed during the pre-pandemic (2000–2019) and pandemic (2020–2024) periods to assess potential deviations associated with COVID-19-related societal changes. Materials and methods Study design and data sources We conducted a nationwide, population-based ecological study examining mortality from external causes among individuals aged 15–24 years in Hungary between 1 January 2000 and 31 December 2024. Mortality data were obtained from the publicly accessible Dissemination Database of the HCSO (2024) [ 2 ]. Causes of death were classified according to the International Classification of Diseases, 10th revision (ICD-10) [ 3 ]. External causes were defined using codes V01–Y89. Within this category, the two most frequent causes in this age group – traffic accidents (V01–V99) and suicides and self-harm (X60–X84, Y87.0) – were analysed in detail. Monthly and annual numbers of deaths were retrieved stratified by sex, five-year age group (15–19 and 20–24 years), and European Union’s Nomenclature of Territorial Units for Statistics, level 2 (NUTS2) region. Corresponding annual population data were obtained from the same database. As official monthly population data for the 15–24-year age group were not available, monthly population denominators were estimated by interpolating between annual mid-year population figures and adjusting for monthly counts of births and deaths. This approach allowed approximation of the population at risk for seasonal analyses. Outcome measures and standardisation Age-specific mortality rates were calculated separately for the 15–19 and 20–24-year age groups. To facilitate regional comparisons and account for potential differences in age structure across regions, age-standardised mortality rates were computed using the direct standardisation method with the European Standard Population (ESP 2013) as the reference [ 11 ]. Territorial classification Regional analyses were performed according to the European Union’s NUTS2 territorial classification system [ 12 ]. During the study period, Hungary comprised eight NUTS2 regions: Budapest (HU11), Pest County (HU12), Central Transdanubia (HU21), Western Transdanubia (HU22), Southern Transdanubia (HU23), Northern Hungary (HU31), Northern Great Plain (HU32), and Southern Great Plain (HU33). Regional mortality rates were directly standardised using the ESP to ensure comparability. Statistical analysis Annual mortality trends were analysed using negative binomial regression models. This modelling approach was chosen because overdispersion may occur in count data when the variance exceeds the mean, thereby violating the assumptions of standard Poisson regression. In such situations, the negative binomial model, which can be interpreted as a Poisson–Gamma mixture, provides a more appropriate fit [ 13 ]. The logarithm of the population size was included as an offset term in all models to estimate mortality rate ratios. Results are presented as incidence rate ratios (IRRs) with 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs). To further characterise temporal changes in sex-specific mortality rate ratios, Joinpoint regression analysis was performed [ 14 ]. Annual percent changes (APCs) and statistically significant joinpoints were estimated using the Joinpoint Regression Program (version 4.9.1.0; National Cancer Institute, Bethesda, MD, USA). Seasonal variation was examined using monthly death counts within a negative binomial regression framework, including month as a categorical variable. To confirm cyclic seasonal patterns, geometric methods were applied, namely the Edwards test [ 15 ], and its generalisation, the Walter–Elwood method [ 16 ]. These complementary approaches allowed assessment of sinusoidal seasonality in mortality data. All analyses were conducted for overall external-cause mortality (V01–Y89) and separately for suicide and self-harm (X60–X84, Y87.0) and traffic accident mortality (V01–V99). Subgroup analyses were performed by sex and age group. Statistical significance was defined as a two-sided p -value below 0.05. All statistical analyses were carried out using STATA version 16.1 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). Ethical considerations The study was based exclusively on anonymised, aggregated, publicly available data provided by the HCSO. No individual-level identifiers were used, and therefore, ethical approval and informed consent were not required under national regulations. Results Overall mortality patterns Between 2000 and 2024, a total of 7,209 deaths from external causes occurred among individuals aged 15–24 years in Hungary. The majority of these deaths were recorded among males ( n = 5,700; 79%), while females accounted for 1,509 deaths (21%) (Table 1 ). Suicides represented 2,382 deaths (33% of all external-cause deaths) (Table 2 ), and traffic accidents accounted for 2,993 deaths (41.5%) (Table 3 ). Together, these two causes were responsible for nearly three-quarters of all external-cause mortality in this age group. The male-to-female mortality rate ratio for all external causes was 3.59 (95% CI: 3.39–3.81). The corresponding mortality rate ratios were 4.32 (95% CI: 3.89–4.79) for suicide and 3.13 (95% CI: 2.88–3.41) for traffic accidents ( Additional file 1: Supplementary Tables S1–S3 ). Age differences were also marked: individuals aged 20–24 years exhibited a significantly higher mortality risk than those aged 15–19 years (IRR = 1.57; 95% CI: 1.49–1.64; p < 0.001). Throughout the study period, suicide mortality remained consistently higher among males than females. The annual male-to-female suicide mortality rate ratio averaged 4.47 and ranged from 2.52 to 8.51. Joinpoint regression demonstrated temporal variation in the magnitude of this disparity, with no significant change between 2000 and 2014, a significant decline between 2014 and 2019, and a significant increase thereafter (Additional file 2: Supplementary Figure S1). The age-standardised mortality rate for all external causes over the study period was 24.17 per 100,000 population. The corresponding age-standardised rates were 7.98 per 100,000 for suicide and 10.06 per 100,000 for traffic accidents. Regional distribution Substantial regional variation was observed in mortality from external causes. Directly standardised mortality rates ranged from 17.61 to 26.73 per 100,000 individuals aged 15–24 years across NUTS2 regions, with the lowest rate observed in Budapest and the highest in the Southern Great Plain (Fig. 1 A). A similar territorial pattern characterised suicide mortality. Age-standardised suicide rates ranged from 6.26 to 9.35 per 100,000, with the highest values in the Southern Great Plain and Northern Hungary and the lowest in Western Transdanubia and Budapest (Fig. 1 B). Traffic accident mortality also displayed pronounced regional differences. Age-standardised rates ranged from 4.9 to 11.75 per 100,000, with Budapest showing the lowest rate and the Southern Great Plain the highest (Fig. 1 C). Sex-specific regional analyses showed that regional inequalities were more consistently evident among males than females (Additional file 2: Supplementary Figure S2; Additional file 1: Supplementary Tables S1–S3). Southern Great Plain was generally among the regions with the highest mortality rates in both sexes, particularly for all external-cause mortality and traffic accident mortality. In contrast, regional differences in suicide mortality were apparent primarily among males, whereas no region differed significantly from Budapest among females. Annual trends A significant decreasing trend was observed in mortality from all external causes over the 25-year study period (IRR = 0.97; 95% CI: 0.96–0.97; p < 0.001) (Fig. 2 A). Suicide mortality also declined significantly (IRR = 0.98; 95% CI: 0.97–0.98; p < 0.001) (Fig. 2 B), as did traffic accident mortality, which demonstrated the steepest reduction (IRR = 0.95; 95% CI: 0.94–0.95; p < 0.001) (Fig. 2 C). Sex-specific analyses demonstrated broadly similar temporal patterns among males and females (Additional file 2: Supplementary Figure S3). Mortality from all external causes, suicide, and traffic accidents declined significantly in both sexes, although absolute mortality rates remained substantially higher among males throughout the study period. The male-to-female suicide mortality rate ratio averaged 4.47 and exhibited significant temporal variation, with a decline between 2014 and 2019 followed by an increase thereafter. Despite these long-term declines, mortality numbers for both suicide and traffic accidents showed relative stabilisation during the final five years of the study period (Figs. 2 B–C). During the COVID-19 restriction period (2020–2021), external-cause mortality continued to decline in the 15–19-year age group. In contrast, mortality in the 20–24-year group remained largely stable during this period and returned to the pre-pandemic trajectory following the lifting of restrictions. title: Vagus-Hepatic-Creatine axis modulates manic-like behaviors via hippocampal MMP19 upregulation in bipolar disorder
abstract: Bipolar disorder (BD) is associated with pronounced alterations in peripheral creatine kinase levels; however, the mechanistic basis of this phenomenon remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we conducted a translational study combining clinical assessments in 55 patients with major depressive disorder, 57 BD patients, and 55 healthy controls, alongside sleep deprivation-induced manic-like mouse models. Our findings revealed significantly elevated peripheral creatine concentrations in both BD patients and model mice, which correlated with increased hepatic expression of guanidinoacetate N-methyltransferase (GAMT), a rate-limiting enzyme in creatine biosynthesis. Behavioral experiments in mice showed that exogenous creatine supplementation recapitulated manic-like phenotypes, whereas administration of the creatine analogue β-guanidinopropionic acid (β-GPA) or surgical subdiaphragmatic vagotomy effectively ameliorated these aberrant behaviors. Mechanistically, peripherally derived creatine was found to modulate neural activity independently of blood-brain barrier penetration, acting instead through interleukin-1α (IL-1α)-mediated inflammatory signaling. Transcriptomic analyses further identified hippocampal matrix metalloproteinase-19 (MMP19) as a critical downstream effector, and genetic knockdown experiments confirmed its indispensability in the expression of manic-like behaviors. Collectively, these results delineate a previously unrecognized vagus-liver-creatine-hippocampal axis in BD pathophysiology, highlighting peripheral creatine metabolic routes as actionable targets for therapeutic intervention. Overall, this work provides compelling evidence that peripheral metabolic disturbances can drive central nervous system dysfunction via neuroimmune crosstalk, offering a new conceptual framework for understanding mood disorder etiology.

title: GluD1 modulates GluN2B-containing NMDAR function and plasticity at subicular synapses
abstract: Dysregulation of the delta-type glutamate receptor GluD1 and N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors (NMDARs) is implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders including schizophrenia and intellectual disability, and GluD1 modulates NMDAR responses in hippocampal neurons. However, the precise mechanisms by which GluD1 influences specific NMDAR subtypes remain undefined, representing a critical gap given the reliance of synaptic plasticity and cognition on NMDAR composition. GluN2A- and GluN2B-containing NMDARs are essential for synaptic long-term potentiation (LTP) and contextual learning and memory. Here, we used CRISPR/Cas9 to generate GluD1 knockout (KO) in cultured hippocampal neurons and observed a selective decrease in GluN2B-containing NMDAR responses. In acute hippocampal slices, GluD1 KO similarly reduced GluN2B-containing NMDAR currents at ventral CA1→subiculum synapses and impaired LTP at these synapses. In vivo, region-specific GluD1 deficiency in the ventral subiculum disrupted long-term contextual memory, indicating a critical role for GluD1 in cognitive processes. These findings demonstrate that GluD1 is indispensable for preserving GluN2B-containing NMDAR function, synaptic plasticity, and memory, providing molecular insight into how GluD1 regulates NMDAR subtypes implicated in synaptic dysfunction in neuropsychiatric disorders. Understanding this mechanism will guide the development of therapeutic strategies that selectively target GluD1-dependent modulation of NMDAR subtypes in brain disease.

title: Comparative effects of various exercise types and doses to improve executive function in children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review with pairwise, network, and dose-response meta-analyses
abstract: Exercise interventions have been demonstrated to effectively improve executive function (EF) in children and adolescents with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). However, evidence comparing effects of different exercise types and doses is limited, and the optimal exercise type and dose that improve EF remain unclear. This study aims to compare the effects of different exercise types and doses on EF improvement in children and adolescents with ADHD. Seven databases (PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Cochrane Library, SPORT Discus via EBSCO, PsycINFO, and CNKI) were systematically searched up to February 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the effects of exercise interventions on EF in children and adolescents with ADHD were included. The outcomes included working memory (WM), inhibitory control (IC), and cognitive flexibility (CF). Pairwise, network, and dose-response meta-analyses using random-effects models were conducted to assess the effects of exercise on EF. Forty RCTs (n = 1563) were included. Network meta-analysis indicated that, among children and adolescents with ADHD, mind-body exercise had the highest probability (SUCRA = 94.9) of being the most effective intervention for improving WM. Combat sports demonstrated the highest probability of being the most effective intervention for enhancing IC (SUCRA = 93.4) and CF (SUCRA = 92.5) in this population. Furthermore, a significant positive non-linear dose-response relationship was identified between total exercise and all EF domains among children and adolescents with ADHD. The minimum effective dose was estimated at approximately 1200 METs-min/week for WM, 340 METs-min/week for IC, and 280 METs-min/week for CF, respectively.

title: Greater Translocator Protein Distribution Volume in Neurocircuitry of Anorexia Nervosa
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Inflammatory stimuli are associated with onset of anorexia nervosa (AN) but whether inflammation occurs in the brain of AN is unknown. The primary objective is to determine whether [ 18 F]FEPPA total distribution volume ([ 18 F]FEPPA V T ), PET index of translocator protein density and inflammatory marker of gliosis, is elevated in AN in anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), ventral striatum (VS), dorsal caudate (DC), dorsal putamen (DP), thalamus, orbitofrontal cortex and insula. Secondary objectives are to determine the relationship of [ 18 F]FEPPA V T  in ACC to rumination severity and [ 18 F]FEPPA V T  to body mass index (BMI).

METHODS: [ 18 F]FEPPA V T  was measured in 20 medication free AN participants and 20 healthy controls. Correlations of [ 18 F]FEPPA V T  with rumination severity, and BMI, were determined.

RESULTS: [ 18 F]FEPPA V T  was elevated in AN in all ROI (linear mixed model (LMM), group effect, P = 4×10 -7 ), particularly ACC, VS, DC and thalamus (mean 52% elevation; LMM, region by group interaction, P = 4×10 -4 ). ACC [ 18 F]FEPPA V T  correlated positively with eating concerns (Eating Disorder Examination, r = 0.58, P = .007; Inventory of Depression and Anxiety Symptoms-II, r = 0.66, P = .002). There were no significant correlations between [ 18 F]FEPPA V T  and BMI.

CONCLUSIONS: Greater [ 18 F]FEPPA V T  is strong evidence for neuroinflammation and gliosis, particularly in ACC, VS, DC and thalamus in AN. Given such, it may be of interest to assess interventions that influence gliosis towards curative roles in future clinical trials in AN.

title: Personalized Functional Network Mapping Across the Lifespan
abstract: Functional brain networks vary substantially across individuals, yet this variability is obscured by conventional group-average atlases. Personalized functional network mapping addresses this limitation by characterizing individual-specific network organization, including the spatial topography of network territories, boundaries, and variants. Personalized mapping can be applied across large developmental and aging cohorts to study lifespan changes in such organization. Precision functional mapping (PFM), a specialized form of personalized mapping, uses extensive functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data per individual to achieve highly reliable and fine-grained characterization of individual functional organization. Here, we review individual-specific functional network organization from infancy through older adulthood. Evidence across life stages suggests a lifespan trajectory in which individual-specific network organization is detectable near birth, continues to refine through childhood and adolescence, and exhibits marked trait-like stability in adulthood, while its evolution in later life remains less well characterized. Across these stages, inter-individual topographic variability is greater in higher-order association than primary sensorimotor systems, positioning the sensorimotor-association axis as a unifying framework for understanding individual-specific network organization across the lifespan. We further review how individualized network features relate to cognition and psychopathology and how they are altered in psychiatric and neurodegenerative disorders. Finally, we discuss advances in MRI acquisition and analysis that facilitate personalized functional network mapping and opportunities for precision clinical translation.

title: PTSD is Associated with Advanced Epigenetic Age in 43,155 US Military Veterans
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) has been associated with advanced biological age in DNA methylation data, but results have been inconsistent. This study evaluated PTSD in association with epigenetic age in the largest cohort to date (by ∼20 fold).

METHODS: Participants were 43,155 US Veterans (92.96% male) enrolled in the VA's Million Veteran Program, with VA electronic health record (EHR), self-report PTSD severity (n = 21,999), and DNA methylation and genotype data. PTSD diagnoses predated the blood draw for obtaining DNA by ≥ one year.

RESULTS: PTSD diagnosis and symptom severity were associated with age-adjusted metrics of epigenetic age ("age residuals") per the Horvath, Hannum, PhenoAge, GrimAge, and DunedinPACE algorithms after multiple testing adjustment. PTSD severity showed the most consistent associations with epigenetic age residuals, ranging from up to ∼7 months (Horvath) to ∼2 years (GrimAge) advanced age and up to 16 days faster pace per year (DunedinPACE). The relationships between PTSD severity and GrimAge, PhenoAge, and DunedinPACE residuals were stronger among younger vs. older Veterans. PTSD was associated with all epigenetic age residuals in the European ancestry subgroup (n = 26,630), but fewer significant associations emerged in the African ancestry participants (n = 11,119). Associations were similar across male and female Veterans.

CONCLUSIONS: PTSD was associated with advanced epigenetic aging in the largest study to date to evaluate this question. Effects were generally small in magnitude, though meaningful when considering the personal and healthcare system impact of advanced aging in the large population of VA users with PTSD.

title: Identity-linked peer stress and internalizing distress: Heterogeneous joint trajectories across two years in adolescence
abstract: Bias-based victimization may function as identity-linked peer stress, yet little is known about how it co-develops with internalizing distress across two years in adolescence. We analyzed four waves of data from  N  = 639 US adolescents (M = 15.23 years, SD = 1.30, range 13-17; 51.3% identified as female; 51.5% White, 23.6% Hispanic/Latino, 19.6% Black, 4.1% Asian, 1.3% multiracial/other) from the AmeriSpeak Teen Panel. Multidimensional growth mixture modeling identified joint trajectories of victimization, depression, and anxiety. A three-class solution emerged (entropy = 0.94): Co-Occurring High-Decreasing (7.5%), High Internalizing, Low Victimization (19.7%), and Low-Stable (72.8%). Higher parenting stress predicted membership in both higher-risk classes relative to Low-Stable (OR = 2.44 and 1.67); the female gender indicator (OR = 2.85,  d  ≈ 0.58) and lower parental education predicted the High Internalizing, Low Victimization class. Both higher-risk classes reported lower school safety and higher peer rejection at Wave 4 than the Low-Stable class but did not differ significantly from each other; classes did not differ in grades. Identity-linked peer stress and internalizing distress followed heterogeneous developmental pathways: comparably elevated internalizing distress emerged with and without frequent victimization.

title: Early adversity, poverty, and positive social development show distinct associations across epigenetic aging measures in childhood
abstract: Adversity and poverty are implicated in biological aging, but epigenetic age research has produced inconsistent findings, and few studies have considered positive developmental factors. Leveraging the Future of Families and Child Wellbeing Study ( N  = 863 with epigenetic data; 51.14% males; 45.67% Non-Hispanic Black), we examined how early adversity, poverty, and social skills trajectories in childhood relate to multiple epigenetic clocks at age 9 ( M   age  = 9.33 ± 0.32), including age-trained (Horvath, Hannum, Skin & Blood, PedBE), health-related (PhenoAge, GrimAge), and pace of aging (DunedinPACE) measures. Early adversity was associated with accelerated GrimAge ( β  = 0.12) and PedBE ( β  = 0.12), but decelerated age on Horvath ( β  = -0.08) and Skin & Blood clocks ( β  = -0.12). Poverty showed more consistent associations with accelerated age on mortality-related clocks. Children with decreasing social skills across childhood had higher GrimAge ( β  = 0.20), and this pattern of social development partially mediated the effect of poverty. This pattern was specific to social skills and not psychopathology symptoms. Together, these findings suggest that early adversity and poverty are implicated in similar and distinct alterations in epigenetic clocks indexing maturation versus disease risk, while social development may play a role specifically in epigenetic aging related to disease risk.

title: Day-to-day peer and family stress as proximal correlates of self-injurious thoughts during adolescence
abstract: Theory and research both highlight interpersonal stressors as precipitants to self-injurious thoughts and behaviors (SITBs) during adolescence. Yet, little is known about near-term risk or which types of interpersonal stressors (e.g., peer and/or family) are most likely to precipitate adolescent SITBs. This study used an intensive longitudinal design to examine whether peer- and family-related stress were associated with adolescents' same- and next-day self-injurious thoughts. Participants were 154 female adolescents aged 12-17 years (77.3% White). Youth were oversampled for risk such that 73.4% ( n  = 113) were at high risk for future SITBs. Youth completed a 30-day ecological momentary assessment procedure assessing interpersonal experiences and SITBs. Multilevel models showed that peer stress predicted same-day nonsuicidal self-injury urges and suicidal ideation (SI), whereas family stress predicted same-day nonsuicidal self-injury urges only. Neither peer nor family stress predicted next-day self-injurious thoughts. Exploratory models examining bidirectional effects showed that non-suicidal self-injury urges predicted next-day peer and family stress while SI predicted next-day family, but not peer, stress. Findings suggest that daily interpersonal stress is proximally associated with self-injurious thoughts during adolescence and underscore the importance of studying these processes in real time. Results may have implications for ecological momentary interventions to interrupt interpersonal risks for SITBs.

title: Children's and adults' metamotivational beliefs about how cognitive reframing shapes motivation
abstract: The ability to overcome motivational challenges depends, in part, on individuals' beliefs about how motivation can be regulated-that is, metamotivational beliefs. Although research with adults shows that such beliefs support more effective motivation regulation and goal pursuit, little is known about how they develop during childhood. The present research examined the development of a foundational aspect of metamotivational beliefs in 4- to 9-year-old North American children ( N  = 379, 58% White, 55% girls) and adults ( N  = 135, 65% White, 54% women): the belief that motivation can be shaped by how one interprets the situation (i.e., cognitive reframing). In Study 1, children as young as 4-5 years attributed stronger motivation to positive than to negative reframing for the same situation, with increases in effects through age 9. In Study 2, children and adults rated reframing as more effective than distracting thoughts for motivation, but the reverse pattern held for emotion. These findings suggest that judgments about reframing cannot be reduced to valence reasoning and that participants recognize that regulating motivation is not identical to regulating emotion. Using a between-subjects design, Study 3 conceptually replicated Study 2's pattern that reframing was considered more effective than distraction for motivation but not for emotion and revealed that, unlike adults, children did not prefer reframing over distraction when selecting a strategy for themselves. Together, the research demonstrates a developing recognition of reframing effects on motivation-a process central to many motivation regulation strategies-with implications for the development of metamotivational beliefs and self-regulation.
