title: Maternal responses to infant positive affect and toddler regulation of positive affect: A longitudinal pilot study
abstract: Children's ability to regulate positive affect (PA) is a crucial yet understudied aspect of early socioemotional development. This pilot study investigated whether maternal responses to infant PA longitudinally predict toddlers' regulation of PA. Participants were 32 mother-infant dyads from a larger longitudinal study in Toronto, Canada. At 11-12 months, dyads were video recorded during naturalistic play at home. Maternal responses to infant PA were assessed using an observational coding system that distinguishes supportive (e.g., elaborative, matching) from nonsupportive (e.g., intrusive, ignoring) responses. At 18-20 months, toddlers completed the gift delay task, which measures regulation of high-arousal PA through latency to touch a desirable toy. Multiple regression analysis controlling for age and family income showed that a greater proportion of supportive responses in infancy predicted better regulation of PA in toddlerhood (β = .37, p = .027). Findings provide preliminary evidence that supportive maternal responses to PA in infancy are associated with capacities to regulate PA in toddlerhood. Results highlight the importance of examining positive as well as negative affect in models of early emotion regulation and suggest potential targets for early intervention.

title: Longitudinal relations between social withdrawal subtypes, internalizing problems, and well-being among Chinese youth: exploring within-person and between-person effects
abstract: To date, the extant literature on the development and implications of social withdrawal is comprised predominantly of studies focused on between-person associations. As such, we have limited understanding of the intra-individual processes that may underlie these relations. The goal of this study was to explore both between- and within-person associations between different subtypes of social withdrawal (shyness, unsociability, social avoidance), internalizing problems, and indices of well-being in a sample of children and early adolescents from mainland China. A total of 1,001 children (563 boys; 100% Han descent) in grades 4-8 ( M age  = 11.71 years,  SD  = 1.45, range = 7.83-14.17) participated in a four-wave longitudinal data collection procedure. Results from random intercept cross-lagged panel models (RI-CLPM) indicated that social withdrawal subtypes were all associated with indices of internalizing problems (depression, loneliness, social anxiety) and poorer well-being at the between-person level (standardized effect sizes ranged from .21 to .61). Within-person analyses revealed reciprocal relations between shyness and well-being, unsociability and depression, unsociability and loneliness, as well as social avoidance and loneliness. These findings offer preliminary evidence that a within-person perspective could be useful for developing tailored interventions to support children's psychological adjustment in Chinese society.

title: Neighborhood poly-victimization and adolescent mental health: Community violence, sexual street harassment, and family cohesion across two waves in urban Mexico
abstract: Violence exposure profoundly disrupts adolescent development, such as in Mexico, where narco-related crime has normalized chronic insecurity. Utilizing a two-wave longitudinal design, we examined poly-victimization (community violence exposure and sexual street harassment), family cohesion, and psychological health among 346 Mexican adolescents ( M age  = 13.02,  SD  = 0.98; 47.9% girls, 52.1% boys) in Uruapan, Mexico. Path models showed poly-victimization was associated with elevated depressive and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) symptoms cross-sectionally, but not longitudinally once baseline symptoms were controlled. Witnessing violence, but not personal victimization, remained cross-sectionally associated with both outcomes. Family cohesion did not buffer these associations; instead, cohesion exacerbated the cross-sectional link between sexual street harassment and PTSD symptoms. Girls reported higher depressive and PTSD symptoms than boys, though gender did not moderate any violence-symptom association. Findings suggest family cohesion, often assumed protective, may intensify rather than buffer the psychological toll of sexual street harassment among Mexican adolescents facing chronic violence.

title: Influence of sex, puberty, and childhood psychopathology on developmental trajectories of the visual P300 across adolescence
abstract:
Research indicates the visual P300 decreases across adolescence due to maturation of neural attention networks. However, there is limited research examining whether assigned sex at birth and puberty influence this neurodevelopment. A blunted visual P300 has also been linked with internalizing and externalizing psychopathology, but it is unclear whether childhood psychopathology predicts changes in the P300 across adolescence. The present study examined whether sex, pubertal development, and childhood internalizing and externalizing symptoms predicted trajectories of the visual P300 across adolescence. The sample included 531 New York youth (45.5% female; 89.4% White; 19.7% Hispanic) who completed a flanker task to elicit the visual P300 at ages 9, 12, 15, 18, and 21 (2010-2025). Multilevel growth modeling indicated that the visual P300 was characterized by a quadratic decrease from late childhood to early adulthood; males showed a slower rate of change than females. Females with greater age 12 pubertal development showed a faster rate of change. Males with higher age 9 externalizing symptoms and depression symptoms had blunted baseline P300s. Age 9 internalizing and externalizing symptoms did not relate to slope. Results highlight the need to better understand the developmental of neural indicators of attentional processing that have been linked to future psychopathology.

The P300 is a neural signal reflecting attention and cognitive processing, which decreases in amplitude during adolescence due to maturation of neural attention networks. The present study involved 531 youth ages 9 to 21, measuring their sex, pubertal development, early psychopathology symptoms, and P300 development across adolescence. The P300 decreased in a curved pattern across adolescence into early adulthood, and females showed a faster decrease than males. The P300 of more physically mature females at age 12 decreased faster. Males with more baseline externalizing problems and depression had a smaller baseline P300, though symptoms did not predict how the P300 changed over time. These findings suggest sex, puberty, and early psychopathology all impact attention-related brain development during adolescence.

title: Parent-Child Physiological Synchrony: Links With Parent Emotion Regulation and Children's Independent Emotion Regulation
abstract:
ABSTRACT Developmental theories propose that physiological synchrony is a key process through which co‐regulatory experiences support children's emerging capacity for independent emotion regulation. Caregivers’ emotion regulation abilities are also theorized to influence their capacity to engage in synchronous interactions, thereby shaping co‐regulatory experiences. Despite these propositions, few studies have empirically examined these developmental processes. The current study examined associations between parent–child respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA) synchrony during dyadic problem solving and children's physiological (i.e, RSA reactivity) and behavioral regulation during a subsequent independent challenge. The study also examined whether parents’ emotion regulation difficulties predicted RSA synchrony and whether synchrony statistically accounted for associations between parents’ emotion regulation difficulties and children's regulatory outcomes. Participants included 57 preschoolers ( M _age = 4.26 years; 49% male) and their parents (50 mothers, 7 fathers). Families were predominantly White (68%), with 62% reporting a master's degree or higher. Greater parent‐driven RSA synchrony during dyadic interactions was associated with reduced reliance on distraction and help‐seeking strategies during the independent problem‐solving task but was not associated with children's physiological regulation. Parents reporting greater difficulties maintaining goal‐directed behavior and less emotional awareness exhibited lower levels of parent‐driven synchrony, and synchrony emerged as an indirect pathway linking these parent characteristics to children's behavioral regulation. Findings provide preliminary support for physiological synchrony as a developmental mechanism linking parent emotion regulation to children's independent emotion regulation during early childhood.

Summary Findings support parent–child physiological synchrony as a potential pathway linking parents’ emotion regulation capacities to children's independent emotion regulation. Greater parent‐driven physiological synchrony during dyadic problem solving was not associated with children's physiological regulation during independent problem solving. Greater parent‐driven physiological synchrony during dyadic problem solving predicted less reliance on external behavioral regulation during independent problem solving. Greater parental difficulty maintaining goal‐directed behavior during distress and lower emotional awareness predicted reduced parent‐driven physiological synchrony.

1 Introduction Emotion regulation is widely recognized as a foundational developmental task of early childhood, with individual differences in children's regulatory abilities associated with functioning across academic (Djambazova‐Popordanoska 2016 ; Wong et al. 2023 ), social (De Neve et al. 2023 ; Qashmer 2023 ), and psychological domains (Klinge et al. 2025 ; Perry et al. 2018 ). Developmental theories propose that emotion regulation emerges within the context of caregiver–child interactions (Morris et al. 2017 ; Sameroff 2010 ; Sroufe 1997 ). Early in life, caregivers must regulate their own emotions while helping children manage physiological arousal and behavioral distress (Eisenberg et al. 1998 ; Morris et al. 2007 ; Snyder et al. 2025 ). Over time, these co‐regulatory experiences are thought to contribute to children's increasing capacity for independent emotion regulation (Perry and Calkins 2018 ). Despite the prominence of these theoretical perspectives, relatively little research has directly examined the distinct processes through which caregiver–child interactions support children's emerging self‐regulation. To address this gap, the current study examined whether parent–child physiological synchrony during dyadic interaction was associated with children's independent biobehavioral emotion regulation and whether synchrony was predicted by distinct aspects of parents’ own regulatory capacities. We also tested whether physiological synchrony represented a potential developmental pathway linking parents’ emotion regulation to children's independent emotion regulation. 2 Parent–Child Physiological Synchrony and Children's Emotion Regulation Caregivers provide behavioral support by modeling appropriate emotional responses and teaching regulatory strategies (Bell 2020 ; Eisenberg et al. 1998 ), but they may also shape the development of neural and physiological systems that support adaptive responses to emotional challenge (Hofer 1987 ; Shonkoff et al. 2012 ). Physiological synchrony, defined as coordination between caregivers’ and children's physiological responses during emotionally salient interactions (DePasquale 2020 ), is thought to reflect mutual attunement to emotional states, potentially allowing caregivers to respond more effectively to children's changing regulatory needs. As such, physiological synchrony has been proposed as one possible mechanism through which co‐regulatory experiences contribute to children's emerging self‐regulatory capacities (Davis et al. 2018 ; Feldman et al. 2010 ). A substantial body of research on physiological synchrony has focused on the parasympathetic nervous system (PNS), given its central role in the regulation of physiological arousal, behavior, and emotion (Porges 2003 , 2025 ). During states of rest, parasympathetic influence via the vagus nerve promotes regulated cardiac activity, whereas environmental challenge can elicit vagal withdrawal, allowing physiological resources to be mobilized in support of active coping (Porges et al. 1996 ). Developmental scientists have proposed that caregivers may facilitate maturation of the vagal system, including greater myelination of vagal fibers, by consistently helping children flexibly upregulate and downregulate arousal (Porges and Furman 2011 ). If so, greater caregiver–child physiological synchrony may be associated not only with more adaptive PNS responses to emotional challenge, but also with the behavioral regulation strategies these biological systems support (Porges 2025 ; Tang et al. 2025 ). PNS functioning is commonly indexed using respiratory sinus arrhythmia (RSA), a component of heart rate variability that occurs at the frequency of respiration (Beauchaine and Thayer 2015 ; Ritz 2024 ). RSA provides a noninvasive index of parasympathetic regulation, with decreases in RSA during environmental challenge generally interpreted as an adaptive physiological response that supports engagement with changing contextual demands (Sacrey et al. 2021 ). Extending this work to the dyadic level, researchers have examined the extent to which caregivers’ and children's RSA responses are synchronized during interaction. To model RSA synchrony, researchers frequently use multilevel coupled autoregressive models (Hu et al. 2021 ; Lunkenheimer et al. 2015 ; Lunkenheimer et al. 2018 ), which allow for a distinction between caregiver‐driven synchrony, in which caregivers’ RSA predicts children's subsequent RSA, and child‐driven synchrony, in which children's RSA predicts caregivers’ subsequent RSA. These time‐lagged associations provide insight into the strength and direction of physiological coupling during caregiver–child interactions. Including person‐average RSA as a covariate further helps distinguish within‐dyad physiological coupling from stable individual differences in RSA. Previous research has linked parent–child RSA synchrony to children's developmental outcomes, but studies have primarily focused on broad indicators of psychological adjustment, such as internalizing and externalizing symptoms (Li et al. 2025 ; Lunkenheimer et al. 2018 ; Lunkenheimer et al. 2021 ; Oshri et al. 2021 ; Somers 2025 ), rather than the specific regulatory processes theorized to develop through parent–child co‐regulation. A growing but limited body of work has begun to address this gap by examining associations between RSA synchrony and children's emotion regulation. For example, Abney et al. ( 2021 ) found that infants exhibited better behavioral regulation of distress when concurrent mother–infant RSA synchrony was concordant (i.e., RSA changing in the same direction) rather than discordant (i.e., RSA changing in opposite directions), particularly among infants demonstrating adaptive RSA reactivity to challenge. Similarly, Xu et al. ( 2024 ) found that greater concurrent parent–child RSA synchrony was associated with better observed emotion regulation in the context of higher parental emotional support. Tang et al. ( 2024 ) found that time‐lagged grandmother‐driven concordance during a collaborative task was associated with better grandparent‐reported emotion regulation, whereas concurrent synchrony during a conflict task was associated with poorer regulation. Together, these findings provide preliminary support for associations between physiological synchrony and children's developing emotion regulation abilities, although important gaps remain. Existing studies have largely examined broad indicators of emotion regulation rather than the specific behavioral strategies children use to regulate arousal during emotional challenge (Perry and Calkins 2018 ). Moreover, relatively little is known about whether caregiver–child physiological synchrony is associated with children's independent physiological regulation of emotional arousal. Addressing these gaps may be particularly important during the preschool period, a time characterized by rapid maturation of stress response systems and acquisition and refinement of behavioral regulatory strategies (Perry and Calkins 2018 ), both of which lay the foundation for independent self‐regulation (Cole et al. 2018 ). Further, children face increasing demands for autonomous regulation as they enter early learning environments, navigate more complex social interactions, and engage in independent problem‐solving. Thus, examining caregiver–child physiological synchrony when children are increasingly transitioning from caregiver‐supported to independent regulation may help elucidate how co‐regulatory experiences contribute to the development of independent behavioral and physiological regulation. 3 Parent Emotion Regulation and Parent–Child Physiological Synchrony Research has linked caregiving risk factors, including parenting difficulties (Ostlund et al. 2017 ), history of maltreatment (Lunkenheimer et al. 2018 ), depressive symptoms and depression history (McKillop and Connell 2018 ; Suveg et al. 2019 ; Woody et al. 2016 ), and elevated life stress (Li and Lunkenheimer 2025 ), to reduced concordance or more discordant patterns of RSA synchrony during caregiver–child interactions. However, relatively little research has examined whether parents’ own emotion regulation abilities contribute to physiological synchrony with their children during challenging interactions. Developmental theories of emotion regulation suggest that effective co‐regulation requires caregivers to manage their own emotional arousal while simultaneously responding to children's regulatory needs (Feldman 2007 ). Consequently, caregivers who struggle to regulate their emotions may not only model less adaptive regulatory behaviors but also have greater difficulty recognizing and responding to children's changing emotional states, potentially limiting their ability to support children in downregulating negative affect (Hajal and Paley 2020 ; Zimmer‐Gembeck et al. 2022 ; Zitzmann et al. 2024 ). The influence of parents’ emotion regulation abilities on physiological synchrony may be particularly evident in parent‐driven patterns of physiological coordination, given caregivers’ central role in supporting children's regulation during early childhood (Feldman 2007 ). Indeed, studies examining directional RSA synchrony have generally found concordant parent‐driven synchrony alongside null or discordant child‐driven synchrony (Helm et al. 2018 ; Lunkenheimer et al. 2021 ). For example, Armstrong‐Carter et al. ( 2021 ) observed concordant parent‐driven but discordant child‐driven RSA synchrony during a parent–child problem‐solving task. These findings suggest that caregivers’ awareness of their own emotional states and ability to modulate their arousal may play an important role in establishing parent‐driven physiological synchrony, especially during emotionally challenging dyadic interactions. 4 Parent–Child Physiological Synchrony Linking Parent and Child Emotion Regulation Although developmental theories propose that parents’ emotion regulation abilities shape children's developing emotion regulation (Eisenberg et al. 1998 ; Morris et al. 2007 ), the mechanisms underlying these associations remain poorly understood. Research has documented similarities in parent and child regulatory strategy use (Bariola et al. 2011 ; Tan and Smith 2019 ) and associations between their emotion dysregulation (Crespo et al. 2017 ; Li et al. 2019 ), but investigations of potential mechanisms have focused primarily on behavioral processes, such as emotion socialization and emotional expressivity (Hajal and Paley 2020 ; Price and Kiel 2022 ). Less attention has been devoted to biological processes that may unfold during parent–child interactions. Physiological synchrony may represent one such pathway, as parents who are better able to regulate their own emotional arousal may be more capable of coordinating their physiological responses with those of their children during challenging interactions. These coordinated physiological experiences may, in turn, support children's developing capacity to independently regulate their physiological arousal and behavioral responses to emotional challenge. 5 The Current Study The first goal of the current study was to examine whether parent–child RSA synchrony during a challenging dyadic problem‐solving task was associated with children's physiological and behavioral emotion regulation during a subsequent independent problem‐solving task. title: Tracing the impact of maternal communication deviance on joint engagement: The mediating role of maternal supportive behaviors
abstract:
Abstract Communication Deviance is a disorganized communicative style that can disrupt shared meaning‐making in parent–child interactions and is considered a risk factor for later mental health difficulties. This longitudinal study, conducted in the UK, examined whether maternal Communication Deviance assessed during pregnancy predicted joint engagement and related processes. Participants were 229 mothers (95.9% White British; M = 27.6 years, SD = 6.1). Maternal Communication Deviance was assessed antenatally, and mother–child dyads were observed during play at 30‐months. Communication Deviance predicted lower total joint engagement, including supported ( β = –.18, p = .007), coordinated ( β = –.17, p = .016), and symbol‐infused joint engagement ( β = –.24, p < .001), and was associated with reduced supportive behaviors ( β = –.40, p < .001) and dyadic attunement ( β = –.31, p < .001). Mediation analyses indicated that supportive behaviors accounted for the associations between Communication Deviance and joint engagement outcomes. These findings suggest that Communication Deviance may constrain children's opportunities for shared attention and meaning making. The study supports developmental models that highlight early communicative processes as foundational to socio‐cognitive and relational development and identifies supportive behaviors as a potential target for interventions promoting early mental health and parent–child interaction. Key Findings Higher maternal Communication Deviance during pregnancy predicted less Total, Supported, Coordinated, and Symbol‐infused joint engagement at 30 months. Reduced maternal supportive behaviors fully explained the link between Communication Deviance and lower joint engagement and dyadic attunement. Maternal Communication Deviance may act as an early environmental risk factor, highlighting the importance of supporting maternal responsiveness to promote healthy development. Statement of Relevance This study examines how maternal Communication Deviance measured during pregnancy predicts joint engagement and dyadic attunement at 30 months, processes central to early socio‐cognitive and relational development. By identifying maternal supportive behaviors as a key mechanism linking Communication Deviance to interactional quality, the research highlights a modifiable target for early intervention. Findings advance understanding of early environmental risk factors and inform strategies to support parent–child interactions, directly addressing foundational processes relevant to child and early childhood mental health.

1 COMMUNICATION DEVIANCE AS A RISK FACTOR FOR PSYCHOPATHOLOGY Communication Deviance refers to a communicative style characterized by vagueness, ambiguity, and disruptions in shared meaning between interlocutors (Singer, 1965a , b ; Singer et al., 1978 ; Tienari & Wahlberg, 2008 ; Wynne, 1963a ; Wynne et al., 1963 , 1977b , 1984 ). It encompasses a range of linguistic and interactional disturbances that can hinder mutual understanding during social exchange (e.g., unclear referents, contradictory statements, or poorly timed contributions). Communication Deviance has been most extensively studied in the context of schizophrenia‐spectrum disorders, where elevated levels in parents have been associated with increased risk of thought disorder and broader psychopathology in offspring (de Sousa et al., 2014 ; Roisko et al., 2014 ). Longitudinal findings indicate that Communication Deviance precedes the onset of such difficulties, supporting its role as an environmental risk factor rather than a response to child characteristics (Goldstein, 1987 ). However, Communication Deviance is not specific to schizophrenia; similar communicative patterns have been observed in families experiencing other forms of psychopathology, relational distress, and needs, suggesting it is better conceptualized as a dimensional and transdiagnostic construct (Miklowitz & Stackman, 1992 ). Evidence from adoption studies further suggests that Communication Deviance interacts with genetic vulnerability, such that its impact on offspring outcomes depends on broader risk context (Wahlberg et al., 1997 , 2000 ). Overall, this body of work supports the view that parental CD constitutes an environmental risk factor in the development of psychopathology. However, the mechanisms through which CD operates in early caregiving contexts remain poorly understood. 2 PLAUSIBLE DEVELOPMENTAL MECHANISM One proposed pathway is through the disruption of early interactional processes in childhood. In particular, Communication Deviance may interfere with joint engagement which refers to episodes of mutual attention, communication, and emotional connection between caregiver and child around a common interest or task (Adamson et al., 2004 , 2009 , 2012 ). These interactions are critical for the development of social understanding, emotional regulation, and cognitive skills (Adamson et al., 2019 ) and the quality of nonverbal and verbal interactions (e.g., dyadic connectedness and fluency) seemed to be important for the child's cognitive and social development (Hirsh‐Pasek et al., 2015 ). If caregiver communication is vague, inconsistent, or poorly timed, opportunities for sustained shared attention and meaning making may be reduced. In this way, Communication Deviance may constrain the quality of early interactional experiences that support development. Although this account is theoretically plausible, it has not yet been directly tested. 2.1 Joint engagement Joint engagement refers to sustained, reciprocal interactions between a child and a social partner in which both participants are actively involved in a shared activity and maintain a common focus over time (Adamson, 2018 ; Adamson et al., 2014 ; Trevarthen & Aitken, 2001 ). These engagement states are characterized not only by shared attention, but also by the quality of the interaction, including affective attunement, reciprocity, and the use of gestures, actions, and language. This construct is grounded in sociocultural developmental theory (Vygotsky & Cole, 1978 ) and early work on infants’ emerging capacity to share attention with caregivers (Scaife & Bruner, 1975 ). Within these broader engagement states, joint attention is best conceptualized as a set of social‐communicative skills that enable the coordination of attention between partners, including behaviors such as responding to joint attention, initiating joint attention, gaze following, and pointing (Adamson et al., 2019 ; Mundy, 2018 ). Rather than being synonymous with joint engagement, these skills support the initiation, maintenance, and elaboration of joint engagement episodes. Thus, joint attention reflects the child's moment‐to‐moment attentional coordination abilities, whereas joint engagement captures the broader, dynamic context in which these skills are embedded and expressed (Adamson et al., 2019 ). Disruptions to both joint attention skills and joint engagement states are well documented in autism and are thought to contribute to broader differences in social communication and cognition (Adamson et al., 2009 ; Nyström et al., 2019 ). These early social interactions are supported by developing perceptual‐motor capacities (Butterworth & Jarrett, 1991 ) and neurocognitive mechanisms that orient the child toward social information (Baron‐Cohen, 1997 ), but they are fundamentally shaped within relational and affective contexts (Hobson, 2005 ; Hobson & Hobson, 2011 ; Racine & Carpendale, 2007 ). During the first year of life, infants begin to engage in behaviors that recruit others’ attention, such as gaze following and pointing, with more consistent use emerging toward the end of the first year (Salter & Carpenter, 2025 ). Across the second year, episodes of joint engagement become increasingly sustained, differentiated, and socially coordinated (Bakeman & Adamson, 1984 ; Charman et al., 2000 ; Mundy & Gomes, 1998 ). These interactions provide a critical context for development, supporting the emergence of social understanding (Mundy, 2018 ; Tomasello, 2014 ), language acquisition (Loy et al., 2018 ; Mundy et al., 2007 ; Tomasello & Farrar, 1986 ), cognitive development (Mundy & Newell, 2007 ; Mundy & Sigman, 2015 ), and emotion regulation (Morales et al., 2005 ). Joint engagement episodes are inherently multi‐modal, integrating gaze, gesture, touch, and language (Schatz et al., 2022 ; Suarez‐Rivera et al. et al., 2022 ). Caregivers play a central role in structuring and sustaining these interactions through sensitivity, contingent responding, and scaffolding (Bakeman & Adamson, 1984 ; Hustedt & Raver, 2002 ). For example, following the child's focus of attention supports the emergence of coordinated joint engagement, whereas more directive behaviors may characterize supported joint engagement (Mendive et al., 2013 ). In naturalistic contexts, caregiver involvement, particularly when it is multi‐modal, substantially increases the duration and complexity of play interactions (Schatz et al., 2022 ). Indeed, caregiver behaviors such as sensitivity, cognitive stimulation, and positive affect are positively associated with both the frequency and duration of joint engagement episodes (Koşkulu et al., 2021 ), whereas difficulties in affective attunement may reduce the likelihood of initiating shared engagement (Annie Yoon et al., 2014 ). Importantly, the quality of parent‐child interaction appears to be a strong predictor of developmental outcomes. For example, dyadic fluency and connectedness during interaction predicts language outcomes beyond the quantity of linguistic input, particularly in socioeconomically disadvantaged contexts (Hirsh‐Pasek et al., 2015 ). Similarly, early caregiver attunement predicts later joint attention abilities, which in turn mediate associations with executive function development (Brandes‐Aitken et al., 2020 ). Time spent in joint engagement and caregivers’ responsiveness to the child's attentional focus are also associated with the development of gesture and early language (Carpenter et al., 1998 ), while infants’ responsiveness to joint attention bids predicts later vocabulary outcomes (Morales et al., 2000 ). Across development, joint engagement becomes increasingly symbol‐infused, providing a foundation for language use and meaning‐making (Adamson et al., 2004 ). By early childhood, these interactions expand to include references to absent objects and events, supporting more complex communicative exchanges about the past and future (Adamson & Bakeman, 2006 ; Adamson et al., 2014 ). 3 PRESENT STUDY The study examined whether antenatal maternal Communication Deviance (at 32 weeks’ gestation) predicts reduced Joint Engagement and related interactional processes at 30 months in primiparous mothers. It was hypothesized that higher maternal Communication Deviance would be associated with less time in Joint Engagement states, less Maternal Scaffolding, Symbol Highlighting, Following the Child's focus, less Fluency and Connectedness of communication and Sustainability of Shared topic in the dyad and poorer Expressive Language, and that the relationships between maternal Communication Deviance, Joint Engagement, dyadic attunement variables, and the child's Expressive Language would be mediated by maternal behaviors such as Scaffolding, Symbol Highlighting, and Following the Child's Focus. 4 METHOD 4.1 Recruitment and sample The study draws on data from the Wirral Child Health and Development Study (WCHADS; Sharp et al., 2012 ) which is a longitudinal study that aimed to identify early social, emotional, and biological factors involved in the development of conduct disorder. The study employed a stratified two‐stage cluster design, recruiting a larger sample of primiparous mothers during pregnancy, from which a random subsample was drawn for intensive assessment ( n = 316). Participants were English‐speaking, aged ≥18, and sought antenatal care at 12 weeks’ gestation between February 2007 and October 2008 in the Northwest of the UK. A detailed flowchart of sampling, recruitment and attrition rates is available elsewhere (Sharp et al., 2012 ). Only data from the intensive subsample were used, as this included detailed observational data on mother‐child interactions. Of the 316 participants, 29 declined or were unable to complete the 5‐min speech sample task. Of the 287 who provided a 5‐min speech sample task during pregnancy, 230 attended the 30‐months’ assessment involving mother‐child play observations. Reasons for non‐attendance included withdrawal from the study, illness, and other commitments. Participants were required to be English‐speaking, and the sample was predominantly monolingual English‐speaking; however, formal mother‐tongue language status was not systematically recorded. 5 PROCEDURE 5.1 weeks speech samples (antenatal) At 32 weeks’ gestation, mothers were invited to provide speech samples about their unborn child (Leeb et al., 1991 ). The mother was instructed using the following prompt: “I would like to hear your thoughts and feelings about your baby at the moment, in your own words without me interrupting. When I ask you to begin, I would like you to speak for 5 minutes, tell me what your impressions have been of your baby whilst you've been pregnant. Have you got any questions before we start?” All interaction samples were reviewed to ensure they reflected continuous, naturalistic engagement; no minimum word‐count threshold was set a priori for inclusion. 5.2 Communication Deviance Communication Deviance was scored with the Interactional Communication Deviance scoring scheme which was originally developed for family interaction (Velligan, 1985 ). The scheme focuses on eight types of communication disturbances derived from research on Communication Deviance (Doane & Singer, 1977 ; Singer, 1965a , b ; Wynne, 1963a , b ; Wynne et al., 1977 , 1963b): (1) abandoned, abruptly ceased, uncorrected remarks, (2) unintelligible remarks, (3) contradictions, denials and retractions, (4) ambiguous referents, (5) extraneous questions and remarks, (6) tangential, inappropriate responses to questions or remarks, (7) odd word usage/odd sentence construction, and (8) reiteration. Code examples are available in a previous publication (de Sousa et al., 2019 ) and in Table 1 . The scheme demonstrates good reliability and construct validity (Velligan et al., 1990 ) and has been applied in clinical (Velligan et al., 1995 , 1996 ), high‐risk (Velligan et al., 1988 ) and natural speech samples (Docherty, 1993 ), including 5‐min speech samples (Kymalainen & Weisman de Mamani, 2008 ; Kymalainen et al., 2006 ). title: Gene discovery and pleiotropic architecture of multidimensional pain in a genome-wide association study of >1.2 million individuals
abstract: Chronic pain is highly prevalent worldwide, yet its genetic architecture remains to be fully elucidated. Here we leveraged data from 1,235,695 European-ancestry individuals across three biobanks. In a meta-analytic genome-wide association study of multidimensional pain (MP), we identified 343 independent loci, 92 of which were new pain associations. Sex-specific meta-analyses revealed 115 independent loci (12 of which were new) among males (n = 583,066) and 12 loci (2 of which were new) among females (n = 241,266). Multi-omic gene prioritization analyses highlighted 490 genes associated with MP through their effects on brain-specific and blood-specific regulation. Mendelian randomization analyses showed causal associations between MP and psychiatric disorders, substance use disorders and C-reactive protein levels. MP variants also showed pleiotropic associations with several brain imaging-derived phenotypes. This study expands our knowledge of the genetics of pain and its pathogenesis, highlighting the importance of its pleiotropy with multiple disorders and elucidating its multi-omic pathophysiology.

title: Human stem cell neuroscience
abstract: In neuroscience, the most relevant human biology has often been the least accessible. Stem-cell-based models, such as organoids and assembloids, are opening ways to generate, assemble, probe, and perturb neural cells and circuits, helping define "stem cell neuroscience." In this issue of Neuron, this and other reviews and commentaries discuss the current state of this emerging field.

title: Toward functional oversight of neural organoid research: A report from the 2025 Asilomar Conference
abstract: In November 2025, an international multistakeholder group convened at Asilomar, California, to address oversight of rapidly advancing neural organoid and assembloid research. This process report documents the convening's design, outcomes, and lessons, and it asks what it will take to turn this momentum into ongoing monitoring and practical guidelines that ensure responsible research without constraining scientific progress.

title: Hypersensitivity to adrenomedullin in post-traumatic headache: a randomized crossover study
abstract: Adrenomedullin (ADM), a vasoactive member of the calcitonin peptide family with receptor-signalling overlap with calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), has emerged as a candidate therapeutic target in migraine. Given the striking clinical parallels between migraine and persistent post-traumatic headache (PTH), we investigated whether ADM-responsive signalling contributes to migraine-like headache in adults with persistent PTH attributed to mild traumatic brain injury. We conducted a single-centre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-way crossover study in adults with persistent PTH and no pre-trauma history of migraine. On two experimental days separated by at least 7 days, participants received 20-minute intravenous infusions of ADM (19.9 pmol kg⁻¹ min⁻¹) and isotonic saline as the matched inactive comparator (placebo) in randomised sequence. Headache outcomes were recorded for 12 hours. The primary outcome was the within-participant incidence of experimentally induced migraine-like headache. The secondary outcome was the within-participant difference in baseline-corrected area under the curve (AUC) for headache intensity from 0 to 12 hours. Of 158 individuals assessed for eligibility, 21 were randomised, completed both periods and were analysed. Participants had a mean age of 34.3 years, 19 (90%) were female, and 18 (86%) reported a migraine-like phenotype. Migraine-like headache occurred in 17 of 21 participants (81%) after ADM and four of 21 (19%) following placebo. Fourteen participants developed migraine-like only after ADM and one only following placebo, yielding a paired absolute risk difference of 61.9 percentage points (95% CI 29.7-80.6; one-sided P < 0.001; two-sided P = 0.001). Baseline-corrected headache-intensity AUC was higher after ADM than placebo (median 1,110 [IQR 315-2205] versus 420 [-160 to 565]; P = 0.006). Median time to onset of migraine-like headache was 30 minutes after ADM and 390 minutes following placebo. Fifteen participants reported that the ADM-induced headache resembled their usual migraine-like headache episodes, and rescue medication was used by 10 participants after ADM and two after placebo. These findings identify pronounced responsiveness to ADM-linked signalling in persistent PTH and support the ADM pathway as a candidate target for mechanism-based therapeutic development, pending confirmation in independent cohorts and complementary preclinical studies.

title: Mosaic CDKL5 deficiency drives progressive inhibitory circuit remodelling
abstract: CDKL5 deficiency disorder predominantly affects heterozygous females, in whom random X-chromosome inactivation generates cellular CDKL5 mosaicism. Although mosaicism is a defining feature of the disease, whether it actively drives disease progression or simply reflects the genetic mode of inheritance remains unknown. Here, we combined age-comparative electrophysiology, quantitative synaptic imaging, transcriptomic profiling and postmortem human brain analyses to determine how mosaic CDKL5 deficiency shapes inhibitory circuit remodeling during disease progression. Heterozygous Cdkl5 female mice exhibited striking age- and region-specific remodeling of inhibitory neurotransmission. Hippocampal inhibition was initially enhanced but progressively declined with age, whereas cortical inhibitory transmission remained preserved at 3 months and increased in middle-aged animals. These functional changes were accompanied by dynamic remodeling of inhibitory presynaptic terminals, persistent disruption of inhibitory synapse organization and reduced hippocampal gephyrin-positive puncta despite preservation of the major inhibitory interneuron populations. At 12 months, heterozygous females also exhibited a higher density of IBA1/CD68 double-positive microglia in both regions compared with age-matched wild-type controls. Importantly, complete Cdkl5 deficiency failed to reproduce the progressive loss of inhibitory presynaptic terminals observed in heterozygous females, indicating that this phenotype is specific to the mosaic condition rather than a simple consequence of complete Cdkl5 loss. Transcriptomic profiling revealed a temporal transition from alterations detected at 3 months in immune-synaptic regulatory pathways to activity-dependent transcriptional programs associated with reduced structural and homeostatic support, consistent with progressive hippocampal circuit reorganization. Exploratory analyses of postmortem cortical tissue from individuals with CDD revealed differences in inhibitory presynaptic labeling between the available young and adult cases, suggesting that inhibitory alterations may also vary with age in human CDD. Together, these findings identify mosaic CDKL5 deficiency as a biologically distinct circuit state characterized by progressive, region-specific inhibitory circuit remodeling and provide a mechanistic framework for disease progression in CDKL5 deficiency disorder.

title: The Neural Correlates of Sickness
abstract: The brain protects animals during infection by detecting immune activity, coordinating behavioral and physiological defenses, anticipating potential infectious threats, and limiting excessive inflammation. Collectively termed sickness, these centrally organized responses include changes in body temperature, activity, energy balance, appetite, fluid intake, social behavior, neuroendocrine function, and autonomic output. Rather than constituting a single uniform state, sickness is generated by distributed and partially dissociable neural pathways that translate immune signals into responses appropriate to the nature and stage of an infection. Work presented at a symposium at the 2026 Society for Neuroscience meeting highlights how humoral and cranial sensory pathways detect ongoing immune responses; how social cues, expectations, and prior experience prepare the organism for anticipated threats; and how endocrine and autonomic circuits constrain inflammation and promote recovery. Together, these findings establish the brain as an active regulator of immunity across the full course of illness.

title: Arousal state fluctuations destabilize speech intelligibility in older adults
abstract: Understanding speech in noisy, multi-talker environments is fundamental for social communication but becomes increasingly challenging as we age. Age-related hearing loss reduces audibility and degrades speech encoding, yet these deficits do not fully explain the momentary lapses in speech understanding that frustrate real-time communication. Here, we tested whether brain state fluctuations immediately before speech onset predict forthcoming speech recognition errors in older listeners. We measured the accuracy, speed, and consistency of speech recognition in 183 adults aged 18-76 years (103 female) using a brief, trial-based multi-talker listening task while tracking pupil dynamics before and during speech presentation. Prestimulus pupil-linked arousal predicted trial-level speech recognition in older, but not younger, adults, independent of hearing status, cognitive load, and task accuracy. In adults over 50 years of age, lower and higher extremes of prestimulus pupil size were associated with less accurate and slower responses, producing a striking inverted-U relationship between prestimulus arousal and forthcoming behavioral performance. Older adults exhibited lower extremes of pupil-linked arousal that were specifically associated with greater self-reported difficulty listening in everyday life. By contrast, stimulus-evoked pupil dilation during speech encoding, a measure of listening effort, did not predict trial-level performance at any age. These findings identify prestimulus pupil-linked arousal as a hidden marker of forthcoming lapses in speech intelligibility in older adults. When considered alongside conventional measures of peripheral hearing status in mixed-effects regression models, these measures provide a more complete accounting of biological changes underlying speech intelligibility deficits that frustrate social communication in older adults .   Significance statement  As we age, following a conversation in crowded environments becomes more difficult and frustrating, even when hearing tests appear normal. This study shows that fluctuations in arousal level (measured through prestimulus pupil size) are tightly linked to fluctuations in the speed and accuracy of speech processing in adults over 50 years of age. Changes in arousal state regulation uniquely accounted for the moment-to-moment variations in speech intelligibility and were more closely associated with self-reported listening challenges than other conventional measures. These findings highlight the contribution of brain-wide arousal systems to real-world listening challenges and identify a straightforward measure that could be used to more comprehensively assess and potentially improve speech understanding in social settings.

title: Information formatting in neuronal populations predicts differential functional contributions to behavior
abstract: Neurons throughout the brain encode essentially everything, so why have distinct areas? We proposed that areas format different information sources differently, implying their computational role. Here we compared the middle temporal (MT) area, involved in visual motion perception, and the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC), implicated in decision-making and reward. In a task that required monkeys to combine motion and reward information, both regions encoded both motion and reward, but formatted differently. Area MT represented them separably, whereas the dlPFC combined them in a decision-related format. A recurrent network model trained to reproduce that formatting predicted a distinct effect of stimulating those areas. Consistent with predictions, MT stimulation biased choices whereas dlPFC stimulation produced 'winner-take-all' outcomes. Our findings suggest that a modular structure flexibly reformats information to enable complex behaviors.

title: An astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 axis promotes synapse engulfment in early amyloid pathology
abstract: Region-specific synapse loss is an early hallmark of Alzheimer's disease, yet the upstream signals that render synapses vulnerable remain unclear. In a mouse model of amyloidosis, we identify an early astrocyte state that emerges in vulnerable brain regions before widespread plaque deposition and overt gliosis. These astrocytes exhibit bulbous-looking perisynaptic processes enriched in p62 and glycogen, impaired autophagic flux and calcium signaling, and diminished astrocyte-synapse coverage. Rather than exhibiting increased synapse engulfment, bulbous astrocytes show elevated milk fat globule-epidermal growth factor 8 (MFG-E8) and are associated with increased local microglial synapse engulfment. Astrocyte-specific gain- and loss-of-function experiments demonstrate that astrocyte-derived MFG-E8 is required for microglial synapse engulfment and acts through microglial β3 integrin signaling. Astrocytic Mfge8 deletion reduces microglial engulfment and synapse loss across amyloidosis models and is associated with reduced amyloid pathology, gliosis, and cognitive impairment. Together, these findings define an astrocyte-microglia MFG-E8 signaling axis that contributes to region-specific synaptic vulnerability during early amyloid pathology.

title: Neural organoid models of human brain evolution
abstract: The human brain has structural and functional differences to our closest living relatives, the other great apes. It is thought that these differences give rise to many of the traits we associate with being human, such as our prodigious capacity to learn and be creative. However, the molecular mechanisms that underpin these differences are mostly unknown. In this review, we describe how neural organoids, an in vitro model of brain development, enable questions of human brain evolution to be functionally investigated in evolutionarily relevant developmental contexts. We discuss new insights at the genetic, cellular, and developmental scales and highlight current challenges in organoid generation, in long-term culture, and in establishing multimodal phenotypic measurements. We anticipate expanding the application of organoid models across Mammalia to help us better define species- and lineage-specific traits and improve our understanding of how complex traits emerge and evolve across developmental and evolutionary timescales.

title: Expanding the genetic landscape of moyamoya angiopathy: insights from 74 trios
abstract: Moyamoya angiopathy (MMA) is a rare cerebrovascular disorder characterized by progressive stenosis of intracranial arteries and the development of abnormal collateral vessels. While RNF213 is a major susceptibility gene in East Asian populations, the genetic architecture of MMA beyond RNF213, particularly in Europeans, remains largely undefined beyond a few known syndromic causes. We performed whole-exome sequencing on 74 sporadic MMA trios (proband and unaffected parents) of predominantly European ancestry. An additional cohort of 200 probands was screened for gene recurrence. We applied a stringent filtering strategy to identify de novo and rare inherited variants, followed by gene prioritization based on structural modeling, expression data, and biological plausibility. Gene-based burden tests were conducted against large control databases (gnomAD). We identified causative variants in 20 of the 74 probands (27%). Six probands with severe syndromic infant-onset phenotypes harbored de novo variants in the E3 ligase domain of RNF213. Fourteen probands carried a causative copy number variant (n = 3) or a short variant (n = 11) in a known MMA-associated gene (CBL, NF1, PTPN11, DIAPH1, ANO1, JAG1, NOS3, HBB). Beyond these established genes, we identified strong candidate variants in 11 probands from the discovery cohort, involving 11 novel candidate genes. Screening the additional cohort of 200 unrelated MMA probands identified recurrence of the gain-of-function SMAD4 p.Arg496Cys variant, which was de novo in the discovery-cohort proband, linking MMA to dysregulated TGF-β signaling. Other candidate findings included de novo loss-of-function variants in genes regulating epigenetic modulation and RNA splicing (SETD2, HNRNPL, UBAP2L, TOP2B, PRPF40A) and variants affecting vascular stress response (EPAS1, SVEP1, PDCD4). RNF213 was the only gene reaching exome-wide significance in burden testing (P = 2.11 × 10⁻11). This study establishes that MMA in non-East Asian populations is characterized by a strong genetic heterogeneity. These findings expand the molecular landscape of MMA and highlight the utility of trio-based sequencing for uncovering very rare molecular players in this disease. Additional analyses will now be needed to investigate the convergence of MMA pathways.

title: Subliminal beauty engages the brain's valuation circuits
abstract: Neuroeconomic models propose that the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) are key regions for computing subjective value (SV) signals that guide choice. However, the role of conscious awareness in this process remains debated. Here we examined whether SV can be automatically computed in these regions without conscious awareness. In an fMRI experiment, human participants (24 females, 5 males) viewed faces that varied in attractiveness under three conditions: (i) suppressed from awareness via continuous flash suppression (CFS), (ii) clearly visible without suppression, or (iii) absent (background only) with CFS. Participants reported trial-wise facial identity (objective) and visibility (subjective) measures of facial awareness. In a post-fMRI session, they rated the attractiveness of each face as a measure of SV. When faces were seen, task performance (d') exceeded chance and responses were faster than in absent trials. When faces were unseen, performance was at chance but responses were slower than absent trials. Neurally, seen and unseen faces elicited greater neural signal than absent trials and showed similar neural patterns in the fusiform face area (FFA). Critically, neural signal in vmPFC correlated with SV for both seen and unseen faces, with similar neural patterns. In aVS, SV-related signal was only observed for unseen faces. Furthermore, mean face-related signal in FFA correlated with SV-related signals in aVS and vmPFC for unseen faces. These findings demonstrate that SV can be automatically computed in aVS and vmPFC without conscious awareness, suggesting a neural pathway by which subliminal information can influence value-based choice. Significance statement  A central question in consciousness research and decision neuroscience is whether the brain's valuation circuitry - particularly the anterior ventral striatum (aVS) and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) - can compute subjective value automatically without conscious awareness. This question is important because prevailing accounts often assume that cognitive functions supported by the prefrontal cortex require conscious awareness of task-relevant information. Using continuous flash suppression and neuroimaging, we found that faces reported unseen nevertheless evoked value-related signals in aVS and vmPFC that scaled with subjective attractiveness ratings. These findings demonstrate that subjective value can be computed automatically from social information in the absence of conscious awareness.

title: Enhancer-targeted CRISPR-A rescues haploinsufficiency and mutant phenotypes in organoid models of autism
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a highly heritable condition with diverse clinical presentations. Approximately 15% of the genetic susceptibility of ASD is imparted by de novo haploinsufficient mutations of major effect. We mapped enhancers of two high-confidence autism genes, CHD8 and SCN2A, and used CRISPR-based gene activation targeting enhancers (eCRISPR-A) in human pluripotent stem cell (hPSC)-derived excitatory neurons and cerebral forebrain organoids to correct the effects of haploinsufficiency, taking advantage of the presence of a wild-type allele of each gene and endogenous gene regulation. Here we show that eCRISPR-A induced a sustained increase in CHD8 and SCN2A expression specifically in mutant neurons and cortical organoids, with rescue of gene expression levels and mutation-associated phenotypes, including gene expression and physiology. These data support gene activation via targeting enhancers of haploinsufficient genes as a therapeutic intervention in ASD and other neurodevelopmental disorders.

title: Brain organoids: Experimental access to human-specific brain development
abstract: Human cerebral cortical development includes species-divergent cellular programs and unusually prolonged trajectories that remain difficult to investigate experimentally. These processes support human-specific cognitive abilities and are thought to be associated with vulnerability to neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric disorders. Human brain organoids provide a tractable system for studying these processes across developmental time and under controlled perturbation. Here, we review how cortical organoids model human-specific features of progenitor biology and cell diversification, as well as progressive cellular maturation and circuit formation. We consider the limitations that constrain later-stage maturation and how approaches including the addition of missing cell types, the use of assembloids, and transplantation can extend the developmental processes accessible to study. Finally, we examine how patient-derived, isogenic, chimeric, and perturbation-based organoid systems are being used to investigate neurodevelopmental disorders and, in turn, reveal mechanisms of typical human development.

title: Unbundling the ethical and social issues in human neural organoid research
abstract: As human neural organoid research advances, some key concepts in its ethical analysis need to be unbundled to keep pace with scientific developments. These include interests involved in informed consent, distinct dimensions of consciousness and their implications for welfare, approaches to engaging public concerns, and governance and oversight of both organoids themselves and their uses.

title: Insight discordance differentiates behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia from false positives
abstract: Behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) can present with behavioural symptoms similar to psychiatric mimics of the disease (sometimes termed 'phenocopies'). Despite this overlap, loss of insight is a cardinal feature of bvFTD unlike most psychiatric disorders. This study tested whether insight could be quantified to improve diagnostic accuracy in distinguishing these conditions, and examined neuroimaging correlates of impaired insight. In this prospective cohort study, 27 patients with frontotemporal lobar degeneration (FTLD) presenting as the bvFTD phenotype and 25 false-positives of bvFTD who ultimately had a psychiatric disorder underwent patient, informant, and clinician symptom ratings on a modified Frontal Behavioural Inventory (FBI). Discrepancy scores were calculated, diagnostic discrimination was evaluated by area under the curve (AUC) with leave-one-out cross-validation, alongside a neuroimaging analysis of network-level associations of insight in bvFTD. Patients with bvFTD endorsed fewer symptoms than false-positives (FBI 6.62 ± 8.80 vs 15.36 ± 8.42, P < 0.001), whereas clinician observations were markedly greater in bvFTD (27.67 ± 8.35 vs 5.64 ± 3.85, P < 0.001). Informant ratings did not differ between groups (25.15 ± 11.11 vs 21.32 ± 12.61, P = 0.14), even though bvFTD informants had more knowledge of the disease (FTD Knowledge Scale 16.20 ± 6.68 vs 9.41 ± 8.19, P = 0.003). A model incorporating patient-clinician and informant-clinician discrepancy showed excellent cross-validated discrimination (AUC 0.99, 95% confidence interval (CI) 0.97-1.00). A model independent of expert clinician ratings, the patient-informant discrepancy, showed fair cross-validated discrimination across the full cohort (AUC 0.71, 95% CI 0.56-0.85) and good discrimination in those who did not develop another FTLD syndrome on follow-up ('pure bvFTD'; AUC 0.78, 95% CI 0.63-0.94). In bvFTD, reduced insight was associated with salience and semantic appraisal network degeneration but not control frontotemporal regions. BvFTD, false-positives, and their informants demonstrated opposing patterns of symptom endorsement. Symptom under-endorsement (lack of insight) by patients relative to clinician and informant observation supports neurodegeneration, whereas informant and patient over-endorsement without clinician-observed disturbance suggests a false-positive. Unfamiliarity with bvFTD may contribute to over-reporting. Though the clinician-dependent findings may not translate to non-expert settings, the patient-informant model retained good discrimination. Formal quantification of discrepancy patterns in behaviour may reduce misdiagnosis in bvFTD. The neuroimaging findings support salience and semantic appraisal networks as the neuroanatomical basis for insight in bvFTD. Future studies should validate the FBI clinician version and examine factors underlying over-reporting by false-positives and their informants.

title: Btbd11 regulates glutamatergic synapse organization in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons
abstract: The mechanisms that underlie glutamatergic synapse organization and function in GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) are not well described, despite evidence that impaired glutamatergic excitation of INs is implicated in psychiatric disorders such as schizophrenia and anxiety. Glutamatergic synapses received by INs have unique basal transmission properties and exhibit distinct synaptic plasticity compared to those received by excitatory neurons, likely due to cell-type specific differences in postsynaptic density (PSD) composition and maintenance mechanisms. In the present study, we show that the interneuron-specific protein Btbd11 regulates excitatory synapse transmission in mixed-sex primary cultured rat and mouse hippocampal interneurons through promotion of phase separation and support of postsynaptic nanoarchitecture. Btbd11 forms a phase separated protein complex with Psd-95 and TARPγ2 and impacts the stability of TARPγ2 and GluA1 within glutamatergic IN synapses in an expression- and phase separation-dependent manner. Using super resolution imaging, we show that Btbd11 displays nanoscale clustering properties within IN synapses that correlate with Psd-95 nanostructure. Furthermore, genetic deletion of Btbd11 decreases PSD protein expression, reduces synapse size, and disrupts Psd-95 nanocluster organization. These effects manifest as a drastic reduction in glutamatergic synaptic transmission onto INs when Btbd11 is deleted. Together, these data provide insights into a novel cell type-specific synaptic regulatory mechanism in an understudied synapse population. Significance Statement  Although glutamatergic excitation of GABAergic inhibitory interneurons (INs) is essential for maintenance of balanced signaling in the brain and dysregulation has been linked to neuropsychiatric disorders, the molecular mechanisms underlying IN-specific glutamatergic transmission are not well characterized. Using protein modeling, molecular biology, live-cell and super-resolution imaging, we describe a unique mechanism of glutamatergic synapse organization in INs by Btbd11, an IN-specific synaptic protein. Btbd11 promotes liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) and regulates PSD protein mobility, the abundance of key synaptic proteins, and nanoscale synaptic organization. Collectively, this is critical for glutamatergic synaptic transmission within INs. Understanding Btbd11's role at the synapse highlights the importance of synaptic LLPS, providing insight into the regulatory mechanisms in an understudied synapse with psychiatric disease relevance.

title: Guided self-help for depression adapted for autistic adults: a multi-centre randomised controlled phase 3 trial (ADEPT-2)
abstract: Introduction Autistic people are disproportionately affected by depression and access recommended first line treatments such as Guided Self-Help (GSH)) which has not been developed to meet their needs. This study aims to test the effectiveness of autism adapted GSH for depression compared to treatment as usual. Methods A two parallel group multi-centre randomised controlled trial investigated the effectiveness of GSH adapted for autism. The RCT was registered on 09th August 2022 (ISRCTN: 17547011). Adults, ≥18 years, with a confirmed autism diagnosis and symptoms of depression (PHQ-9 ≥ 10) recruited from community settings were randomised to GSH or Treatment as Usual (TAU). Adapted GSH comprised psychoeducation and behavioural activation supported by nine meetings with a coach. Beck Depression Inventory (BDI-II) scores at 16-weeks post-randomisation were analysed on an intention to treat basis. Additional measures at 16-weeks captured anxiety, well-being and service use with follow up at 32- and 52-weeks. Results Participants (n=266) were randomised to GSH (n=132) or TAU (n=134). Of participants randomised to GSH, 110 (81%) completed the minimum 6 session dose, five did not begin the intervention and 28 discontinued. Estimated between group mean difference in BDI-II scores at 16 weeks was -5.05 (95% CI: -7.85 to -2.24, P<0.001, d=0.47) in favour of GSH, with the difference sustained at 52-weeks. Conclusion The intervention named Autism Affirming Accompanied Self-Help for depression (AASH-DEP) needs to be rolled-out so clinicians and autistic people can be confident to access effective treatment for depression adapted for autism.

title: Evaluation of low-intensity, family-based behavioral treatments for youth with anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders
abstract:
OBJECTIVE: To examine the efficacy of two different low-intensity, family-based treatments (internet-based, therapist assisted CBT and parent training) relative to relaxation and mentorship training (RMT) for youth with anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders (OCD).

METHOD: 151 youth (age 7-13 years) with anxiety or OCD and their parent/caregiver were randomized to receive four telehealth sessions of either an internet-based, therapist-assisted CBT protocolknown as Learning to Understand and Navigate Anxiety (LUNA), parent training with bibliotherapy (SPACE-Light), or RMT over 12 weeks. Participants were assessed by blinded raters at baseline, post-treatment, and one-month follow-up.

RESULTS: Across measures, participants in all three treatment arms showed significant improvements from baseline to post-treatment and one-month follow-up on continuous outcomes. Clinician-rated outcomes indicated greater improvement forLUNA relative to parent training and RMT, particularly at follow-up. Differences in continuous outcomes between treatments were less consistent for child- and parent-reported outcomes, though still favored LUNA. Rates of treatment response and remission from all anxiety disorders were higher in LUNA relative to parent training and RMT in completer-only analyses, but not in intent-to-treat analyses. Dropout rates did not differ significantly between treatment arms.

CONCLUSION: A low-intensity internet-based, therapist-assisted cognitive behavioral therapy protocol demonstrated significant benefits for youth with anxiety and/or OCD, outperformed low-intensity parent training and relaxation approaches which were also effective.
