title: Online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy for people with multiple sclerosis with mild-to-moderate depression- protocol for a type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT) is an effective treatment for recurrent depression in the general population and is recommended in clinical guidelines for those with mild-moderate depression. However, the effectiveness of MBCT in people with multiple sclerosis (PwMS) with mild to moderate depression is unknown. Further, how best to tailor and implement MBCT for PwMS is largely unstudied. This manuscript describes the study protocol for a hybrid-effectiveness study to evaluate online MBCT tailored for PwMS.

METHODS: This type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation study will employ an embedded mixed methods experimental design. Quantitative findings will be collected through a powered waitlist randomized controlled trial examining online MBCT in a minimum of 152 PwMS with case-ness of mild-moderate depression (Clinical Trials Gov #NCT07742579). The intervention will consist of an online 8-week MBCT course with weekly sessions conducted by qualified mindfulness instructors experienced int the care of PwMS. Questionnaires will be collected at baseline, post-intervention, and 3 months later. The primary outcome will be depression, measured using the Hospital Anxiety and Depression Score - Depression (HADS-D). An intention-to-treat analysis will be conducted. Qualitative findings will be collected through semi-structured interviews with 30-40 MBCT participants, HCPs, MBCT instructors, and MS decision makers. Thematic analyses will be used to analyze interview data. The RE-AIM PRISM tool will be used to evaluate implementation and mixed data assessed in a joint display.

CONCLUSION: The results from this study will provide evidence regarding the effectiveness of online MBCT in PwMS with mild to moderate depression, recommendations for intervention tailoring and implementation. Findings will be disseminated through traditional and novel, creative knowledge mobilization methods.

title: Effects of acceptance and commitment therapy on psychological and health-related outcomes in stroke patients: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract:
Background Stroke is a leading cause of disability worldwide and is frequently accompanied by psychological and functional impairments. Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT), a third-wave behavioral intervention focusing on psychological flexibility, has been increasingly applied in stroke rehabilitation. Although previous reviews have suggested beneficial effects of ACT in stroke patients, whether these benefits persist in the short term after the intervention ends, and the certainty of the evidence, remain unclear. Methods A systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted according to PRISMA guidelines and registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261325108). Randomized controlled trials evaluating ACT in stroke patients were included. Pooled effects were calculated using random-effects models, with separate analyses for post-intervention and follow-up outcomes. Sources of heterogeneity were explored using subgroup analyses and meta-regression. Risk of bias was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 tool, and certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework. Results Twenty-two RCTs involving 1,975 participants were included. ACT may be associated with reductions in depressive symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = −1.32, 95% CI: −1.80 to −0.84; follow-up: SMD = −0.76, 95% CI: −1.07 to −0.45) and anxiety symptoms (post-intervention: SMD = −1.36, 95% CI: −1.90 to −0.82; follow-up: SMD = −0.51, 95% CI: −1.42 to 0.40, not significant); depressive symptoms remained statistically significant at follow-up. Heterogeneity was considerable for both outcomes at post-intervention ( I 2 = 93.68% for depression and 93.60% for anxiety), so the pooled estimates represent average effects across studies. ACT may also be associated with improvements in psychological flexibility, quality of life, and sleep quality; however, these outcomes were based on a limited number of studies and showed considerable heterogeneity ( I 2 = 74.68 to 92.26%), so they should be interpreted cautiously. However, no statistically significant effects were observed for activities of daily living, neurological function, or hope. ACT did not appear to increase dropout rates in the available studies ( K = 16; RR = 0.99, 95% CI: 0.58–1.69). Meta-regression analyses indicated that intervention duration may not be a significant moderator of treatment effects. The certainty of evidence ranged from very low to moderate, mainly due to risk of bias and inconsistency. Conclusion Acceptance and Commitment Therapy may be a useful adjunctive intervention for improving psychological outcomes in people with stroke. However, evidence for functional recovery remains insufficient. Future high-quality RCTs with standardized protocols, larger samples, and longer follow-up are needed to confirm the long-term effectiveness of ACT. Systematic review registration https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/ , identifer CRD420261325108.

1 Background Stroke is defined as a sudden onset of focal neurological deficit lasting ≥24 h or associated with acute brain imaging evidence of infarction or hemorrhage ( 1 ). Stroke is a leading cause of death and disability worldwide ( 1 ). Many survivors are left with persistent disability: in a large cohort of patients with ischemic stroke, approximately 40% had moderate-to-severe or persistent severe disability during the first year ( 2 ). Post-stroke depression affects roughly 10–35% of patients during the first 3 months ( 3 ), and anxiety affects about one in four patients when assessed with rating scales ( 4 ); anxiety after stroke has been described as the “other” poststroke mood disorder ( 5 ). Depression is associated with poorer functional outcomes over the first 5 ears after stroke ( 3 ), and at 6 months, with cognitive impairment ( 6 ). These symptoms are often not transient: long-term cohort data show that a considerable proportion of survivors still report elevated depressive and anxiety symptoms several years after stroke, and that these rates are relatively stable over time ( 7 ). Current management of post-stroke psychological distress relies mainly on pharmacological treatment and general psychosocial or rehabilitation support. Antidepressants are widely prescribed, but a Cochrane review found that the evidence for pharmacological and psychological interventions for depression after stroke is of very low certainty, and that antidepressants were associated with adverse events involving the central nervous system and the gastrointestinal tract ( 8 ). At present, traditional intervention methods such as cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) have been shown to reduce depressive and anxiety symptoms after stroke, with large effects at the end of treatment and moderate maintenance at 3 months, although the evidence comes from a small number of generally small studies ( 9 ). Psychological treatment is recommended in stroke care ( 10 ). Acceptance and Commitment Therapy (ACT) is the third wave of behavioral intervention, and it has gained increasing attention due to its focus on psychological flexibility ( 11 ). ACT emphasizes psychological flexibility, helping individuals accept distressing experiences and engage in value-based behaviors despite ongoing health challenges. This approach may be particularly relevant for stroke survivors who face persistent functional limitations and emotional distress during recovery ( 11 ). Rather than attempting to reduce or control distressing thoughts and feelings, ACT seeks to increase psychological flexibility — the capacity to remain in contact with the present moment and to persist in, or adjust, behavior in the service of personally meaningful values — through acceptance, cognitive defusion, and committed action ( 11 ). This process-oriented approach may be particularly relevant after stroke, where disability and uncertainty about recovery are often not modifiable: cognitive fusion has been found to predict depressive symptoms and to mediate the association between psychological flexibility and depression, suggesting that cognitive defusion may be a relevant treatment target ( 12 ). Previous evidence has primarily focused on immediate post-intervention outcomes, while the durability of ACT effects after intervention remains unclear ( 13 ). A recent systematic review and meta-analysis reported that ACT improved depression, anxiety, and quality of life in stroke patients ( 13 ). Evidence from other populations is mixed: a randomized trial in people with acquired brain injury found no superiority of ACT over an active control on the primary outcomes, although more participants showed long-term, individual-level improvement in depressive and anxiety symptoms ( 14 ); benefits have been reported in older adults with chronic low back pain ( 15 ) and in people with type 2 diabetes ( 16 ), and internet-delivered ACT has been associated with reduced anxiety ( 17 ). Whether the benefits of ACT are maintained after the intervention ends, and which outcomes and patient groups respond most consistently, therefore remain unclear. To address these uncertainties, this systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to provide an updated and comprehensive evaluation of ACT in stroke patients. Specifically, we evaluated the effects of ACT on psychological outcomes (depression, anxiety, and ACT-related psychological processes, including psychological flexibility and cognitive fusion), clinical outcomes (quality of life, sleep quality, activities of daily living, and neurological function), and all-cause attrition (used as an indirect indicator of participant retention rather than as a direct measure of acceptability). We also examined whether the effects of ACT were maintained at follow-up, explored potential sources of heterogeneity through subgroup analyses and meta-regression, and assessed the certainty of evidence using the GRADE framework. By integrating updated evidence from randomized controlled trials, this review aims to clarify the role of ACT in stroke rehabilitation and to inform future clinical practice and research. 2 Methods This meta-analysis followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The study protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420261325108) on 24 February 2026, and the PRISMA checklist is provided in Appendix 1 . No amendments were made to the eligibility criteria or primary outcomes; the final search was updated to 6 March 2026 to ensure coverage of the most recent literature. 2.1 Search strategy We conducted a comprehensive literature search across eight English-language databases (PubMed, MEDLINE [via Ovid], Embase [via Ovid], Cochrane Library, CINAHL, Web of Science, Scopus, and PsycINFO) and four Chinese databases (CNKI, Wanfang, SinoMed, VIP) from their inception to March 6, 2026. Reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were manually examined, and the Journal of Contextual Behavioral Science was screened for additional eligible RCTs. The search combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) with free-text terms, including “Acceptance and Commitment Therapy,” “stroke,” “Apoplexy,” and “Cerebrovascular Accident*.” Detailed search strategies for each database are included in Appendix 2 . 2.2 Eligibility criteria Selection of studies was based on the PICOS framework. Participants (P): Adults diagnosed with stroke (ischemic or hemorrhagic). Interventions (I): ACT-based interventions delivered in any format (face-to-face, group, tele-rehabilitation, or online). An intervention was classified as ACT-based if the authors explicitly described it as ACT and it was delivered as a structured program following the six core ACT processes by a named facilitator; single-technique or generic third wave/mindfulness interventions without an explicit ACT rationale were excluded. Comparisons (C): Conventional care without ACT, including medical treatment, routine nursing, traditional psychotherapy, rehabilitation training, health education, or other standard care. Outcomes (O): Primary: Depression and anxiety. Secondary: Psychological processes (psychological flexibility, cognitive fusion), clinical outcomes (quality of life, sleep quality, activities of daily living, neurological function), and positive psychological resources (self-efficacy, hope, and resilience). Attrition: dropout rates. Only outcomes measured with validated instruments (e.g., PHQ-9, HADS, AAQ-II, SS-QOL, PSQI, and BI) were considered. Study Design (S): Randomized controlled trials (RCTs). For studies with multiple reports, the publication with the most complete dataset or largest sample size was selected. Outcomes were classified as post-intervention or follow-up, with separate meta-analyses performed for each time point to evaluate the durability of ACT effects. 2.3 Study selection and data extraction Records were imported into NoteExpress 2018, and duplicates removed (Y’E). Two independent reviewers (XH and WJ) screened titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of potentially relevant articles. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (GY). Data extraction employed a structured form capturing authorship, publication year, sample size, stroke subtype, intervention and control details, and outcome measures. Inter-rater agreement was quantified using Cohen’s kappa coefficient. Medians and interquartile ranges were transformed into means and standard deviations using published methods ( 18 ). For studies with missing or unclear information, attempts were made to contact the original authors. All outcome measures were harmonized prior to analysis to ensure consistency across studies. 2.4 Risk of bias assessment The Cochrane Risk of Bias tool version 2 (RoB 2) was used to evaluate methodological quality. Two reviewers (XH and WJ) independently assessed five domains: (1) randomization process, (2) deviations from intended interventions, (3) missing outcome data, (4) outcome measurement, and (5) selection of reported results. Each study was rated as low risk, some concerns, or high risk of bias. Discrepancies were resolved via discussion or consultation with a third reviewer (GY). Inter-rater reliability was determined using Cohen’s kappa coefficient. For Domain 5, as no trial had a publicly available protocol, reported outcomes were compared with each paper’s own Methods; absence of registration alone was not sufficient for high risk. Overall risk of bias was rated high only when at least one domain was rated high risk. 2.5 Data synthesis and statistical analysis 2.5.1 Effect size and statistical model Meta-analyses were conducted using Stata 18.0. Continuous outcomes were analyzed using mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs), depending on measurement consistency. Dichotomous outcomes, including dropout, were analyzed using relative risks (RRs) with 95% CIs. Effect sizes were interpreted according to Cohen’s criteria (0.2 = small, 0.5 = medium, 0.8 = large). A random-effects model with the DerSimonian-Lairdτ 2 estimator was applied for pooled estimates; meta-regression and trim-and-fill used restricted maximum likelihood (REML). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 (two-sided). In this review, short-term follow-up was defined as outcome assessment performed within 3 months after the end of the intervention. Post-intervention and follow-up outcomes were analyzed separately. Meta-regression was restricted to outcomes with at least 10 studies per covariate; depression ( K = 13) and anxiety ( K = 10) met this criterion, while the AAQ-II model ( K = 7) was exploratory only. 2.5.2 Heterogeneity, subgroup, and sensitivity analyses Heterogeneity was evaluated using Cochran’s Q test and the I 2 statistic, interpreted as low (25%), moderate (50%), or high (75%). Q test significance was set at p < 0.10. Subgroup analyses and meta-regression analyses were conducted, when sufficient data were available, to explore potential sources of heterogeneity. Subgroup analyses were performed for predefined variables, with between-subgroup differences tested by Cochran’s Q; strata containing a single study were reported descriptively only. Intervention duration was entered as a raw continuous covariate (in weeks), without centering or standardization. Sensitivity analyses employed a leave-one-out approach to assess the robustness of the pooled estimates. 2.5.3 Publication bias and certainty of evidence Publication bias was assessed using funnel plots and Egger’s regression test for outcomes with ≥10 studies. A two-sided p < 0.1 indicated potential bias. When publication bias was suggested, the trim-and-fill method was additionally applied to examine the potential impact of missing studies on pooled estimates. The certainty of evidence for key outcomes was evaluated using the GRADE framework and summarized in a Summary of Findings table. 3 Results 3.1 Study selection

title: Efficacy of Digital Health Interventions for Insomnia: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Insomnia is common, and treatments are limited by tolerability and access. Digital health interventions (DHIs) are increasingly used for sleep management, but evidence comparing multiple outcomes is scarce.

OBJECTIVE: This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of DHIs on 8 sleep outcomes, including insomnia severity, sleep efficiency, total sleep time, and sleep quality.

METHODS: We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Scopus, CINAHL, CNKI, CBM, VIP, Wanfang, ClinicalTrials.gov, and the American Academy of Sleep Medicine's website from inception to July 2026. Two reviewers (SG and BZ) independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2.0 tool. We included randomized controlled trials or controlled clinical trials comparing DHIs with any control in insomnia, without language restriction, and excluded experimental sleep deprivation, conference abstracts, protocols, and nonrandomized or noncontrolled designs. Pooled standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% CIs used restricted maximum likelihood with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman correction; 95% prediction intervals (PIs) used the Nagashima method. We also performed subgroup analyses by intervention category, comparator type, diagnostic criteria, and country income, plus sensitivity analyses, Egger tests, and GRADE (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation) assessment.

RESULTS: We included 44 randomized controlled trials (n=10,521) published between 2004 and 2026 across 14 countries. DHIs significantly improved insomnia severity (SMD -0.91, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.70), sleep efficiency (SMD 0.59, 95% CI 0.45-0.72), total sleep time (SMD 0.20, 95% CI 0.11-0.29), sleep quality (SMD -0.61, 95% CI -0.78 to -0.45), and secondary outcomes (SMDs -0.37 to -0.64). However, 95% PIs crossed the null for insomnia severity (-2.04 to 0.22), total sleep time (-0.05 to 0.46), and all secondary outcomes. Subgroup analyses showed larger insomnia severity effects in high- versus upper-middle-income countries, modality differences for sleep efficiency, and comparator-type differences for total sleep time (all  P <.01). Egger tests suggested small-study effects; sensitivity analyses did not change direction or significance. GRADE certainty ranged from very low to moderate.

CONCLUSIONS: Although DHIs showed statistically significant average effects on multiple sleep outcomes, wide PIs crossing or approaching the null, effects approaching or below Minimum Clinically Important Difference thresholds, and very low-to-moderate GRADE certainty indicate that the evidence remains exploratory. Subgroup analyses revealed effect modifications by country income, intervention modality, and comparator type, underscoring contextual factors. Unlike previous reviews focusing on single DHI formats or average statistical effects, this review provides stratified comparisons and integrates PIs and Minimum Clinically Important Difference conversion to distinguish statistical significance from clinical relevance. This paper provides an evidence synthesis framework showing that DHI benefits are context-dependent and insufficient for a standard clinical role. In practice, DHIs cannot be recommended as a standard substitute for face-to-face cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia, although they may serve as a low-intensity option in stepped care. Large-scale, head-to-head implementation trials in diverse populations with extended follow-up are needed to define their optimal role.

title: Outcomes from a Pilot Trial of a Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) Tobacco Cessation Intervention for Veterans at Heightened Risk for Suicide
abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Tobacco use has consistently been linked to suicide risk, and some data suggest that tobacco cessation may reduce risk. However, higher risk individuals are typically excluded from clinical trials. Dialectical Behavior Therapy is a psychotherapy approach originally designed to reduce suicide risk that may also be beneficial in treating addiction by enhancing emotion regulation and distress tolerance skills.

METHODS: The present study was a randomized pilot trial comparing a standard tobacco cessation intervention to a DBT-based integrated intervention for tobacco cessation and suicide prevention. Veterans (n = 68) who were daily users of cigarettes and/or e-cigarettes were randomized to DBT for cessation (DBT-C) or to treatment as usual (TAU). Participants in both conditions attended 12 weekly group psychotherapy sessions and were followed for a total of 24 weeks to evaluate changes in tobacco use, suicidality, emotion regulation and overall satisfaction with the intervention.

RESULTS: DBT-C and TAU participants did not differ in terms of abstinence at end-of-treatment or 24-week follow-up. There was a trend toward greater improvement in emotion regulation in DBT-C versus TAU. Participants generally were satisfied with the intervention.

CONCLUSIONS: This pilot trial provides preliminary evidence that individuals who use tobacco and are at elevated suicide risk can be effectively engaged in tobacco cessation interventions, and that such interventions may benefit emotional functioning as well as reducing tobacco use. DBT-C appears to be a potentially effective approach but additional, larger-scale research is needed to enable a more thorough assessment.

title: Theoretical frameworks of extended reality interventions for eating and weight disorders and beyond: A systematic umbrella review
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Extended reality (XR) is increasingly used in mental health treatment, including eating and weight disorders (EWD), due to its potential to target disorder-relevant mechanisms in immersive environments. This umbrella review synthesizes theoretical frameworks guiding XR-based psychotherapeutic applications. Our findings have also implications for other mental health disorders as they provide a framework on transdiagnostic mechanisms of XR-based interventions.

METHODS: Systematic searches of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Cochrane identified 44 review articles on XR-based psychotherapeutic interventions in EWD, including systematic and non-systematic reviews. Methodological quality was assessed using AMSTAR 2 and SANRA. The umbrella review was conducted and reported in accordance with PRISMA 20 guidelines.

RESULTS: The majority of reviews (n = 37) reported underlying theoretical frameworks with varying depth and quality. Our synthesis organizes these into a two-level taxonomy comprising first-order therapeutic mechanisms (behavioral, intersectional, and cognitive) and second-order XR-specific modulators (presence, embodiment, and the Proteus Effect).

CONCLUSIONS: XR appears to enhance established psychological mechanisms rather than generate novel therapeutic processes. A mechanism-oriented framework separating therapeutic mechanisms from XR-specific modulators may guide the development of more targeted and clinically precise XR interventions. Further experimental research is needed to validate mechanisms of action and optimize XR applications in EWD and beyond.

title: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy to Optimize Post-Operative Fracture Recovery (COPE): a randomized controlled trial
abstract:
Background: Persistent pain after extremity fracture requiring surgical repair is common and associated with long-term morbidity. We sought to determine whether app-based cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) reduces persistent postsurgical pain after fracture repair. Methods: We performed a randomized controlled trial of adults from 11 American and Canadian hospitals with an extremity fracture treated with internal fixation. We allocated participants 1:1 to an app-based CBT program or usual care, and followed them at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months post-fracture. Our primary outcome was moderate-to-severe persistent post-surgical pain. We constructed a mixed-effects log-binomial model to explore the effect of CBT versus usual care on moderate-to-severe persistent post-surgical pain over 12 months postfracture. Results: We randomized 1009 participants to app-based CBT ( n = 506) or usual care ( n = 503). The mean age of participants was 44.5 years, and 129 (12.8%) presented with an open fracture. Adherence to CBT was modest, with 237/506 patients (46.8%) completing all 7 modules. App-based CBT, compared with usual care, did not reduce the risk of persistent postsurgical pain over 12 months postfracture (30.8% v. 30.3%, adjusted relative risk 1.02, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.89 to 1.16). The 365-day probability of returning to leisure activities without restrictions was 29.0% in the intervention group and 22.4% in the control group (hazard ratio 1.33, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.77). The other secondary outcomes showed no significant differences between treatments. Interpretation: Among adults with an operatively managed extremity fracture, app-based CBT did not reduce the risk of persistent postsurgical pain over 12 months. Future research is warranted to develop more effective CBT approaches for adults with extremity fractures and to evaluate alternative supportive interventions that may be more acceptable to patients with fracture. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov , NCT04274530

The Global Burden of Disease Fracture Collaborators estimated that in 2019, there were 178 million new fractures worldwide. 1 Lower-limb fractures were most common and burdensome, 1 and chronic pain is frequently reported after these injuries. A systematic review of 20 observational studies (1460 patients) found that among patients with tibial fractures, the mean incidence of persistent postsurgical pain was 47% at an average of 24 months after surgery. 2 A subsequent study of 1560 patients with surgically managed upper- and lower-extremity open fractures found that 67% reported moderate-to-severe persistent post-surgical pain at 1 year. 3 Higher somatic preoccupation and poor coping in the acute postoperative period is strongly associated with persistent postsurgical pain, functional limitations, unemployment, and reduced quality of life 1 year after surgery. 3 – 5 Psychological interventions designed to modify unhelpful beliefs and behaviours have the potential to reduce persistent postsurgical pain among trauma patients. A meta-analysis of 15 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) on heterogeneous groups of patients undergoing orthopedic surgery, coronary artery bypass graft, or colonic and colorectal cancer surgery found moderate-certainty evidence that perioperative psychotherapy reduced the severity of persistent pain and improved physical functioning. 6 The study could not, however, confidently address possible population or intervention subgroup differences, 7 and a subsequent trial of 325 patients with traumatic extremity fractures, randomized to receive telephone-delivered cognitive behavioural–based physical therapy versus education, found no differences in physical function, pain interference, pain intensity, or quality of life at 12 months. 8 The objective of the Cognitive Behavioural Therapy to Optimize Post-Operative Fracture Recovery (COPE) trial was to assess the effectiveness of an app-based cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) program for reducing persistent postsurgical pain and impairment among patients with surgically managed extremity fractures, as compared with usual care. Methods Study design This multicentre, randomized, parallel group trial was conducted at 11 academic trauma centres in the United States and Canada between January 2021 and July 2025. The definitive trial was preceded by a pilot trial at 1 centre that enrolled 90 patients. 9 There were no major protocol changes after the pilot, and the 90 participants were included in the definitive trial. Our trial protocol was published 10 and registered on ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT04274530 ; Feb. 25, 2020). This article adheres to the Consolidated Standards of Reporting Trials 2025 statement. 11 Trial oversight The COPE trial was funded by the Canadian Institutes of Health Research, the Orthopaedic Trauma Association, and the Michael G. DeGroote Institute for Pain Research and Care. TELUS Health (formerly LifeWorks; www.telus.com/en/health ), a private health care company, provided the app-based CBT. Neither the funding sources nor TELUS Health had any role in trial design or conduct; the collection, management, analysis, or interpretation of data; or the preparation, review, or approval of this manuscript. The Methods Centre, located at McMaster University, coordinated the trial and was responsible for randomization, data management, data analysis, and clinical site coordination. The steering committee designed the trial and the prespecified statistical analysis plan. Participants The study team enrolled skeletally mature adults (aged ≥ 18 yr), who presented within 2 to 12 weeks of an extremity fracture requiring internal fixation, were willing and able to participate in an app-based, English-language CBT program, and provided written informed consent. Key exclusion criteria included fragility or stress fractures, not experiencing any pain in the fracture region at the time of patient screening, concomitant injuries likely to impair function for as long or longer than the eligible extremity fracture, active psychosis, suicidality, substance use disorder, current participation in psychotherapy, or a high likelihood of loss to follow-up. 10 In cases of patients who had been randomized but were suspected of being ineligible, a central adjudication committee, composed of an orthopedic trauma surgeon and a psychologist blind to treatment allocation, independently evaluated patient eligibility. All baseline demographic information, including ethnicity, was by participant self-report. Specifically, participants were asked to select from the following fixed categories when reporting ethnicity: White, South Asian, East Asian, Middle Eastern, African or Caribbean, Indigenous, Other, and Prefer Not to Answer. Participants who selected “Other” were able to further specify their ethnicity within an open-ended text-box response option. Participants were also asked to specify if they were a first responder from the following response options: police officer, firefighter, emergency medical technician, paramedic, and search and rescue personnel. Randomization Concealed randomization via the REDCap Cloud randomization function was stratified by clinical site, sex, at least 1 open fracture versus no open fracture(s), and greater versus lesser illness beliefs (Somatic Pre-Occupation and Coping [SPOC] score ≥ 48 v. < 48) 4 with randomly varied block sizes of 6 or 8. It was not feasible to blind participants or study personnel. Intervention Participants randomized to the treatment group were given access to an app-based CBT program provided by TELUS Health, available on any Internet-enabled device. 12 Members of our study team that led the development of the CBT modules included 3 board-certified, PhD-level psychologists (R.E.M., M.N., E.G.H.) with 5 to 30 years’ clinical training and research experience in CBT and pain management, and certified in CBT by their national credentialling body. A detailed description of the CBT program curriculum can be found in Appendix 1, Supplementary Table 1 (available at www.cmaj.ca/lookup/doi/10.1503/cmaj.260090/tab-related-content ). The program consisted of 7 self-directed learning modules, each requiring approximately 1 hour to complete, focused on addressing maladaptive beliefs related to pain and recovery, as well as practical strategies to enhance coping and management of pain. Participants allocated to CBT scheduled a telephone call with a licensed therapist who introduced the program. Participants completed modules independently and submitted homework through the application. Their therapist reviewed the homework and provided direction and support via in-app messaging. At the discretion of their attending trauma fellowship-trained surgeon, all participants received standard postsurgical pain management (“usual care”) for their fracture that was generally consistent across sites, including pain medication and referrals to physiotherapy. Outcomes The research team collected outcome data at 3, 6, 9, and 12 months postfracture in clinic, by telephone, or through a secure electronic method. Our primary outcome was patient-reported moderate-to-severe persistent postsurgical pain, defined by the World Health Organization (WHO) as pain that develops or increases in intensity after surgery; persisting for at least 3 months after the initiating event; and not better explained by an infection, malignancy, pre-existing pain condition, or an alternative cause. 13 To meet the criteria for moderate-to-severe persistent postsurgical pain, participants were required to report a score of 4 or higher on a 0- to 10-cm visual analogue scale (VAS) for pain. 14 Secondary outcomes included scores on the 36-Item Short Form Health Survey (SF-36) physical component summary (PCS) and mental component summary (MCS); return to work without limitations among people who were employed before injury; return to household activities without limitations; return to at least 80% of function from before injury; return to leisure activities without limitations; pain severity and pain interference measured by the Brief Pain Inventory–Short Form (BPI-SF) over 12 months postfracture; and the proportion of patients using opioid class medications at 6 and 12 months postfracture. We transformed the SF-36 PCS and MCS scores to a scale ranging from 0 to 100, with 100 representing the highest level of functioning. 15 , 16 Participants indicated their overall level of function at each follow-up visit on a scale from 0% (no ability to function) to 100% (their level of functioning before injury). The BPI-SF average pain severity score averages the scores of four 0- to 10-point numeric rating subscales for “average,” “least,” and “worst” pain severity in the past 24 hours, as well as pain severity “now” (0 = no pain, 10 = pain as bad as you can imagine). The BPI-SF pain interference score uses 7 subscales to measure the degree to which pain interferes with general activity, mood, walking, work, relationships, sleep, and enjoyment of life (NRS for each item; 0 = does not interfere, 10 = completely interferes). A total interference score is calculated by summing these 7 items. Sample size We based the sample size calculation on detecting a 20% relative risk reduction in the prevalence of moderate-to-severe persistent postsurgical pain over 12 months with CBT compared with usual care. We selected a control group event rate of 50% 2 , 3 and a relative risk reduction of 20% with CBT, 6 and our sample size was estimated at 408 per arm. To account for an estimated 20% loss to follow-up, we increased our sample size to 500 participants per arm. Statistical analyses Before any analyses, the study team published a statistical analysis plan on ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT04274530 ). Our primary analyses followed the intention-to-treat principle by analyzing all patients according to the group to which they were allocated. All participants without complete follow-up data were censored at their last follow-up. We used multiple imputation to address missing observations in all analyses unless otherwise specified. The multiple imputation approach relies on the missing-at-random assumption, given that treatment allocation was randomized and loss to follow-up was not known to be related to unobserved outcome values. We conducted data analyses using R (version 4.4.3 or newer, R Foundation for Statistical Computing) with a threshold p of 0.05 or less. We constructed a mixed-effects log-binomial model to explore the effect of CBT versus usual care on moderate-to-severe persistent postsurgical pain over 12 months postfracture. This outcome was recorded at each of the trial time points (3 mo, 6 mo, 9 mo, and 12 mo postfracture). Treatment allocation, time of assessment, the interaction between time and treatment, and stratification variables were included in the models as fixed effects with participants entered as a random intercept. We obtained adjusted percentages from marginal predicted probabilities derived from mixed-effects log-binomial models. We calculated the resulting adjusted percentages from the 12-month observed data alone but estimated them from a longitudinal mixed-effects model informed by all repeated observations. We used linear repeated-measures mixed modelling to assess the effect of CBT versus usual care on SF-36 PCS and SF-36 MCS scores over 12 months, including time of assessment, the interaction between time and treatment, baseline SF-36 scores (PCS or MCS, depending on the model), and stratification variables as fixed effects, with participants entered as a random intercept. We constructed cumulative logit models to investigate the effect of CBT versus usual care on BPI-SF average pain severity scores and total pain interference scores over 12 months, including time of assessment, the interaction between time and treatment, baseline BPI-SF scores (pain or pain interference, depending on the model), and stratification variables as fixed effects, with participants entered as a random intercept. Return to function analyses included time to return to work without restrictions, time to return to household duties without restrictions, time to return to at least 80% of overall function before injury, and time to return to leisure activities without restrictions, using Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for our stratification variables. The proportional hazards assumption was tested and met using Schoenfeld residuals, both graphically and via statistical testing. We asked participants the following prompt regarding overall function before injury: “Please indicate on a scale of 0% to 100% what your overall level of functioning is, with 0% representing no ability to function and 100% representing the level of functioning before your injury.” Participants who self-reported an overall functioning of 80% or higher of their overall function before injury were coded as an event within the time-to-event analyses.

title: Music-based interventions for acute and short-term anxiety in nursing students: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
Background Nursing students encounter acute anxiety during examinations, simulations, clinical skills training, and other health-related student contexts. We evaluated music-based interventions, with acute or short-term self-reported anxiety as the principal outcome and other psychological, physiological, health, and educational outcomes as secondary domains. Methods Following peer review, we repeated searches in PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL Complete, Embase, APA PsycINFO, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Web of Science Core Collection, and ClinicalTrials.gov from their inception to 19 September 2026, without outcome, study design, publication type, or language limits. Two reviewers independently screened, extracted, and assessed the risk of bias. The principal meta-analysis used a uniform post-intervention Hedges’ g from each eligible, individually randomized parallel-group trial. Random-effects models were estimated using Restricted Maximum Likelihood or Residual Maximum Likelihood (REML); Wald confidence intervals were the primary estimate, and Hartung–Knapp and prediction intervals were used to assess small-sample uncertainty. Results Of the 737 records identified, 337 duplicates were removed, and 400 records were screened. A total of 64 reports were sought; 39 unique complete documents were assessed; 26 reports representing 24 studies were included; and 13 full-text reports were excluded. Twenty studies were randomized, and four were non-randomized. Nine parallel-group trials (650 participants) contributed to the principal anxiety synthesis ( g = −0.31, 95% confidence interval (CI): −0.58 to −0.04; p = 0.024; I 2 = 64%; τ 2 = 0.107). The Hartung–Knapp interval (from −0.63 to 0.01; p = 0.055) and the 95% prediction interval (from −1.15 to 0.53) crossed zero. All nine principal trials were at high overall risk of bias, and certainty was very low. Conclusion Music-based interventions may reduce acute or short-term self-reported anxiety on average. However, the results are sensitive to the method used to quantify uncertainty, and the effects are likely to vary across settings. Evidence is insufficient to infer sustained psychological benefits, improved learning, or support for routine implementation. Systematic review registration The review was registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251274752). Public record URL: https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251274752 .

Introduction Investing in nursing education is a health-workforce priority because nurses are central to health service delivery and progress toward universal health coverage ( 1 ). Nursing students encounter examinations, simulations, invasive-skills training, and early clinical placements while managing workloads, responsibilities, observations, and fears of making errors ( 2–5 ). Anxiety and related distress are common across nursing programs ( 6–9 ). Support for students’ mental health is therefore relevant to both their participation in training and the future nursing workforce. In this review, music-based intervention is an umbrella term, not a claim of equivalence. We distinguish passive music listening or music medicine, active music making, and therapist-delivered music therapy. The last category requires a structured therapeutic intervention delivered by a music therapist; researcher- or educator-delivered listening is not labeled as formal music therapy ( 10 , 11 ). We also identify trials in which music was added to a shared co-intervention, such as aromatherapy, because these comparisons estimate only the incremental contribution of music. Music may redirect attention away from threat cues, support emotion regulation, increase perceived control when choice is offered, and alter autonomic arousal ( 12–17 ). The same attentional mechanism may also impose cognitive load or obscure task-relevant auditory information. Listening before a stressor may therefore differ from listening during simulation, skills performance, assessment, or clinical activity, where distraction could impair instruction, communication, alarms, or performance. These mechanisms were proposed more often than they were measured across the included studies. Earlier reviews addressed test anxiety and performance in nursing students ( 18 , 19 ). A 2026 meta-analysis across health sciences programs included 24 nursing-student reports ( 20 ). After conducting a corrective search and full-text reassessment, 15 of the 24 reports were included in the present review (resulting in a 62.5% overlap within each review, with a Jaccard overlap of 45.5% across 33 unique reports). The contribution of this review is therefore a nursing-specific, outcome-free update with design verification, separate analyses of randomized and non-randomized evidence, unit-of-analysis safeguards, an explicitly defined principal anxiety estimand, small-sample sensitivity analyses, and the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE), rather than a largely independent evidence base. The primary review question is as follows: among nursing students, do passive music listening, active music making, structured therapist-delivered music therapy, or music-based educational interventions, compared with no music, usual activity, an attention or sensory control, or a matched co-intervention, reduce acute or short-term self-reported anxiety at the first eligible post-intervention assessment? Other psychological, physiological, student health, and educational outcomes were secondary domains and were not interpreted as evidence that reduced anxiety improves competence or sustains mental health. Methods Protocol and reporting The protocol was prospectively registered in PROSPERO (CRD420251274752), and the review was reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines ( 21 ). In response to peer review, we revised the electronic search by removing outcome and study-design restrictions, while retaining acute or short-term anxiety as the principal outcome. The amendment, search date, and outcome-selection hierarchy were documented before the corrective search was conducted. Eligibility criteria and outcome domains Participants were nursing students or student nurses at any stage of preregistration education. Eligible interventions included passive music listening or music medicine, active music making, structured therapist-delivered music therapy, and a music-based educational intervention. Music added to a co-intervention was eligible only when a comparator receiving the same co-intervention isolated the incremental music component. Studies using music solely as a metronomic or mnemonic cue were excluded if the intervention did not target psychological, physiological, student health, or broader educational outcomes. Comparators included no music, silence, usual education or activity, attention or sensory controls, and matched active controls. The principal outcome was acute or short-term, self-reported state or situational anxiety at the first eligible post-intervention assessment. The context could occur during an examination, a clinical-skill simulation, an early clinical activity, or a student health event. Trait anxiety and test-specific anxiety were reported separately when they did not align with the selected acute construct. Stress, mood, burnout, pain, sleep, comfort, physiological measures, biomarkers, self-efficacy, knowledge, skills performance, and academic outcomes were secondary domains. Randomized and non-randomized controlled studies were eligible to be included; uncontrolled studies, reviews, editorials, case reports, and reports without an eligible controlled comparison were excluded. Information sources and search strategy We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, CINAHL Complete, Embase, APA PsycINFO, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, the Web of Science Core Collection, and ClinicalTrials.gov from their inception through 19 September 2026. The corrective strategies combined only music-based interventions and nursing-student concepts. No outcome, study design, publication type, or language filters were applied. Complete platform-specific syntax, execution dates, and retrieval counts are provided in Supplementary Table S1 . The seven sources provided a total of 737 records: 114 from PubMed/MEDLINE, 191 from CINAHL Complete, 167 from Embase, 72 from CENTRAL, 36 from APA PsycINFO, 133 from the Web of Science Core Collection, and 24 from ClinicalTrials.gov . Database exports were preserved and deduplicated at the report level using DOI or registry identifiers, exact bibliographic matching, and a manual review of similar entries. Reference and companion-report checks supplemented electronic retrieval. The corrective search was a post-peer-review amendment and is reported accordingly. Study selection and data extraction Two reviewers independently screened 400 titles and abstracts and 39 unique full documents; they extracted study and outcome data, and resolved disagreements by discussion; a third reviewer was not required. Of the 64 reports sought, 23 could not be retrieved as complete documents, one was available only as a conference abstract, and one was an exact duplicate. Reports were linked to study families using authors, setting, sample, recruitment dates, intervention, outcomes, registry identifiers, and companion publication information. We did not impute unpublished numerical outcome data. When several anxiety measures were eligible, the hierarchy was as follows: the study-designated primary acute anxiety outcome; a validated state or situational measure; or a test- or event-specific anxiety measure. We selected the first postintervention assessment and did not count any participant twice. Trait anxiety and stress were not used as substitutes for the principal anxiety construct ( 22 , 23 ). We selected the first postintervention assessment and did not count the same participants twice. Accordingly, trait anxiety and stress were not used as substitutes for the principal anxiety construct. In multi-arm trials, the comparison that isolated music was selected; for Öner et al. and Son et al., aromatherapy plus music was compared with aromatherapy alone. Risk of bias assessment Two reviewers independently assessed each target result using Risk of Bias 2 (RoB2), including the cluster and crossover variants where applicable, or Risk of Bias in Non-Randomized Studies of Interventions (ROBINS-I) ( 24–26 ). The target effect was assignment to the music-based intervention for the selected outcome. Prespecified confounders for non-randomized studies included baseline outcome severity, age, and sex; academic level or prior performance; musical experience or preference; and concurrent stress-management activities. Domain judgments and rationales are reported in Supplementary Tables S4, S5 . Reporting bias assessment Funnel plots and regression tests were performed only when at least 10 sufficiently comparable studies were available ( 27 ). No synthesis met this threshold. Therefore, reporting bias was judged as undetermined and was not downgraded solely because formal testing was unavailable. Certainty of evidence We used GRADE to assess the risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias ( 28 ). Publication bias was downgraded only when independent evidence supported a concern, not merely because fewer than 10 studies were available. Data synthesis The principal synthesis included one effect from each individually randomized parallel-group trial that reported usable postintervention arm summaries. Cluster-randomized, crossover, and non-randomized studies were not pooled in this model unless valid design-adjusted effects and standard errors (SEs) were available. Hedges’ g standardized across anxiety instruments ( 29 ). For two independent groups, g = Jd, where J = 1–3/(4df − 1); its variance was (n1 + n0)/(n1n0) + g 2 /(2df). When only a symmetric 95% confidence interval was available, SE was reconstructed as (upper − lower)/(2 × 1.959964). Random-effects models used inverse-variance weights wi = 1/(SEi 2 + τ 2 ), with τ 2 estimated by restricted maximum likelihood. The pooled estimate was Σwiyi/Σwi. The primary 95% confidence interval used the normal quantile. An unmodified Hartung–Knapp sensitivity interval used q * = Σwi(yi − μ ) 2 /( k − 1), SEHK = √( q */Σwi), and a t distribution with k − 1 degrees of freedom. Heterogeneity was described with Q , I 2 , τ 2 , and a 95% prediction interval was also calculated ( 29 , 30 ). The analyses used Python 3.12.13, NumPy 2.3.5, SciPy 1.17.0, and Matplotlib 3.10.8 ( 31 ). The principal estimand was deliberately uniform: the unadjusted postintervention standardized mean difference across all included trials. As a sensitivity analysis, post-minus-pre–change-score effects were calculated for eight trials with compatible baseline and follow-up data. When a change-score SD was not reported, SDchange = √(SDpre 2 + SDpost 2 − 2 r ·SDpre·SDpost), using r = 0.50 primarily and r = 0.25 and 0.75 in sensitivity analyses. We also examined passive listening, the exclusion of add-on interventions, standalone passive listening, the exclusion of the high-risk trial from the randomization domain, and leave-one-out analyses. The crossover trial by Lai et al. lacked paired variance or first-period data. The two cluster-randomized trials lacked sufficient cluster-adjusted information. These studies were not included in the principal pool. Stress, dysmenorrhea-related pain, physiological outcomes across different stressors, and educational constructs were not pooled because the number of comparable studies was small and clinical or methodological heterogeneity was substantial. Non-randomized effects were presented separately. Results Study selection The corrective search identified 737 records. After 337 duplicates were removed, 400 titles and abstracts were screened, and 336 of these were excluded. A total of 64 reports were sought; 23 could not be retrieved. title: Effects of Group-Based CBT/ERP and ACT on Emotion Dysregulation, Sleep, Anxiety Sensitivity and Psychological Flexibility in Adults With OCD
abstract:
ABSTRACT Introduction Cognitive behavioural therapy with exposure and response prevention (CBT/ERP) is the recommended first‐line psychological treatment for obsessive‐compulsive disorder (OCD). Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) has emerged as a promising alternative, yet treatment comparisons have primarily focused on symptom severity and even less is known about their effects on other domains. Study Aim We examined the effect of group‐based ACT and CBT/ERP on emotion regulation, anxiety sensitivity, insomnia and psychological flexibility in adults with OCD. Methods 176 adults with OCD were randomized to CBT/ERP or ACT and assessed with the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS), Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI), Anxiety Sensitivity Index‐Revised (ASI‐R) and Acceptance and Action Questionnaire for Obsessions and Compulsions (AAQ‐OC) at baseline, post‐treatment, 6‐month and 12‐month follow‐up and analysed with Mixed‐Model Repeated Measures (MMRM). Results Both treatments showed similar improvements in the four domains across timepoints. Conclusions In line with our hypotheses, our results indicated that ACT may be non‐inferior to CBT/ERP for all secondary outcomes. However, as the trial was powered for the primary outcome (symptom severity) rather than for these secondary measures, our findings should be interpreted as suggestive. Nonetheless, these findings add to the growing evidence that ACT may be considered a viable treatment for OCD.

Practitioner Points Group‐based ACT and CBT/ERP produced comparable improvements in emotion regulation difficulties, sleep quality, anxiety sensitivity and psychological flexibility, providing preliminary support for non‐inferiority under the chosen margin across these secondary outcomes. The findings suggest that both ACT and CBT/ERP may have benefits extending beyond reductions in core OCD symptoms, including improvements in broader psychological difficulties that commonly affect patients with OCD. Our results provide additional support for ACT being a viable treatment for OCD.

1 Introduction Obsessive‐compulsive disorder (OCD) is a chronic and potentially disabling mental disorder affecting approximately 1%–3% of the population worldwide (Santomauro et al. 2026 ). OCD is associated with substantial impairment across multiple areas of life and symptoms often persist without adequate treatment (Öst et al. 2015 ). Meta‐analytic evidence shows that cognitive behavioural therapy including exposure and response prevention (CBT/ERP) is an effective treatment for OCD, with large effects relative to waitlist and placebo conditions (Reid et al. 2021 ). Accordingly, CBT/ERP is recommended as a first‐line psychological treatment in clinical guidelines (NICE 2005 ). CBT/ERP helps patients systematically confront obsession‐related triggers while refraining from compulsions and other neutralizing behaviours, thereby facilitating new learning and reducing reliance on avoidance and ritualized responses (Foa 2010 ). Nevertheless, not all patients benefit sufficiently from treatment or complete it. A meta‐analysis reported pooled rates of response and clinically significant change of 65.0% and 50.0%, respectively, for ERP, although definitions varied across studies. Pooled dropout rates were 15.5% for CBT, 19.1% for ERP and 32.0% for ERP/CBT combined with antidepressant medication (Öst et al. 2015 ). These limitations highlight the need to evaluate alternative treatment approaches. Acceptance and commitment therapy (ACT) has emerged as a potentially effective treatment for OCD (Evey and Steinman 2023 ). Rather than primarily targeting the content or frequency of intrusive thoughts, ACT aims to encourage value‐based living, change how individuals relate to internal experiences and strengthen psychological flexibility (Twohig et al. 2006 ). Although studies indicate that ACT can reduce OCD symptom severity, relatively few trials have compared ACT directly with CBT/ERP (Evey and Steinman 2023 ). In their systematic review, Evey and Steinman ( 2023 ) included 17 studies on ACT, with 8 of them including a control condition and 1 comparing ACT combined with ERP to ERP. Recently, group‐based ACT was found to be non‐inferior to group‐based CBT/ERP in reducing OCD symptoms (Nielsen, Stuart, Winding, Øllgaard, et al. 2025 ). Treatment outcomes in studies of CBT/ERP and ACT for OCD have predominantly been evaluated using measures of OCD symptom severity, particularly the Yale–Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale (Y‐BOCS) (Goodman et al. 1989 ). Although symptom reduction is a central treatment objective, it may not fully capture changes in psychological functioning and associated clinical difficulties. OCD is indeed also characterized by sleep disturbance, emotion regulation difficulties, anxiety sensitivity and psychological inflexibility. These domains have been associated with the severity or maintenance of OCD (Bluett et al. 2014 ; Olatunji and Wolitzky‐Taylor 2009 ; Paterson et al. 2013 ; See et al. 2022 ) and may remain clinically relevant even when obsessive‐compulsive symptoms improve. We therefore included sleep disturbance, emotion regulation difficulties, anxiety sensitivity and psychological inflexibility to assess clinically relevant difficulties and theoretically relevant dimensions of functioning that are not fully captured by measures of obsessive‐compulsive symptom severity. Together, they allow us to examine whether the benefits of treatment extend beyond reductions in obsessions and compulsions. Establishing whether these domains change during treatment may also provide a preliminary foundation for subsequent research investigating potential mediators and mechanisms of change (Kazdin 2007 ). 1.1 Anxiety Sensitivity Several studies have found associations between anxiety sensitivity and OCD symptoms specifically (e.g., Robinson and Freeston 2014 ). Anxiety sensitivity refers to the tendency to fear anxiety‐related sensations because they are believed to have harmful physical, cognitive, or social consequences (Reiss et al. 1986 ). Within this expectancy model, such interpretations amplify fear responses to bodily sensations and other anxiety‐related experiences and repeated amplification of fear is thought to maintain anxiety over time (Olatunji and Wolitzky‐Taylor 2009 ). Intervention studies have found that both CBT and ACT can reduce anxiety sensitivity (Kraemer et al. 2020 ; Smits et al. 2008 ). However, their comparative effects on anxiety sensitivity have not, to our knowledge, been examined specifically among patients with OCD. 1.2 Emotion Regulation Emotion regulation difficulties are consistently associated with OCD symptoms and symptom severity (See et al. 2022 ). In particular, difficulty tolerating negative emotions and maintaining behavioural control under emotional distress may be relevant to OCD (Nielsen, Stuart, Winding, et al. 2025 ). Compulsions can temporarily reduce distress, thereby reinforcing avoidance behaviours and limiting opportunities to develop more adaptive responses to unwanted emotions. CBT has been associated with improved emotion regulation in mixed samples of patients with anxiety‐related disorders (e.g., Asnaani et al. 2020 ). Nevertheless, comparatively little is known about changes in emotion regulation following CBT/ERP or ACT among patients with OCD, or whether the two treatments differ in their effects on this domain. 1.3 Psychological Inflexibility Psychological inflexibility involves rigid patterns of responding to internal experiences. Cognitive fusion and experiential avoidance represent two central manifestations of psychological inflexibility (Twohig et al. 2006 ). Cognitive fusion involves responding to thoughts as literal truths rather than as transient mental events, which can result in individuals becoming entangled with and governed by their thoughts. Experiential avoidance refers to attempts to suppress, control, or escape unwanted thoughts, emotions, bodily sensations and memories (e.g., Twohig et al. 2006 ). In OCD, cognitive fusion may lead individuals to interpret intrusive thoughts as meaningful indicators of threat or responsibility. Experiential avoidance may subsequently be expressed through compulsions and other neutralizing behaviours intended to reduce the distress experienced by the individual. Both cognitive fusion and experiential avoidance have been associated with greater OCD symptom severity (e.g., Bluett et al. 2014 ). ACT explicitly targets these two processes and has been shown to increase psychological flexibility among patients with OCD (Evey and Steinman 2023 ). Improvements in psychological flexibility have also been observed following CBT/ERP (Schubert et al. 2022 ). 1.4 Sleep Quality The persistent and time‐consuming nature of obsessions and compulsions may interfere with sleep initiation and maintenance. Although sleep disturbances are common across psychiatric disorders, including depression and anxiety disorders, the relationship between OCD and sleep remains comparatively understudied (Paterson et al. 2013 ). A large cohort study found that OCD was associated with approximately sevenfold higher odds of insomnia (Sevilla‐Cermeño et al. 2020 ). Similarly, a review of eight studies found evidence of an elevated prevalence of insomnia among adults with OCD, with commonly reported difficulties including prolonged sleep‐onset latency, disrupted sleep maintenance and reduced sleep quality (Santiago et al. 2025 ). Taken together, these findings suggest that sleep disturbance represents an important but insufficiently investigated domain of impairment in OCD. Studies conducted outside the OCD field have also indicated that CBT and ACT may produce comparable improvements in insomnia (e.g., El Rafihi‐Ferreira et al. 2024 ). However, the comparative effects of ACT and CBT/ERP on sleep difficulties have not, to our knowledge, been examined in an OCD sample. 1.5 The Present Study Although CBT/ERP and ACT are based on distinct theoretical models, both treatments may influence shared psychological processes (Arch and Craske 2008 ; Fang and Ding 2023 ; Nielsen et al. 2026 ). CBT/ERP encourages patients to approach feared situations and internal experiences while refraining from compulsive responses. ACT similarly promotes willingness to experience unwanted thoughts, emotions and bodily sensations without engaging in avoidance, while supporting behaviour guided by personally meaningful values. Both treatments may therefore reduce rigid or avoidant responses to internal distress and increase psychological flexibility (Arch and Craske 2008 ). This proposition is consistent with comparative evidence suggesting that CBT and ACT may have overlapping effects across symptom‐based and broader psychological outcomes (Fang and Ding 2023 ). The present study compared the effects of group‐based ACT and group‐based CBT/ERP on the secondary outcomes sleep, emotion regulation, anxiety sensitivity and psychological inflexibility among adults with OCD from baseline to post‐treatment and through 12‐month follow‐up. We hypothesized that ACT would be non‐inferior to CBT/ERP in improving sleep quality, measured with the Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI); emotion dysregulation, measured with the Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale (DERS); anxiety sensitivity, measured with the Anxiety Sensitivity Index–Revised (ASI‐R); and psychological flexibility, measured with the Acceptance and Action Questionnaire for Obsessions and Compulsions (AAQ‐OC). 2 Methods 2.1 Study Design The present study is based on data from a multicenter randomized controlled trial comparing group‐based ACT and CBT/ERP for OCD (Nielsen, Stuart, Winding, Øllgaard, et al. 2025 ). The original trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID NCT03852186 ) and approved by the Danish Research Ethics Committees (ID H‐18046928) and Danish Data Agency (VD‐2018‐376, I‐Suite number: 6626) (Nielsen, Stuart, Winding, Øllgaard, et al. 2025 ). Participants were recruited from two public outpatient hospital‐based mental health clinics in the Capital Region of Denmark between January 2019 and September 2023. The present study is a secondary analysis of the data from the original trial. 2.2 Setting Participants were referred to the outpatient mental health clinics by general practitioners, hospital departments, or private psychiatrists because of substantial functional impairment related to a mental disorder, complex symptomatology and/or an insufficient response to psychological or pharmacological treatment in primary care. 2.3 Participants Participants were adults aged 18–65 years with a primary diagnosis of OCD according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM‐5) criteria. Eligibility required that participants were not receiving psychotherapy at baseline and, if on psychopharmacological treatment, had been on a stable dose of medicine for at least six weeks before study intervention. Participants were required to be fluent in Danish and free of current alcohol or substance use disorder. All referred patients underwent a comprehensive psychiatric examination conducted by a psychiatrist, who assigned a preliminary diagnosis according to ICD–10 criteria. Eligible participants who provided written informed consent were invited to a baseline assessment conducted by the first author. This assessment included clinical interviews including the Y‐BOCS (Goodman et al. 1989 ) to assess OCD symptom severity and the MINI International Neuropsychiatric Interview (Sheehan et al. 1998 ) to establish whether participants met DSM–5 criteria for OCD and comorbid psychiatric disorders. The outcome variables used in this study were assessed using self‐reports. Written informed consent was obtained prior to baseline assessment. Self‐report measures were administered via the secure online data capture platform REDCap and post‐treatment assessments were conducted within 14 days of treatment completion (Nielsen, Stuart, Winding, Pedersen, et al. 2025 ). Sample characteristics are presented in Table 1 and participant flow for the outcomes examined in this study is presented in Figure 1 . 2.4 Randomization and Blinding Participants were stratified by clinic and randomly allocated to either CBT/ERP or ACT using block randomization with varying block sizes. Allocation concealment was maintained and the randomization sequence was generated using the blockrand package in R; further detail on the randomization procedure is provided in the original trial article (Nielsen, Stuart, Winding, Pedersen, et al. 2025 ). Participants were informed of their treatment allocation at the first therapy session. 2.5 Interventions and Therapists The intervention consisted of two individual sessions (1 h each) and 14 group sessions (2.5 h each), delivered in groups of up to eight patients (M = 4.41, SD = 1.67, range = 2–7), each led by two therapists.
