title: The Effects of Mindfulness-Based Programs on Pain-Related Cognitions in Individuals With Chronic Musculoskeletal Pain: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
abstract:
Objectives Chronic musculoskeletal pain is a complex condition influenced by psychological factors, including pain‐related cognitions. This systematic review and meta‐analysis of randomized controlled trials aimed to evaluate the effects of mindfulness‐based programs on pain‐related cognitions in individuals with chronic musculoskeletal pain. Secondary outcomes included depression, anxiety, psychological distress, pain intensity, disability, intervention adherence, and mindfulness‐related adverse events. Methods Eight databases were searched from inception to January 2026. Evidence was synthesized using random‐effects models and reported as standardized mean differences with 95% confidence intervals. Risk of bias was assessed using the revised Cochrane risk of bias tool. Evidence certainty was rated using GRADE. Results Fifty‐one studies ( n = 5997) were included and had a moderate‐to‐high risk of bias. Compared to no intervention, mindfulness‐based programs reduced pain catastrophizing (SMD: 1.00, 95% CI: 0.56–1.45) and increased pain acceptance (SMD: 1.12, 95% CI: 0.31–1.92) post‐intervention. They also reduced depression (SMD: 0.94, 95% CI: 0.50–1.38), anxiety (SMD: 1.08, 95% CI: 0.57–1.59), psychological distress (SMD: 0.75, 95% CI: 0.12–1.38), pain intensity (SMD: 0.80, 95% CI: 0.38–1.23), and disability (SMD: 0.48, 95% CI: 0.04–0.92) compared to no intervention. Minimal significant differences were observed between the effect of mindfulness‐based programs and cognitive behavioral therapy on these outcomes. Discussion Mindfulness‐based programs appear to be an effective self‐management strategy for individuals with chronic musculoskeletal pain. However, the certainty of evidence is mostly low with intervention adherence varying. Future research should clarify the direction and nature of the relationship between adherence and outcomes. Reporting of mindfulness‐related adverse events was insufficient to evaluate safety; future trials should incorporate comprehensive measurement.

1. Introduction Chronic musculoskeletal pain can profoundly impact psychological well‐being, increasing the risk of mental health disorders such as depression and anxiety [ 1 – 6 ]. In turn, psychological factors such as stress [ 2 , 7 , 8 ], depression [ 9 , 10 ], and anxiety [ 11 ] can contribute to the onset and persistence of chronic musculoskeletal pain. This affective distress is associated with increased pain intensity and worse physical function [ 12 , 13 ]. There is also substantial evidence that other psychological factors, particularly pain‐related cognitions, contribute to the trajectory of chronic musculoskeletal pain. Pain‐related cognitions are the thoughts, beliefs, and attitudes individuals hold regarding their pain experience. Maladaptive pain‐related cognitions such as pain catastrophizing and kinesiophobia can exacerbate pain and disability in people with chronic musculoskeletal pain [ 14 – 18 ]. Conversely, positive cognitions such as pain acceptance and pain self‐efficacy are associated with lower pain intensity and better physical function [ 19 – 21 ]. Further, several studies suggest that among people with comorbid chronic musculoskeletal pain and depression or anxiety, pain‐related cognitions can mediate the bidirectional relationship between these conditions [ 22 – 24 ]. Addressing psychological factors within chronic musculoskeletal pain management is crucial [ 25 – 29 ]. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is widely considered the gold‐standard psychological treatment for depression and anxiety [ 30 , 31 ] and is the main psychological intervention recommended in chronic musculoskeletal pain management guidelines [ 25 , 26 ]. However, barriers to widespread implementation persist. CBT is typically delivered by mental health professionals, such as psychologists and psychiatrists, yet growing workforce shortages and rising demand have limited service availability [ 32 – 34 ]. Moreover, the conventional one‐on‐one format of CBT is resource‐intensive and more costly than group‐based approaches [ 35 ]. Additional scalable, accessible, and cost‐effective options are needed. Mindfulness‐based programs have emerged as one potential alternative for addressing psychological well‐being in individuals with chronic musculoskeletal pain [ 36 , 37 ]. Practicing mindfulness involves paying attention, on purpose, as nonjudgmentally and open‐heartedly as possible, to the present moment—to what one is experiencing in their body, their mind, and the world around them [ 38 ]. Mindfulness‐based programs involve sustained, intensive training in mindfulness meditation, complemented by inquiry—a reflective practice that employs questioning to examine one’s experiences with curiosity and nonjudgment and distinguish direct experiences from habitual reactions and conceptions. They are thought to reduce the stress associated with living with a chronic condition by fostering decentering and equanimity—defined as even‐mindedness in the face of challenging experiences—and by enhancing emotional and behavioral self‐regulation [ 39 ]. Various mindfulness‐based programs are described in the literature; the two most widely adopted are mindfulness‐based stress reduction (MBSR) and mindfulness‐based cognitive therapy (MBCT) [ 40 ]. Hundreds of studies have investigated the health impacts of mindfulness across various populations [ 36 , 40 , 41 ]. Among people with chronic musculoskeletal pain, they have been shown in randomized controlled trials (RCTs) to positively influence pain‐related cognitions [ 42 – 44 ], reduce symptoms of depression and anxiety [ 45 ], decrease perceptions of pain severity, and improve physical function [ 46 ]. However, findings across studies have been inconsistent. The rapid growth of research and inconsistent findings in this area present challenges for clinicians and people living with chronic musculoskeletal pain by contributing to uncertainty in decision‐making and creating barriers to evidence‐based practice. While several reviews have endeavored to synthesize the evidence for the impact of mindfulness among people with chronic pain, important limitations remain. First, no reviews have specifically focused on the effect of mindfulness‐based programs on pain‐related cognitions, despite their known relevance to clinical outcomes. Additionally, limited attention has been given to intervention adherence and mindfulness‐related adverse events (MRAEs). Second, many reviews examining important outcomes—including psychological well‐being, pain intensity, and disability—have been narrow in scope, focusing on a single pain condition such as chronic back pain or rheumatoid arthritis [ 47 – 52 ], or overly broad, including interventions with minimal mindfulness content such as acceptance and commitment therapy [ 53 – 55 ]. Third, as advised in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [ 56 ], the inclusion of nonrandomized studies in several reviews increases the risk of bias, potentially leading to inaccurate conclusions [ 50 , 54 , 57 , 58 ]. Finally, many meta‐analyses have pooled heterogeneous comparators, for instance, passive and active controls [ 51 , 59 – 61 ] or diverse active controls [ 58 , 59 , 62 ], limiting the precision and interpretability of the findings. A rigorous synthesis of evidence addressing these limitations is needed to clarify the effects of mindfulness‐based programs in people with chronic musculoskeletal pain and to inform clinical practice. Therefore, this systematic review and meta‐analysis of RCTs aimed to evaluate the effects of mindfulness‐based programs on pain‐related cognitions among people with chronic musculoskeletal pain. Secondary outcomes included depression, anxiety, psychological distress, pain intensity, disability, intervention adherence, and MRAEs. 2. Methods This systematic review is reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines [ 63 ]. The protocol was registered prospectively with PROSPERO (CRD42023495026); no deviations occurred. There was no patient or public involvement in this review. 2.1. Search Strategy Eight databases were searched from inception to January 9, 2026: Medline (Ovid), Embase (Ovid), Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL) (Ovid), Cumulative Index of Nursing and Allied Health Literature (CINAHL) (EBSCO), APA PsycINFO (Ovid), Allied and Complementary Medicine Database (AMED) (Ovid), Web of Science, and Scopus. Additionally, three clinical trial registries were searched from inception to January 9, 2026: the United States National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register (ClinicalTrials.gov), the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform, and the Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry. Search strategies incorporated a combination of keywords and Medical Subject Headings related to mindfulness and chronic musculoskeletal pain (Supporting Digital Content 1 ). The search strategies were reviewed by an experienced librarian and validated by confirming their ability to retrieve two known eligible studies [ 46 , 64 ]. Reference lists of relevant studies were also hand searched by TBH. Titles and abstracts of retrieved studies were screened by two of six independent reviewers using predefined eligibility criteria (TBH, FP, EP, LR, JP, and AA). Full‐text articles of potentially eligible studies were subsequently assessed by two of four independent reviewers (TBH, FP, LR, and AA). Disagreements regarding eligibility at either stage were resolved through discussion to reach consensus or arbitration by a third reviewer not involved in the initial decision. Authors of identified studies were contacted via email if additional information was required. 2.2. Eligibility Criteria 2.2.1. Study Design Only published RCTs were included. No restrictions were placed on language or publication date. 2.2.2. Participants Eligible trials were those involving participants of any age reporting chronic primary or secondary musculoskeletal pain, as defined by the International Classification of Diseases, 11th revision [ 65 ]. Trials involving participants with chronic back pain were included when all participants had back pain classified as chronic primary or secondary musculoskeletal pain or when a subset of participants may have had radicular pain. Trials that exclusively included participants with radicular pain as well as trials involving participants with other forms of chronic neuropathic pain were excluded. Trials involving participants with chronic cancer‐related pain, chronic postsurgical pain, chronic headache (including tension‐type headache), or chronic visceral pain were excluded. 2.2.3. Interventions Trials were included if the intervention was aligned with Crane et al.’s [ 39 ] definition of a mindfulness‐based program as an intervention that a. is informed by theories and practices that draw from a confluence of contemplative traditions, science, and the major disciplines of medicine, psychology, and education; b. is underpinned by a model of human experience which addresses the causes of human distress and the pathways to relieving it; c. develops a new relationship with experience characterized by present‐moment focus, decentering, and an approach orientation; d. supports the development of qualities such as joy, compassion, wisdom, equanimity, and greater attentional, emotional, and behavioral self‐regulation; and e. engages participants in sustained intensive training in mindfulness meditation practice, in an experiential inquiry‐based learning process, and in exercises to develop understanding [ 39 ]. Examples include MBSR and MBCT. Adaptations of these programs were eligible if an emphasis on the practice of mindfulness meditation remained the central pedagogical component. Interventions that incorporated practices informed by mindfulness but did not have training in mindfulness meditation as the primary focus, such as acceptance and commitment therapy, dialectical behavioral therapy, or compassion‐focused therapy, were excluded. 2.2.4. Comparators No restrictions were placed on the type of comparator. 2.2.5. Outcome Measures Trials were required to measure at least one of the following: pain‐related cognitions (i.e., pain catastrophizing, pain self‐efficacy, chronic pain acceptance, kinesiophobia, or pain control), depression, anxiety, psychological distress, pain intensity, disability, intervention adherence, or MRAEs. 2.3. Data Extraction Data were independently extracted by two of three reviewers (TBH and LR or JM) and verified by a further reviewer (AA). Discrepancies were resolved by consensus. Extracted information included study design, participant characteristics, comparator characteristics, funding sources, and conflicts of interest. Intervention characteristics were extracted according to the Template for Intervention Description and Replication (TIDieR) framework [ 66 ]. Outcome data collected immediately following intervention completion were extracted for analysis of post‐intervention effects. If data were also available from a time point ≥ 12 months post‐randomization, these scores were used to analyze long‐term effects. If multiple eligible outcome measures were available for an outcome domain, the measure more commonly used across the included trials was extracted. Where this guideline could not be applied, the most appropriate measure was determined through consensus among the reviewers. 2.4. Data Analysis Clinical heterogeneity was assessed through structured comparison of key study characteristics, including participant characteristics, intervention and comparator characteristics, outcome measures, and assessment time points. This assessment was used to inform decisions about whether studies were sufficiently similar to combine in meta‐analyses, whether subgroup or sensitivity analyses were appropriate and feasible, and how findings should be interpreted. Disagreements regarding the implications of clinical heterogeneity for evidence synthesis were discussed among reviewers until consensus was reached. Meta‐analyses were conducted only for outcomes and comparisons for which at least four eligible studies were available, in line with current standards in the field [ 67 ]. Random‐effects models were used to account for anticipated heterogeneity. All meta‐analyses included studies that used varied outcome measures. As such, treatment effects were expressed as standardized mean differences (SMDs; Hedges’ g) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). SMDs were calculated using the post‐intervention mean and standard deviation (SD) for each group. Effect sizes were categorized as small (0.2–0.4), medium (0.5–0.7), or large (≥ 0.8) [ 68 ]. title: Depression in autism spectrum disorder: a scoping review of pharmacologic, neuromodulation, and psychosocial interventions
abstract:
Introduction Major depressive disorder is common in autism spectrum disorder, but diagnosis and treatment are complicated by symptom overlap, atypical presentations, alexithymia, and limited ASD-specific evidence. Methods We conducted a scoping review of PubMed, PsycINFO, and reference lists for studies published from 1995 through 2025 examining pharmacologic, neuromodulation, and psychosocial interventions for depressive symptoms in ASD. Results Psychosocial interventions, including autism-adapted cognitive behavioral therapy, mindfulness-based therapy, dialectical behavior therapy-informed approaches, behavioral activation, PEERS, exercise, and animal-assisted therapy, were associated with improvements in depressive symptoms in open-label studies and small randomized trials. Neuromodulation findings were preliminary, while evidence for electroconvulsive therapy and deep brain stimulation was primarily case-based. Pharmacologic recommendations were based largely on expert consensus and indirect evidence rather than ASD-specific controlled trials. Discussion Depression treatment in ASD remains understudied. Larger controlled trials using ASD-validated depression measures, broader representation across support needs, and assessment of functional and long-term outcomes are needed.

1 Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD), defined by social communication differences, restricted/repetitive behaviors, and sensory processing variations, affects almost 1 in 31 children, with prevalence rising globally ( 1 ). Psychiatric comorbidities are common in ASD, with Simonoff et al. reporting that 70% of children had at least one comorbid disorder and 41% had two or more. Joshi et al. demonstrated a substantial psychiatric comorbidity burden in psychiatrically referred youth with ASD. Depressive disorders are also prevalent, with pooled lifetime estimates of 14.4% in ASD overall and 37% in adults with ASD. ( 2 – 5 ). Major depressive disorder (MDD) manifests as persistent low mood, anhedonia, worthlessness, and cognitive/somatic symptoms, driving individual morbidity, relational strain, and more than $300B annual U.S. economic costs ( 6 , 7 ). In individuals with ASD, social adversities amplify risk: bullying, employment barriers, social isolation, and loneliness, all recognized contributors to depression ( 8 – 11 ). Yet evidence remains fragmented. Prior studies exhibit methodological heterogeneity (e.g., age, unvalidated scales, diagnostic overshadowing), likely underestimating burden. No standardized treatment pathway exists; clinicians extrapolate from neurotypical data despite sparse ASD-specific evidence across pharmacologic, psychosocial, and neuromodulation domains ( 5 , 12 ). Throughout this review, the term “individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)” is used for consistency, while recognizing that both person-first and identity-first language are preferred by different members of the autism community. This PRISMA-ScR-guided scoping review synthesizes evidence from PubMed, PsycINFO, and reference list searches from 1995 to 2025 on pharmacologic, neuromodulation, and psychosocial treatments for depressive symptoms in individuals with ASD, with the goal of providing clinicians, patients, and families with a clearer overview of available options and the strength of the supporting evidence. 2 Materials and methods 2.1 Study design We conducted a scoping review of pharmacologic, neuromodulation, and psychosocial interventions for depressive symptoms in ASD guided by the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR) framework ( 13 ). Given the limited number of ASD-specific depression intervention studies, the review also included indirect or clinically relevant evidence from ASD studies targeting related psychiatric symptoms (e.g., anxiety, emotional dysregulation, irritability) when these interventions are commonly used or recommended in the management of depression in ASD. 2.2 Data sources and search strategy We searched PubMed and PsycINFO databases for studies published between December 1, 1995, and December 1, 2025. Search terms combined Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) and keywords related to autism spectrum disorder (‘autism spectrum disorder,’ ‘autism,’ ‘Asperger syndrome’), depression (‘major depressive disorder,’ ‘depression,’ ‘depressive symptoms’), and intervention-related study designs (‘clinical trial,’ ‘randomized controlled trial,’ ‘intervention’). Reference lists of included primary studies and relevant systematic reviews were manually screened to identify additional eligible primary studies. Records identified through manual reference-list screening were imported into Covidence along with records retrieved from the electronic database searches. Duplicate records were removed in Covidence prior to title and abstract screening. Only articles published in English were included. PubMed and PsycINFO were selected because they provide broad coverage of biomedical and mental health literature relevant to ASD and depression. To improve study identification, reference lists of included studies and relevant reviews were also manually screened for additional eligible articles. Because the original database-specific search strings were not retained, a PubMed search strategy was reconstructed based on the documented methodology and scope of the review and is provided in the Supplementary Material. This reconstructed strategy is intended to provide readers with a more concrete representation of the search approach and should not be interpreted as the original search string. 2.3 Eligibility criteria Inclusion criteria comprised peer-reviewed articles reporting clinical outcome data in participants of any age with a confirmed ASD diagnosis (based on ADOS/ADI-R, DSM/ICD criteria, or clinical judgment). Eligible studies included interventions targeting depressive symptoms, major depressive disorder, internalizing symptoms, emotional dysregulation, suicidality, anxiety, or other psychiatric outcomes clinically relevant to depression management in ASD. Outcomes could include validated depression scales [e.g., Hamilton Depression Rating Scale (HDRS), Beck Depression Inventory-II [BDI-II], Patient Health Questionnaire–9 (PHQ-9), Children’s Depression Inventory–2 (CDI-2), Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS)], clinician-rated depressive symptom improvement, or related affective and internalizing outcomes. Interventional study designs included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-experimental studies, open-label trials, pilot studies, case series, and case reports. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were used to identify additional eligible primary studies through manual reference-list screening and to provide contextual background where appropriate but were not included as evidence units in this review. Interventions included pharmacologic treatments (e.g., antidepressants, antipsychotics, cannabinoids, and ketamine/esketamine), neuromodulation approaches (e.g., repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation [rTMS], intermittent theta burst stimulation [iTBS], electroconvulsive therapy [ECT], deep brain stimulation [DBS], transcranial direct current stimulation [tDCS]), and non-pharmacological approaches (e.g., CBT, DBT, Mindfulness-Based Interventions, behavioral activation, social skills interventions, exercise, animal-assisted therapy, nutraceuticals, and microbiota-focused interventions.). Given the limited number of ASD-specific intervention studies targeting major depressive disorder or depressive symptoms, we intentionally adopted broader eligibility criteria. Studies evaluating clinically related outcomes (e.g., anxiety, emotional dysregulation, irritability, suicidality, repetitive negative thinking, internalizing symptoms, and psychological well-being) were included when the intervention was considered clinically relevant to depression management in individuals with ASD. Studies that directly assessed depressive symptoms or MDD were classified as providing direct evidence, whereas studies assessing only clinically related psychiatric outcomes were classified as providing indirect evidence. Studies assessing both depression-specific and adjacent psychiatric outcomes were classified as direct evidence at the study level, with both outcome types recorded during data extraction. At the intervention level, “direct plus indirect” indicated that the evidence base included both depression-specific studies and studies assessing only related psychiatric outcomes. Classification was performed independently by C.S. and L.A. during data extraction based on the prespecified eligibility criteria. Discrepancies were resolved by consensus or, when necessary, through consultation with a third reviewer (U.G.). Throughout the review, direct evidence was interpreted separately from indirect evidence when evaluating the evidence supporting depression treatment in ASD. Exclusion criteria included studies involving mixed ASD and non-ASD populations unless results for individuals with ASD were reported separately, non-interventional or associative studies without an eligible intervention, preclinical or mechanistic studies without clinical outcomes, narrative reviews without primary or synthesized clinical data, conference abstracts without sufficient methodological detail, and studies unrelated to psychiatric or emotional outcomes relevant to depression in ASD. 2.4 Study selection C.S. and L.A. independently screened titles/abstracts, then full texts using standardized forms. Discrepancies were resolved by discussion between the two primary reviewers or consultation with a third reviewer, U.G. The PRISMA-ScR flow diagram is shown in Figure 1 . 2.5 Data extraction An individually developed data extraction form captured study characteristics, including study design (randomized controlled trials [RCTs], open-label studies, and case series); population characteristics (age, sex, ASD diagnostic method, IQ and verbal communication proficiency, and depression severity); intervention details for psychopharmacologic and neuromodulation studies (agent, protocol, dose, duration, and ASD-specific adaptations); comparator (placebo, treatment as usual, or waitlist); outcomes (primary depression scale scores, response and remission rates, adverse events, and follow-up timing); and findings (effect sizes, p-values, and confidence intervals, where reported). 2.6 Intervention categorization and evidence hierarchy Interventions were categorized into three domains: non-pharmacological (psychotherapy including CBT, DBT, mindfulness; skills training such as PEERS; lifestyle and complementary interventions including exercise, animal-assisted therapy, nutraceuticals, and microbiota-focused interventions), pharmacologic (antidepressants comprising SSRIs, SNRIs, atypical antidepressants; antipsychotics; cannabinoids; ketamine/esketamine), and neuromodulation (TMS protocols including rTMS and iTBS; ECT; DBS). Evidence from included primary studies was summarized according to study design, including case reports and case series, open-label studies, observational studies, and randomized controlled trials. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses were used only for citation searching and contextual synthesis. 2.7 Data synthesis Substantial heterogeneity across studies, including differences in participant age ranges, depression outcome measures, intellectual and verbal functioning, and intervention protocols, precluded quantitative meta-analysis. Therefore, findings were synthesized narratively by intervention domain. Studies were further distinguished according to whether depressive symptoms were directly measured or whether they evaluated clinically related psychiatric outcomes. Direct evidence was given greater interpretive weight when discussing treatment efficacy for depression, whereas findings derived from adjacent symptom domains were interpreted as indirect, hypothesis-generating evidence. Additional emphasis was placed on ASD-specific adaptations, methodological limitations, and major gaps within the literature. Because this review was conducted as a scoping review, a formal risk-of-bias or certainty-of-evidence assessment was not performed. Instead, evidence was interpreted descriptively with consideration of study design, sample size, presence of comparator groups, directness of the depression outcome, duration of follow-up, and methodological limitations. The evidence-strength categories presented in Figure 2 represent a pragmatic descriptive summary of the available literature rather than a formal certainty-of-evidence assessment or comparative ranking of treatment efficacy. Greater interpretive weight was given to larger or controlled studies directly assessing depressive symptoms or MDD, whereas smaller uncontrolled studies, case series, case reports, and studies assessing only related psychiatric outcomes were interpreted more cautiously. 3 Results Study selection: The search yielded 552 records after duplicate removal. Title and abstract screening excluded 440 records, and 112 full-text articles were assessed for eligibility. Of these, 55 full-text records were excluded: 8 for ineligible outcomes, 26 for ineligible study design, 11 for ineligible patient population, and 10 secondary reviews or contextual sources that were not treated as evidence units. This left 57 unique primary studies included in the review ( Figure 1 ). 3.1 Study characteristics The 57 included studies spanned non-pharmacological, pharmacologic, and neuromodulation interventions relevant to depression in individuals with ASD. Of these, 38 studies provided direct evidence by assessing depressive symptoms or MDD, whereas 19 provided exclusively indirect evidence through clinically related psychiatric outcomes. By intervention domain, 34 non-pharmacological studies included 27 providing direct evidence and 7 providing exclusively indirect evidence; 16 pharmacologic studies included 6 direct and 10 exclusively indirect studies; and 7 neuromodulation studies included 5 direct and 2 exclusively indirect studies. Most studies focused on adolescents and adults with verbally fluent profiles and without intellectual disability, although several pediatric and mixed-age samples were also represented. Study designs included randomized controlled trials, open-label and pilot studies, case series, and case reports, with substantial variation in intervention type, duration, and outcome measures. Depression outcomes were assessed using a wide range of validated scales, including clinician-rated and self-report instruments, which contributed to methodological heterogeneity across studies. title: Imagery-based fear conditioning and extinction learning in individuals with psychotic liability: an EEG study
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Pavlovian fear conditioning using aversive imagery rather than physical stimuli as the unconditioned stimulus (US) provides a powerful paradigm to study fear learning in psychosis, in which threat expectations often develop in the absence of proximal external threats. This preregistered study aimed to identify behavioral, psychophysiological, and neural aberrancies in imagery-based fear acquisition and extinction learning associated with psychotic liability.

METHODS: Participants at-risk for psychosis (n = 70 with elevated psychosis proneness, n = 28 with verified clinical high-risk status) and non-clinical controls (n = 55) underwent an imagery-based fear conditioning paradigm. Participants learnt to produce aversive, neutral (US), or no imagery in response to cues (shapes) that were systematically paired with a different neutral face (conditioned stimulus; CS). Behavioral ratings, EEG (late positive potential; LPP), and psychophysiological responses (skin conductance responses; SCRs) were assessed.

RESULTS: The at-risk group showed more pronounced acquisition learning in fear and arousal ratings and LPPs than controls. This pattern was driven by elevated affect ratings to the CS+ that had been paired with aversive imagery. In contrast, explicit expectancy ratings indicated less CS discrimination in at-risk individuals. The at-risk group also showed reduced extinction learning in expectancy but faster extinction learning in fear and arousal ratings than controls.

CONCLUSIONS: Psychotic liability is associated with an increased susceptibility to acquire fear through negative mental imagery, even in the absence of actual threat. These findings provide novel insights into the pathogenesis of psychosis, suggesting that imagined threat beliefs could contribute to delusion formation.

title: Effects of mindfulness-based interventions on sleep quality in university students: a meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
abstract:
Background Sleep problems are common among university students due to academic stress, lifestyle factors, and psychological distress and may adversely affect physical and mental health, academic performance, and social functioning. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) have increasingly been used as a non-pharmacological approach to improve sleep health; however, previous findings remain inconsistent, and evidence specifically addressing sleep quality in university students remains limited. This study aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of MBIs on sleep quality in university students and explore factors that may account for variations in intervention effects. Methods We searched seven databases—PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCO, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, Embase, and ScienceDirect—from inception to June 26, 2026. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating MBIs for sleep quality in university students were included. Two reviewers independently conducted study selection, data extraction, and risk-of-bias assessment using the RoB 2 tool. Meta-analysis was conducted in Stata 17.0 using a random-effects model. Subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses, publication bias assessment, and GRADE assessment were also performed. Results Ten RCTs involving 638 university students were included, with 335 participants in the intervention groups and 303 in the control groups. MBIs significantly improved sleep quality [SMD = −0.97, 95% CI (−1.43, −0.51), p < 0.001], although substantial heterogeneity was observed ( I 2 = 85.1%). Subgroup analyses revealed statistically significant between-group differences with respect to sleep-outcome measurement instrument ( p = 0.001), intervention type ( p = 0.009), and session duration ( p = 0.030), indicating that these variables may partially account for the observed heterogeneity. Sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the pooled results. Egger’s test revealed no evidence of significant publication bias ( p = 0.270). The certainty of the evidence was rated as low according to the GRADE framework. Conclusion MBIs may improve sleep quality in university students. However, given the substantial heterogeneity and low certainty of evidence, further high-quality RCTs are needed to confirm these findings. Systematic review registration CRD420261458068, https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261458068 .

1 Introduction Sleep is a fundamental physiological need essential for maintaining human health and normal functioning and plays a critical role in cognitive performance, emotional regulation, mental health, and cardiovascular and metabolic function ( 1 ). The university years represent a critical transitional period from adolescence to adulthood. During this period, students are exposed to multiple stressors, including academic competition, examination pressure, and career planning, while also commonly engaging in behaviors such as irregular sleep schedules and caffeine consumption, all of which may adversely affect sleep quality. A meta-analysis of 48 studies involving 95,938 undergraduate students reported a pooled prevalence of insomnia symptoms of 46.9% ( 2 ). Similarly, a systematic review and meta-analysis of university students in Africa reported pooled prevalences of poor sleep quality of 62.34% among general university students, 64.81% among health science students, and 60.33% among medical students ( 3 ), further highlighting the high prevalence of sleep problems among university students. Importantly, poor sleep quality may have a range of adverse consequences. It may impair learning and academic performance among university students ( 4 , 5 ). In addition, sleep problems are closely associated with anxiety, depression, elevated stress levels, and reduced quality of life ( 6 , 7 ). Taken together, these findings indicate that sleep problems are common among university students and may adversely affect both their academic performance and their physical and mental health. Current approaches to improving sleep quality among university students can generally be classified as pharmacological or non-pharmacological interventions. Although pharmacological treatments may alleviate sleep problems to some extent, uncertainty remains regarding their long-term benefits and safety. A study of university students found that continued melatonin use was associated with subsequent increases in sleep disturbance and depressive symptoms ( 8 ). Therefore, pharmacological treatment may not be an appropriate routine long-term strategy for managing sleep problems in university students. In contrast, mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs), as a non-pharmacological approach, have increasingly been applied to the management of sleep and psychological health in university populations. These interventions are predominantly meditation-centered and train individuals to observe present-moment bodily sensations, emotions, and cognitive experiences with an open, accepting, and non-judgmental stance, thereby diminishing automatic reactivity to negative thoughts and stressful stimuli ( 9–11 ). Greeson et al. reported that the Koru mindfulness program, developed for university students and emerging adults, significantly reduced stress and alleviated sleep problems ( 12 ). Another study found that a low-intensity mindfulness intervention improved subjective sleep quality, sleep latency, and habitual sleep efficiency, with some benefits persisting into the later stages of the intervention ( 13 ). Collectively, these findings suggest that MBIs may represent a useful adjunctive approach to promoting sleep health in university settings. Although several randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have suggested that MBIs may improve sleep quality in university students, findings from previous systematic reviews and meta-analyses remain inconsistent. A meta-analysis including five studies found only a small improvement in sleep quality following MBIs, and the pooled effect did not reach statistical significance ( 14 ). Another meta-analysis specifically examining mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) among university students included 29 RCTs overall; however, only three studies contributed data on sleep quality, and the pooled effect was likewise not statistically significant ( 15 ). In contrast, another meta-analysis including only two studies found that MBIs may significantly improve sleep quality in university students ( 16 ). Notably, previous meta-analyses have generally examined MBIs as one subgroup among several psychological interventions or have treated sleep quality as one of multiple secondary outcomes of MBIs. Consequently, systematic evaluations specifically focusing on the effects of MBIs on sleep quality in university students remain relatively limited. Moreover, previous analyses of sleep quality have included relatively few studies and small overall sample sizes, which may have resulted in unstable pooled effect estimates and limited the precision and reliability of their conclusions. Given these limitations in the existing literature, the present study aimed to systematically evaluate the effects of MBIs on sleep quality in university students and to conduct exploratory subgroup analyses to examine whether intervention characteristics, delivery modalities, and outcome measurement instruments may influence the observed intervention effects. By doing so, this study sought to provide more robust evidence regarding the effectiveness of MBIs and the conditions under which they may be most applicable, while also informing the design of future university-based sleep health interventions and related research. 2 Materials and methods This systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in strict accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement and the methodological guidance provided in the Cochrane Handbook ( 17 ). The protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO), with the registration number CRD420261458068. 1 2.1 Literature search strategy We systematically searched seven databases—PubMed, Web of Science, EBSCO, the Cochrane Library, Scopus, Embase, and ScienceDirect—from inception to June 26, 2026. Searches combined subject headings with free-text terms to identify RCTs evaluating the effects of MBIs on sleep quality in university students. Search terms were developed around four key concepts: “university students,” “mindfulness-based interventions,” “sleep quality,” and “randomized controlled trials.” The detailed PubMed search strategy is presented in Table 1 . 2.2 Inclusion and exclusion criteria for literature The inclusion and exclusion criteria were developed according to the PICOS framework, and studies were systematically screened based on five components: Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome, and Study design ( 18 ). 2.2.1 Inclusion criteria for literature Population (P): Participants were students enrolled in higher education institutions, including associate degree students, undergraduate students, master’s students, and doctoral students ( 19 ). Intervention (I): The intervention group received interventions centered on mindfulness training, including MBSR, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy (MBCT), and mindfulness meditation (MM) ( 20 , 21 ). Comparison (C): Control conditions included wait-list control, no intervention, usual care, health education, sleep hygiene education, or other comparable control conditions. Outcome (O): Studies were required to report at least one sleep quality-related outcome, assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), Insomnia Severity Index (ISI), Sleep Condition Indicator (SCI), Medical Outcomes Study Sleep Scale (MOS Sleep Scale), or other validated sleep assessment tools. Study design (S): Only RCTs were included because randomization helps minimize confounding and strengthens causal inference regarding intervention effects ( 22 ). 2.2.2 Literature exclusion criteria Studies involving participants who were not students enrolled in higher education institutions were excluded. Studies were excluded if mindfulness training was not the core component of the intervention, or if mindfulness was combined with other interventions in a way that did not allow the independent effect of the mindfulness intervention to be evaluated. Studies were excluded if they did not report sleep quality-related outcomes, or if the outcome data were incomplete and could not be extracted or used to calculate an effect size. Studies published in languages other than English were excluded. 2.3 Literature screening and data extraction Study selection and data extraction were independently performed by two reviewers (Junbo Wang and Zhaoxuan Chen). Following the prespecified inclusion and exclusion criteria, the two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, assessed potentially eligible articles in full text, and extracted relevant data. Their results were subsequently cross-checked to ensure consistency in study selection and data extraction. Any disagreements between the two reviewers were resolved through discussion with a third reviewer (Longkang Guo) until consensus was reached. After study selection, the two reviewers independently extracted and verified relevant information from the included studies using a prespecified standardized data extraction form. The extracted information included publication year, country or region, participant characteristics, sample size, mean age, intervention, comparator, mode of intervention delivery, intervention duration, intervention frequency, duration of each intervention session, and sleep quality assessment instruments. For studies with incomplete reporting or unclear data, the original study authors were contacted to obtain additional information. If the required data could not be obtained, they were handled according to the prespecified procedures. 2.4 Risk assessment of bias To assess the methodological quality of the included studies, two reviewers (Junbo Wang and Zhaoxuan Chen) independently evaluated the risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk of Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool. The assessment covered five domains: Randomization process, Deviations from intended interventions, Missing outcome data, Measurement of the outcome, and Selection of the reported result. An overall risk-of-bias judgment was then made based on the assessments across these domains ( 23 ). Each domain was rated as “low risk,” “some concerns,” or “high risk.” A study was judged to be at low overall risk of bias when all domains were rated as low risk. A study was judged to have some concerns when one or more domains raised some concerns but none were rated as high risk. A study was judged to be at high overall risk of bias when at least one domain was rated as high risk, or when multiple domains raised some concerns that could substantially reduce confidence in the study findings. After completing the assessments independently, the two reviewers cross-checked their judgments. Any disagreements were reviewed and discussed with a third reviewer (Longkang Guo) until consensus was reached. 2.5 Statistical analysis Data synthesis and meta-analysis were performed using Stata version 17.0 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, United States) ( 19 ). Because different measurement instruments were used across the included studies, resulting in differences in measurement units and scoring systems, standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were used as the pooled effect measure ( 24 , 25 ). Before data synthesis, the direction of all outcome measures was standardized so that lower effect estimates consistently indicated an improvement in sleep quality. Accordingly, an SMD < 0 with a 95% CI entirely below zero indicated that the mindfulness intervention favored improvement in sleep quality among university students. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q test and quantified using the I 2 statistic and corresponding p -value. When I 2 ≤ 50% and p ≥ 0.01, heterogeneity among studies was considered not statistically significant, and a fixed-effect model was used for data synthesis. When I 2 > 50% and p < 0.01, substantial heterogeneity was considered to be present, and a random-effects model was applied. When evident clinical heterogeneity was identified, subgroup analyses or qualitative synthesis were performed as appropriate ( 26 ). Sensitivity analysis was conducted using a leave-one-out approach to assess the robustness of the pooled results. Publication bias was visually assessed using funnel plots and statistically evaluated using Egger’s test, with p < 0.05 indicating potential publication bias ( 27 ). In addition, the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach was used to assess the certainty of evidence for the primary outcome ( 28 ). 3 R

title: Written exposure therapy as treatment for comorbid PTSD and SUD: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
Purpose of review This study aimed to evaluate the effectiveness, feasibility, and acceptability of Written Exposure Therapy (WET) when it is used as a component in integrated treatment of comorbid PTSD and Substance Use Disorder (SUD). A systematic review and meta-analysis was used to synthesise foundational knowledge regarding WET. Recent findings Twelve studies were included and analysed in the review. Random-effects meta-analysis of six studies showed large overall pre/post decrease in PTSD severity (Hedges’ g = 1.18, 95% CI [0.68, 1.72], p < 0.001). Rate of retention (69.03%) was higher than typically seen in integrated prolonged exposure treatments for PTSD-SUD. The majority of participants and providers found WET feasible and acceptable. A minority of participants found concurrent treatment for both disorders burdensome. Summary Findings suggest that can be an effective component in integrated treatment of PTSD-SUD, owing to its efficacy, brevity, and low-burden of integration. Limitations of the current findings include small samples, lack of comparator groups, and limited information regarding treatment components and change in SUD. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1007/s11920-026-01724-x .

Introduction Post Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and Substance Use Disorder (SUD) are significant mental health concerns that are frequently comorbid. Prevalence of this comorbidity ranges from 25–49% in the general population, and is typically higher in clinical populations [ 1 – 3 ]. Patients with comorbid PTSD-SUD experience a more severe, complex, costly, and chronic course of illness compared to patients with either disorder alone. Unfortunately, both disorders maintain each other, impede recovery for either condition, and are more difficult to treat when comorbid [ 1 , 4 – 9 ]. PTSD and traumatic exposure exert significant influence over the impacts and outcomes of PTSD-SUD. Substance use is more common in individuals who report trauma exposure or meet criteria for PTSD, with a higher number of traumatic events becoming increasingly predictive of SUD severity [ 10 , 11 ]. PTSD severity predicts faster relapse following SUD treatment, with patients endorsing elevated PTSD symptoms prior to and immediately following relapse [ 7 , 12 , 13 ]. Finally, a reduction in PTSD severity accounts for a greater and more sustained reduction in SUD, while a reduction in SUD severity does not account for a similar or greater reduction in PTSD [ 7 , 8 , 12 , 14 ]. Treatment of comorbid PTSD-SUD Growing evidence suggests that exposure-based integrated interventions are safe, tolerable, and more effective than non-exposure-based interventions in the treatment of PTSD-SUD, without exacerbating or compromising outcomes for SUD [ 12 , 14 – 20 ]. However, existing treatments have inherent constraints that limit their accessibility and retention. Integrated treatments are typically longer than treatment for either disorder [ 21 ], requiring between 12–15 sessions that each last 60–90 min [ 20 , 22 , 23 ]. Most clinicians manage high clinical workloads, and are typically trained for either PTSD or SUD but not both. The burden of resources and time required by specialized integrated treatments is quite high [ 4 , 24 ]. Finally, studies show that less than 40% of participants receive an adequate dose of exposure before dropping out of integrated treatment, and more than 40% leave prior to completion [ 25 – 28 ]. In this landscape, Written Exposure Therapy (WET) is emerging as a modality of interest. WET is a brief therapy utilising exposure through writing, across 5–7 60-min sessions, with no between-session homework [ 29 ]. It has been established as an effective treatment for PTSD across a variety of demographic and cultural contexts [ 30 ] and is shown to be non-inferior to existing exposure-based therapies [ 31 , 32 ]. Recent literature has started to explore its use for the treatment of PTSD-SUD, as it offers several potential advantages. Its brevity can allow for easier integration into existing SUD treatment programs. Its highly structured delivery and low training burden may make it more feasible for clinicians. And in its less cognitively-demanding nature, it may also be more accessible to a broader range of clients. Finally, by both frontloading the exposure in the first session and via writing, WET may also reduce treatment dropout. To date, only exploratory and pilot studies with small samples have explored the potential of WET as a treatment for PTSD-SUD. However, no systematic collation of WET’s effectiveness for PTSD-SUD treatment exists in the current literature. Therefore, we conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of the international literature to: Examine changes in PTSD symptoms following Written Exposure Therapy (WET) among individuals with comorbid PTSD and substance use disorders (SUD). Evaluate preliminary evidence regarding the impact of WET integrated within SUD treatment settings on substance use–related outcomes.. Assess the feasibility and acceptability of WET as a component of integrated treatment for PTSD-SUD. Method The Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis guidelines were followed for conducting this review (PRISMA 2020) [ 33 ]. The review was registered with the Prospero International Prospective Register for Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; ID CRD42024602565) [ 34 ]. Studies that implement or plan to implement WET as treatment for adults presenting with co-morbid PTSD/trauma and SUD were included. Detailed inclusion criteria and search terms used are detailed in Appendix A. The initial search was conducted in November 2024 and included publications from January 2000 to October 2024. Studies short-listed for inclusion were screened by two reviewers and any disputes were resolved by discussion among all three reviewers. Data extraction and analysis A data extraction template was created in Covidence. Data were extracted by two reviewers regarding the publication, sample size and demographic characteristics, retention, any comparators or control treatments, psychometric measures, data analysis strategy, reported outcomes, conclusions, and limitations of the study. A risk of bias assessment (RoB) was conducted for studies that reported quantitative outcomes for change in PTSD or SUD, as these were considered most relevant to the goals of this review. The Cochrane RoB in Non-Randomised Studies – of Interventions Version 2 (ROBINS-I-V2) [ 35 ] was used to assess pilot studies, and the RoB 2 [ 36 ] was used to assess RCTs. The RoB was completed independently by two reviewers, and discrepancies were resolved with discussion among all three reviewers. A meta-analysis was considered where results were reported by 3 or more studies for psychometric tools that measure change in PTSD or SUD. Only the PCL-5 met these criteria, results for which were reported by six studies. Standardized mean change effect sizes (Hedges’ g ) were calculated using pre- and post-treatment PTSD symptom scores among participants receiving WET. Change-score standard deviations were derived from reported baseline and follow-up standard deviations using an assumed pre–post correlation of r = 0.50 when change-score standard deviations were not reported. Small-sample bias was corrected using Hedges’ adjustment. Random-effects meta-analysis models were fitted using restricted maximum likelihood estimation (REML). Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using Cochran’s Q , I 2 and τ 2 statistics. Effect sizes were coded such that positive values reflected improvement in PTSD symptoms from pre- to post-treatment. Egger’s regression test was conducted to examine potential small-study effects and publication bias. Qualitative findings were sparse, varied, and distributed across different studies. A Narrative Synthesis approach was used to consolidate findings regarding change in PTSD and SUD, and feasibility and acceptability of WET. Reviewers followed guidelines for using narrative synthesis for systematic reviews outlined by Economic and Social Council Methods [ 37 ]. Results The preliminary search resulted in the identification of 8563 articles. Duplicates ( n = 5361) were removed using Covidence software followed by manual screening by a reviewer. 3202 studies were screened at the title and abstract level, and 14 full-text studies were assessed for eligibility. Following inclusion criteria, 9 articles were included in the review at this stage. Given the small number of studies, searches were repeated in November 2025 and May 2026 via the Monash Library Database, with the goal of finding new publications. Three additional studies met inclusion criteria and included in the review. A total of 12 studies were included and analysed in the review. Figure 1 shows a PRISMA flowchart of the identification, screening, and inclusion of studies from the initial database search and repeated searches. Table 1 summarises key information extracted from each study. An identifier number (#1–12) is assigned to each study for ease of reference. Study descriptions All twelve studies were based in the United States. Six studies reported quantitative findings, five from single-arm pilots (#1–5) and one from a feasibility RCT (#6). Nillni et al. [ 38 ] (#1) provided WET to pregnant women in a specialised addictions-obstetrics outpatient clinic. Schacht et al. [ 39 ] (#2) and Shaw et al. [ 40 ] (#5)conducted non-randomised feasibility pilots of WET in residential SUD treatment. Van Doren et al. [ 41 ] (#3) did the same, but adapted the WET protocol for delivery in group therapy format. Finally, Hahn et al. [ 42 ] (#4) reported on a proof-of-concept study of WET combined with CBT for Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD), delivered to female survivors of recent sexual assault. This study was unique in specifying the traumatic event (recent sexual assault) that would be the focus of exposure, compared to the usual protocol where participants may select any traumatic event that they consider most distressing. Finally, Schacht et al. [ 43 ] (#6) conducted a feasibility RCT comparing outcomes from treatment as usual (TAU) in residential SUD care versus when TAU is combined with WET. Thus far, this is the only study to use a comparator group. Four studies (#7–10) reported qualitative findings, and one quantitative study (#4) included a blended case example. The pilot conducted by Nillni et al. [ 38 ] was part of a larger project that also reported interview data gathered from WET providers [ 44 ] (#7) and users [ 45 ] (#8). Two studies used case studies to understand the experience of participants receiving WET, namely Schumacher et al., [ 46 ] (#9) who delivered WET in a bi-weekly group therapy format in residential SUD care, and Hahn et al. [ 47 ] (#10) who delivered WET in conjunction with coping skills for Cannabis Use Disorder (CUD) in female survivors of recent sexual assault. Finally, two studies were protocols and methodologies for future pilot RCTs. Hahn et al. [ 48 ] (#11) plan to build on their pilot with WET combined with CBT for AUD, comparing its efficacy against WET alone for female survivors of sexual assault. Meshberg-Cohen et al. [ 49 ] (#12) plan to evaluate with WET combined with TAU for SUD is superior to neutral topic writing combined with TAU with a sample of veterans. Overall, 75% of studies integrated WET into existing SUD treatments (inpatient and outpatient), while the remaining 25% were based at study clinics. In terms of population, 41.7% of study samples were women only, 25% were veterans, and 25% were patients in residential SUD treatment. Only one study (8.3%) gathered perspectives from WET providers. With regards to primary substance(s) used by participants, 75% of studies used a broad inclusion criteria allowing any or poly-substance use. Most studies applied the standard WET protocol delivered to individuals. Two studies (#3, 9) tested an adapted bi-weekly delivery of WET. Finally, an additional three studies (#4,10,11) integrated or plan to integrate WET with CBT-based interventions for AUD or CUD. Risk of bias assessment Results from the RoB assessments are displayed in Table 2 . Of the 5 non-randomised studies evaluated using the ROBINS-I-V2, four (#1–2, 4–5) were at moderate risk of bias and one (#3) was at serious risk. The pilot RCT (#6) assessed using the RoB 2 was at low risk of bias. Thus overall, 16.7% are at low risk of bias, 66.7% are at moderate risk, and 16.7% are at serious risk. Some sources of bias included participant selection into analysis (#3), protocol deviation (#2), and missing data (#3). The most common source of bias in non-randomised pilots were unblinded treatment conditions (#1, 3–5), which is difficult to avoid in their design. However, even the pilot RCT (#6), despite taking some measures, was ultimately unable to achieve blinding as the comparison group (receiving only TAU) would inevitably become aware that they were the ‘control’. All studies favoured the intervention or experimental condition, possibly influenced by the awareness of receiving treatment. All studies acknowledge potential bias and limitations inherent in their design. None of the studies were biased in selection and reporting of results. These findings suggest that these studies offer valuable and foundational insights for future studies, though their results must be interpreted with caution. Change in PTSD symptoms All studies used valid, reliable, and appropriate tools to establish the presence of and measure change in PTSD severity, most commonly the PCL-5. Some studies used variations of the PCL-5 and provided rationale for their use. Two studies (#3, 5) used the Weekly version as symptoms were assessed at each session; this approach is in line with the WET protocol. Two studies (#4, 10) used the Past-Week version, as they included participants whose traumatic exposure occurred less than 1 month ago. Two studies (#2, 6) administered the Trauma Coping Self-Efficacy scale (CSE-T) [ 50 ] as an additional trauma-related instrument, and both report statistically significant improvements following WET. A pilot study, using pre/post scores (#2) reported a large effect size for increased coping efficacy (CSE-T: t [ 25 ] = − 5.79, p < 0.001, d = − 1.14). Similarly, a pilot RCT (#6), comparing improvement on the CSE-T for participants receiving TAU + WET versus TAU only reported significantly greater improvements among participants receiving TAU + WET (CSE-T: M diff = 12.46, SE = 2.50, p < 0.001, 95% CI [− 17.51, − 7.40]), while the TAU group did not. Meta-analysis measuring change in PTSD severity A random-effects meta-analysis identified a large overall pre/post effect across all six studies (Hedges’ g = 1.18, 95% CI [0.68, 1.72], p < 0.001). title: A tailored online mindfulness intervention for junior doctors: a mixed-methods study
abstract:
Background Junior doctor training is stressful and associated with significant challenges, including poor mental health and burnout. Mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) are increasingly being offered within junior doctor education programs to support junior doctor wellbeing, with online platforms for delivery attracting interest. Methods This mixed-method randomised waitlist control trial was conducted with junior doctors across two hospitals in Western Australia. The intervention was an 8-week online mindfulness training program, with usual training as control. Outcome measures were changes from baseline to program completion (eight weeks) and then one-month follow-up for self-reported surveys of trait mindfulness, perceived stress, self-compassion, occupational stress, and work engagement. Intervention and control participants completed surveys at all three time points. Semi-structured interviews and focus groups were conducted with participants at program completion. Results Seventy-two (35 intervention, 37 control) junior doctors were randomised. Seventeen did not complete the baseline measures. Data for the remaining 55 participants (28 Intervention, 27 Control) were retained for analysis. Most intervention participants formally practiced mindfulness two to three times per week for five to seven minutes however quality of formal and informal practice was low. For the intervention group, perceived stress increased at program completion (-1.4, 95% CI − 2.6, -0.3, p = 0.0151) while work engagement was decreased (-2.9, CI − 5.6, -0.2, p = 0.0355) at final follow-up. There were no significant changes in any of the outcomes for the control group at any follow-up point. Thirteen intervention participants undertook focus groups or individual interviews about their experience. Despite lack of positive quantitative findings, benefits reported regarding the program during interview included: improved self-awareness, emotion regulation, self-compassion and work productivity, as well as professional and personal relationships. Barriers to participation in the program included limited time, work stress, and challenges with elements of the intervention. Conclusion This novel online mindfulness training program was not associated with improvements in measured outcomes including trait-mindfulness, perceived stress, self-compassion, occupational stress or work engagement for participating junior doctors. This contrasts with our qualitative findings suggesting that junior doctors experience some wellbeing benefits from participating, and with the results of our similar trial in medical students. While the dose of mindfulness practice was the same for both trials, junior doctors’ adherence to practice was lower than medical students’ adherence. Organisational factors such as stressful workplaces and time limitations likely minimised the impact of the mindfulness intervention in this group. Open Science Trial Registry: Australian New Zealand Clinical Trials Registry (ANZCTR). Trial Registration ID: ACTRN12622001248752. Protocol and statistical analysis plan: https://anzctr.org.au/. Request ID: 384649. Date of Registration: 16th September 2022. Data sharing: De-identified participant data, data dictionary, analytical code used to process data and materials associated with the intervention may be shared with researchers providing a methodologically sound proposal on a case-by-case basis at the discretion of the Primary Sponsor. Funding and conflicts of interest: Funding was provided by University of Western Australia and Fiona Stanley Hospital. There are no conflicts of interest to declare.

Background The first few years of junior doctor training have been recognised as a particularly stressful period in a doctor’s career [ 1 , 2 ] with significant impact on both the mental health [ 3 – 5 ] and work efficiency of junior doctors [ 6 ]. Burnout during early stages of junior doctor training has negative effects on trainees’ professional behaviour and impacts patient safety through poor communication and high medical error rates [ 7 – 9 ]. Further, personal impacts of burnout such as depression [ 10 , 11 ] and suicidal ideation [ 12 ] are worrisome, as many Australian doctors, particularly junior doctors, do not seek help due to concerns regarding privacy, confidentiality, feelings of humiliation, and fear of being reported to medical registration bodies [ 13 ]. Underlying reasons for junior doctor stress and burnout have been well documented in the literature and include poor work-life balance, anxieties about suboptimal practices and poor patient outcomes, high workloads and on-call commitments, low job satisfaction, poor career development and poor work environment [ 14 ]. In response to these significant problems for junior doctors worldwide, statements have been issued by national medical associations recommending evidence-based change at national, hospital, program and non-work levels to optimise junior doctor wellbeing. These organisations include the Collaborative for Healing and Renewal in Medicine (CHARM) - a group of experts in medical education and burnout interventions based in the United States [ 15 ], the British Medical Association in the United Kingdom [ 16 ] and the Australian Medical Association in Australia [ 17 ]. The list of wellbeing interventions recommended by most of these bodies, including CHARM, incorporate system-level changes as well as programs aimed at the individual, including the development and research of evidence-based mindfulness and resilience training for medical students and trainee doctors for best practice [ 15 ]. Meta-analyses of studies investigating the effectiveness of mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) for reducing the symptoms of depression, anxiety and stress in patient populations with psychological problems report positive results [ 18 , 19 ]. MBIs have also been found to increase the trait of self-compassion amongst non-clinical populations [ 20 , 21 ]. Higher levels of self-compassion are associated with lower levels of stress and more effective coping strategies [ 22 ], better emotion regulation in times of adversity [ 23 ] and protection from burnout [ 7 ]. Additionally, studies have demonstrated that mindfulness practice may improve engagement with work [ 24 , 25 ], and higher levels of work engagement are generally regarded as an antidote to burnout [ 26 ]. In line with the CHARM and other recommendations, MBIs have been introduced to medical school curricula around the world and their effectiveness for reducing psychological distress and promoting wellbeing in medical students has been documented [ 27 , 28 ]. MBIs have also been taken up by hospital medical education units to provide junior doctors with tools to manage their stress, optimise their wellbeing and reduce the risk of burnout. Quantitative studies evaluating these interventions have demonstrated improvements in wellbeing outcomes for junior doctors, including in objective measures such as trait-mindfulness, perceived stress, mood, self-compassion and burnout [ 29 – 34 ]. Qualitative and mixed-methods studies have also assessed MBIs delivered to junior doctors, reporting their utility for stress-management at work, improved self-care and enhanced relationships [ 30 , 35 – 38 ]. Nevertheless, systematic reviews of MBI studies have not been entirely consistent, with objective effects of these interventions on junior doctor wellbeing and burnout not always observed. It has been suggested that this is mainly due to the methodological limitations of the primary studies (such as study design and sample size) but may also represent limited impacts of the interventions themselves in the junior doctor cohort [ 39 – 41 ]. Possible reasons for the limited impact of such programs may relate to the mode of delivery of the interventions. Traditional Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction programs make up the majority of MBIs introduced to junior doctors at hospitals in studies. These usually involve between one to 2.5 h per week of face-to-face training over approximately eight weeks [ 39 – 41 ]. Junior doctor participants in studies of such face-to-face MBIs however report challenges with attendance due to conflicting clinical commitments [ 33 ] and inadequate support for ‘protected time’ to attend sessions [ 42 , 43 ]. They may also not feel comfortable openly discussing challenges and mental health topics in a group of their peers. Despite reports that junior doctor working hours have improved over the past few decades, this may paradoxically increase pressure on junior doctors to complete their work in a shorter period [ 3 ] making it even more challenging to participate in intensive mindfulness training programs. Delivering mental health support via online platforms, including mindfulness training, has therefore become increasingly popular for health care professionals, including junior doctors [ 44 , 45 ]. Online wellbeing programs are accessible, offer flexibility, and teach health practitioners practical skills that can be implemented immediately into practice [ 44 , 45 ]. Less intensive programs offering short, face-to-face workshops [ 46 , 47 ], very brief 10-day interventions [ 48 ] and four-to-six-week programs using mobile mindfulness apps with no facilitator contact [ 49 – 52 ] as well as facilitated teaching sessions via Zoom [ 53 – 55 ], have been appraised with junior doctors. However, most were single arm studies, with only one bespoke online MBI for health practitioners evaluated in a randomised control trial [ 50 ]. Study measures have included various outcomes such as burnout, trait mindfulness, self-compassion, mood and stress [ 46 – 48 , 50 – 55 ] as well as qualitative evaluation [ 49 , 53 – 55 ]. Although these studies suggest that both brief workshops and online programs that teach mindfulness skills to junior doctors are associated with positive trends in wellbeing, several limitations have been identified, including small sample sizes, lack of control groups, high dropout rates and selection bias. The RCT evaluating an online MBI of 3-months duration reported a significant increase in self-compassion and mindfulness from baseline to post-intervention within the intervention group, with improvements in self-compassion maintained at 6-month follow-up, with no changes reported in the control group at either follow-up time point [ 50 ]. This finding warrants further high-quality research to strengthen the evidence for the efficacy of online MBIs at improving wellbeing in junior doctors [ 39 – 41 ]. As tailored online mindfulness training programs for health care professionals have been associated with lower dropout rates from trials and may have greater potential for effectiveness amongst junior doctors, priority should be given to interventions specifically designed for this group [ 44 ]. Of note, there are currently no studies conducted with junior doctors that directly compare the efficacy of in-person and online MBIs. We have previously reported on the positive findings of a feasibility pilot study and randomised control trial evaluating the effects of a tailored 8-week online mindfulness training program on wellbeing outcomes in medical students [ 56 , 57 ]. The aim of this study was to assess the effectiveness of the same tailored 8-week online mindfulness training program in reducing junior doctors’ perceived and occupational stress levels, and improving their trait-mindfulness, self-compassion, and work engagement, in comparison to a control group, who only undertook the normal junior doctor training curriculum. The focus groups and individual interviews aimed to understand the experiences of junior doctors during the online MBI, their perceptions of the benefits of the intervention with regards to their wellbeing and work engagement, and the difficulties they encountered during the 8-week intervention. We anticipated that online mindfulness training would be a valuable tool for stress management, wellbeing, and professional development for junior doctors at the commencement of their hospital training. Methods Study design This was a mixed-methods evaluation of a randomised waitlist control trial of individual participants with a 1:1 allocation ratio based on a superiority framework. There were no changes to the original protocol after the trial commenced. See the CONSORT Flow Diagram (Fig. 1 ) for an overview of the study design. The qualitative part of the study involved conducting focus groups or individual interviews with a subset of trial participants, who were sampled using a convenience method via an email invitation and follow-up telephone call. Setting The trial was conducted within the South Metropolitan Health Service (SMHS), including Fiona Stanley Hospital (FSH), a large tertiary hospital, and Fremantle Hospital (FH), a secondary hospital, both located in Perth, Western Australia. Participants Inclusion criteria: all interns (first year post-graduation) and resident medical officers (post-graduate doctors, predominantly not yet on a specialty training program) employed by SMHS during the years of 2022 and 2023, aged 18–60 years. Exclusion criteria: medical students, registrars (specialty-trainees) and consultants. Ethics approval and consent to participate This study was approved by SMHS Human Research Ethics Committee (Ref RGS0000005076). All participants provided informed, written consent to participate prior to commencement of the study. Intervention & comparator The intervention was a tailored, 8-week online Mindfulness Training Program (referred to as the MTP) in addition to the usual junior doctor curriculum. The comparator was the usual junior doctor curriculum alone. This ‘waitlist’ control group were guaranteed access to the MTP on completion of the study. The comparator condition was chosen for pragmatic reasons, as this was a low-budget trial with limited resourcing. The MTP was originally developed for medical students by the coordinating principal investigator, SM, an experienced mindfulness practitioner and medical educator, with input from two mindfulness experts, CH and RC, from Monash University (Moore et al., 2020; Moore et al., 2024). The program was adapted for use by junior doctors by SM and a medical education registrar at FSH, LO, and involved making small modifications to the original MTP to ensure that the lectures were relevant to the junior doctor context with provision of information describing the applications of mindfulness relevant to work rather than its study-related applications. The MTP provides junior doctors with short, regular mindfulness teaching videos and meditation practices in order to minimise time spent engaging with the program content within their busy schedules, while encouraging them to complete the mindfulness training daily. title: The impact of cognitive behavioral therapy and third-wave therapies on the quality of life of patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract:
Objective The aim of this study is to evaluate the impact of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) and third-wave therapies on the quality of life of patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Methods A systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Web of Science and the Cochrane Library databases, up until June 20, 2026, to identify randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that used quality of life as an outcome measure. Quality assessment was performed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Assessment Tool. Meta-analysis was conducted using Stata 18.0 software, and subgroup analyses, sensitivity analyses and tests for publication bias were performed. Results A total of 13 randomised controlled trials ( N = 1,324) were included. The meta-analysis revealed that CBT and third-wave therapies improve quality of life in patients with OCD (SMD = 0.18, 95% CI: 0.06 to 0.29, P = 0.004), with no overall heterogeneity ( I² = 0.0%). The results of sensitivity analyses were stable, and the risk of publication bias was low. Subgroup analyses indicated that CBT and third-wave therapies were effective in improving quality of life in non-European countries, early studies (≤ 2020), short-term interventions (≤ 12 weeks), adult populations, standard CBT, third-wave therapies, active control groups, and subjective experience/satisfaction scales; however, statistical significance was not achieved in some subgroups. Since the differences between subgroups aren’t significant, the subgroup analysis is just exploratory, so the results should be interpreted with caution. Conclusion CBT and third-wave therapies can improve the quality of life of patients with OCD to a certain extent, but the overall effect is modest. Future research should be larger in scale, multi-center, and prospective. It’s also necessary to further clarify the mechanisms behind different intervention modules, optimize intervention plans, and improve long-term follow-up, so that we can provide stronger evidence to support clinical practice.
