Introduction Obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD) is a mental disorder characterised by persistent intrusive thoughts (obsessions) and repetitive behaviours or mental acts (compulsions) [ 1 ]. Several multinational studies show that the lifetime prevalence of OCD in the general population is 4.1% [ 2 ], and the average age of onset for obsessive-compulsive symptoms in adult patients seeking treatment is 16.9 years [ 3 ], and it is listed as one of the top ten causes of disability worldwide [ 4 ]. Several studies [ 5 , 6 ] have confirmed that OCD significantly impairs patients’ quality of life, affecting a range of areas including social, occupational and family functioning, subjective well-being, and the ability to participate in leisure activities [ 5 ]. Furthermore, in the absence of effective intervention, OCD can develop into a chronic condition, significantly impairing patients’ quality of life [ 7 ]. Early detection and appropriate intervention for OCD can therefore alleviate individual suffering and reduce the public health burden associated with the condition [ 8 ]. Treatment for OCD primarily comprises two main categories: psychotherapy and medication [ 9 ]. Psychotherapy is usually recommended first because it’s safer and has better long-term effects [ 8 ]. Among various psychological interventions, cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT), including exposure and response prevention (ERP), as a first-line treatment, has been widely proven to effectively relieve obsessive-compulsive symptoms and holds a central place in clinical guidelines [ 10 ]. CBT has evolved through the classical development of traditional behavioural and cognitive techniques, the widespread adoption of internet-based remote interventions, and the emergence of the third wave centred on acceptance and mindfulness, resulting in a diverse and more accessible system of interventions [ 11 – 15 ]. Previous studies have demonstrated that third-wave therapies helps to alleviate symptoms associated with OCD [ 16 ]; however, existing research has found that symptom relief does not necessarily equate to an improvement in quality of life [ 17 ]. Quality of life is a multidimensional, subjective outcome measure distinct from disease symptoms, encompassing various aspects such as physical well-being, emotional state, social interaction and daily functioning [ 18 , 19 ]. Furthermore, most previous reviews have focused their analysis solely on core symptoms, paying little attention to the important dimension of patients’ quality of life [ 20 , 21 ], and thus there are certain limitations to the research. Given the current state of research and the limitations of previous reviews, this study systematically reviewed relevant randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and employed meta-analysis to comprehensively evaluate the effectiveness of CBT in improving the quality of life of patients with OCD, compare differences in efficacy across different intervention settings, and focus on exploring the asynchronous nature of the improvement in obsessive-compulsive symptoms and the enhancement of quality of life. The aim is to supplement the evidence base for cognitive behavioural therapy interventions in OCD, refine the clinical efficacy evaluation system, and provide a scientific basis for optimising CBT intervention protocols, implementing targeted quality-of-life interventions, and improving patient prognosis. Methods The entire process of this systematic review and meta-analysis was conducted in accordance with the internationally recognised PRISMA 2020 reporting guidelines. This research project has been registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261287363). Inclusion and exclusion criteria Inclusion criteria: (1) Patients diagnosed with OCD in accordance with internationally recognised diagnostic criteria (e.g. DSM-5, ICD-10/11); (2) Studies investigating the impact of psychological interventions—such as CBT, mindfulness-based cognitive therapy, and acceptance and commitment therapy—on the quality of life of patients with OCD; (3) Study design: randomised controlled trial (RCT); (4) Outcome measures must relate to quality of life; (5) Studies must be in English. Exclusion criteria: (1) Studies where the population doesn’t primarily have OCD, or mixed samples where OCD patient outcome data can’t be extracted separately; (2) Studies including participants with serious mental disorders (like schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, substance use disorders) or neurological diseases; (3) Studies with missing relevant information or data; (4) Studies where the full text can’t be obtained or isn’t publicly available; (5) Duplicate publications. Search strategy Using a combination of subject headings and free text, a systematic search was conducted in PubMed, Web of Science, Embase and the Cochrane Library, covering the period from the inception of each database to 20 June 2026. Search terms were formulated using a combination of MeSH subject headings and free text. The subject headings included: Cognitive Behavioural Therapy, Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder. During the literature selection process, relevant synonyms were used flexibly to ensure the comprehensiveness of the search. Boolean operators (AND/OR) were used to combine numbered search lines. Synonymous terms were linked via OR, while separate thematic search blocks were combined using AND. The specific search strategy is provided in Appendix 1. Literature screening and data extraction Literature screening and data extraction were carried out independently by two researchers (ZCW and YHT) in accordance with pre-defined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Duplicate publications were first removed; subsequently, all search results were screened by title and abstract to exclude irrelevant studies. Full texts of potentially relevant publications were then obtained and assessed to determine whether they met the inclusion criteria. Data extraction was carried out using a pre-designed data extraction form. The information extracted included authors, year of publication, country of the study, sample size, participant characteristics, study design, intervention, control measures, outcome measures and follow-up duration. In the event of disagreement between the two researchers, consensus was reached through discussion; if the disagreement could not be resolved, a third researcher (YY) made the final decision. Inter-rater reliability was assessed using Cohen’s k coefficient. The k value was 0.69 for title and abstract screening and 0.77 for full-text screening, indicating substantial inter-rater agreement. Statistical analysis All data were entered into Stata 18 software for statistical analysis. Where P > 0.05 and I² < 50%, this indicated that heterogeneity between studies was acceptable, and a fixed-effects model was used for the meta-analysis; where P ≤ 0.05 and I² ≥ 50%, this indicated that heterogeneity between studies was substantial, and a random-effects model was used for the meta-analysis. For quantitative data, the standardised mean difference (SMD) was used as the pooled statistic, and 95% confidence intervals (95% CI) were calculated. According to Cohen’s criteria for effect sizes, an SMD of 0.2 represents a small effect, 0.5 a moderate effect, and 0.8 a large effect. This study combined the overall effect size using a fixed-effects model, chosen because the included studies had relatively low overall statistical heterogeneity. For subgroup analyses stratified by follow-up duration, a random-effects model was adopted; all remaining subgroup comparisons were conducted using the fixed-effects model, owing to the relatively high heterogeneity observed within follow-up subgroups and low heterogeneity across other stratified groups.To check the robustness of the results, we also did a sensitivity analysis. We used funnel plots for visual assessment of publication bias and performed quantitative tests including Egger’s linear regression test and Begg’s rank-correlation test. A P -value > 0.05 indicated that no significant publication bias was detected based on the included data. Study risk of bias assessment The Cochrane Randomised Controlled Trial Risk of Bias Assessment Tool (RoB 1.0) was used to assess the risk of bias in the included studies. The included studies were evaluated across six domains: selection bias, performance bias, measurement bias, follow-up bias, reporting bias and other biases. Specific assessment criteria included random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and testers, and triple-blind assessment of outcomes; incomplete outcome data; selective reporting of study results; and other sources of bias. Each type of bias was classified into three levels of quality: low risk, high risk and unclear. We will use a funnel plot to detect the risk of publication bias, in which the dotted line perpendicular to the horizontal axis represents the pooled effect size; ideally, studies should be evenly distributed on both sides. Studies with large sample sizes and high precision are distributed at the top of the funnel plot, whilst those with small sample sizes and low precision are distributed at the bottom. The bias risk plot was generated using Review Manager 5.4 software. Two reviewers independently assessed the risk of bias. The Kappa coefficient for the risk of bias assessment in the literature was 0.73, indicating good agreement between the reviewers. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or by consulting a senior third reviewer. Results Literature search A preliminary search of four major databases yielded a total of 3,248 articles. After deduplicating the results using EndNote reference management software, 1,341 duplicate articles were excluded, leaving 1,907 articles. Two researchers then independently screened the titles and abstracts, excluding a total of 1,876 articles that did not meet the inclusion criteria; ultimately, 31 articles proceeded to the full-text assessment stage. During the full-text screening process, the two researchers again independently assessed all 31 articles. Of these, 18 were excluded due to inconsistent intervention measures, missing outcome measures, mismatched study participants, incomplete or unpoolable data (e.g., studies only reporting subscale scores of quality of life without total scores), or non-original research (e.g., reviews and meta-analyses); ultimately, 13 studies [ 1 , 4 , 22 – 32 ], involving a total of 1,324 participants, were included. The study selection process is shown in Fig. 1 . A list of studies excluded during the full-text screening stage and the brief reasons can be found in Appendix 1. Study and participant characteristics The trials included in this study were conducted in seven countries worldwide, specifically Germany (3 trials) [ 24 , 26 , 29 ], the United States (2 trials) [ 23 , 32 ], Japan (2 trials) [ 25 , 27 ], the United Kingdom (1 trial) [ 4 ], Denmark (2 trial) [ 1 , 28 ], Spain (1 trial) [ 30 ] and Australia (2 trial) [ 22 , 31 ]. The sample sizes ranged from 18 to 228 participants, with a median of 89. The types of interventions include traditional CBT (4 trials) [ 22 , 23 , 25 , 28 ], internet CBT (4 trials) [ 4 , 24 , 27 , 29 ], and third-wave therapies (5 trials) [ 1 , 26 , 30 – 32 ]. The study population was divided based on the participants’ ages. There are 3 trials [ 23 , 24 , 28 ] focused on children and adolescents, and 10 trials [ 1 , 4 , 22 , 25 – 27 , 29 – 32 ] focused on adults. The characteristics of participants, intervention details and outcome measures are detailed in Table 1 . Risk of bias According to Cochrane standards, the results of the risk of bias assessment are shown in Figs. 2 and 3 . Twelve studies [ 1 , 4 , 23 – 32 ] reported the random sequence generation methods in detail, with only one study [ 22 ] being unclear; seven studies [ 4 , 24 – 28 , 32 ] clearly used allocation concealment, while the remaining six [ 1 , 22 , 23 , 29 – 31 ] had unclear details on allocation concealment. Due to the specific nature of the interventions, 11 studies [ 1 , 4 , 22 – 24 , 26 – 30 , 32 ] clearly did not blind participants or researchers, and only two [ 25 , 31 ] had unclear blinding. Only six trials [ 23 – 28 ] reported blinding of outcome assessors, while the remaining seven [ 1 , 4 , 22 , 29 – 32 ] were unclear in this regard. In addition, eight studies [ 4 , 22 – 26 , 31 , 32 ] fully reported outcome data with no obvious risk of loss to follow-up, while the remaining five [ 1 , 27 – 30 ] did not clearly explain missing data and how it was handled. title: Older yet faster: Representational development explains accelerated semantic processing in older adults
abstract: Slower responses in older age are often taken as evidence for cognitive decline, yet they may also stem from representational changes shaped by lifelong learning. Building on the information-accumulation perspective on aging, we argue that behavioral change across the lifespan can arise from representational systems continuously updated through learning from the environment. This view predicts that aging may bring both benefits and costs: Performance improves when task demands are congruent with accumulated knowledge but declines when they conflict. We provide convergent evidence for this account across three studies, each comprising the following components. First, in tasks requiring participants to access word meanings (i.e., when task demands were congruent with representation), we found that older adults (70-80 years old) exhibited faster semantic processing speed than younger adults (18-25 years old), a finding that cannot be explained by decline-based accounts. Second, we traced this processing advantage to systematic changes in older adults' conceptual representations inferred from semantic rating tasks. Third, using learning simulation models, we demonstrated how such representational changes could emerge naturally from cumulative language experience. Replications across different samples, task requirements, and word stimuli strengthen the robustness of these findings. Finally, we identified a boundary condition: When learned representations contain information incongruent with task demands, older adults' greater learning experience not only attenuates their representational changes but also reduces processing-speed advantage. Altogether, our research challenges the explanatory framework of cognitive aging that emphasizes decline and compensation, advancing a more balanced view grounded in representational development and lifelong learning. title: Repetition bias in self-directed learning
abstract: Self-directed learning is a major part of individual knowledge formation. People often autonomously organize their own learning into "blocks": they practice a certain task for some continuous stretch of time, then switch to another task for another period of time, and so on. Yet current models of intrinsic motivation highlighting epistemic factors such as novelty, competence, and learning progress make various predictions about the extent to which learners block, as opposed to interleaving, their practice. In this study, we demonstrate that people tend to block in a multi-task setting where existing models of intrinsic motivation based on epistemic factors make ambiguous predictions. We show that while epistemic factors can partially explain blocking, a simple repetition bias substantially improves our ability to predict choices.

title: Communication about color over the life span
abstract: Color communication is more than a naming game where the informant names each color: the color terms must also be understood by the listener. Here, we studied how participants' productive and receptive vocabularies affect communication about color over the life span. Human participants, 3-72 years old, played a color communication game. As "senders", participants named 15 or 30 color samples presented singly. Then, as "receivers", they selected from their palette of 15 or 30 colors the sample that corresponded to color term "messages," which were either their own color terms (self-communication) or another participant's color terms (interpersonal communication). The number of color terms in participants' vocabularies, their fraction correct performance for self-communication, and their fraction correct for interpersonal communication, all matured continuously until at least age 21, and were highly correlated with each other. Simulations using a quantitative model of the communication task showed that performance for self-communication was determined by the number of color terms the participant provided in the color-naming phase (color term production), with some forgetting of how they had previously named the samples. The simulation predicted no association between participant age and performance on the interpersonal communication task. Contrary to that prediction, interpersonal communication improved throughout the age range. Further analysis showed that performance for interpersonal communication was independently controlled by life-long improvement in participants' ability to understand terms provided by others (color term comprehension). Therefore, color term production and color term comprehension are distinct abilities, which mature independently across the life span.

title: Testing a secondary motor integration account of confidence computation
abstract: A growing body of empirical evidence suggests that confidence judgments are modulated by action-related cues, yet the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. Recent decision-making models propose that the evidence accumulation variable is continuously transmitted to the motor system, allowing motor plans to evolve in parallel with decision formation. At the motor level, a secondary leaky integration process acts as a filter that regulates the speed-accuracy tradeoff: the stronger the filter, the slower and more accurate the responses. Here, we tested whether action-related effects on confidence are mediated by this secondary motor integration process. We manipulated sensory noise using a doubly stochastic random dot motion task and varied the motor-level filter via speed-accuracy instructions. We reasoned that the positive effect of sensory noise on confidence observed in previous studies should be attenuated by stronger filtering in the accuracy condition compared to the speed condition. However, we found strong empirical evidence against this qualitative prediction. Computational modeling further revealed that the predicted attenuation was extremely small and that confidence predictions based on secondary motor integration offered no advantage over those based on evidence accumulation. Together, these results show that confidence need not be computed from secondary motor integration to account for the observed pattern.

title: Young children engage in choice-relative moral reasoning
abstract: A central challenge in moral reasoning is evaluating actions not only by their outcomes, but also by the alternatives that were available at the time of choice. The present study examined whether preschool-age children engage in this form of choice-relative moral reasoning. Using a child-friendly version of the trolley problem, 3- to 5-year-old children (N = 124, 51% girls) judged a protagonist who moved a barrier to protect three children's cookies from being eaten by a mean squirrel. Children typically judged this action as morally good when no better alternative was available, even when it caused harm to another child. However, they judged the same action as morally bad when a non-harmful alternative was available but not chosen. These findings suggest that preschool-age children evaluate actions in light of available alternatives rather than solely on the basis of outcomes. Thus, even young children appear to consider what else could have been done when making moral judgments.

title: Do parental questions and gestures support executive functions in toddlers born preterm and full-term?
abstract: This study examined parental questions and gestures in the development of executive functions (EF) in preterm (PT) and full-term (FT) toddlers. Sixty-four Turkish-speaking parent-child dyads (32 girls, Mage = 26.1 months, SD = 1.33, 25 PT) were observed in free-play sessions. The form (i.e., WH, yes/no) and function (i.e., pedagogical, information-seeking, rhetorical) of parental questions and gestures accompanying them were coded. Children's working memory and cognitive flexibility skills were measured using Hide the Pots and Reverse Categorization (pre- and post-switch) tasks, respectively. Results showed that PT and FT children had similar EF skills. Parental WH questions were associated with PT children's working memory skills. Parental WH questions, not pedagogical ones, were related to children's cognitive flexibility skills, regardless of neonatal status. When accompanied by gestures, both WH and pedagogical questions were associated with PT children's working memory and cognitive flexibility skills. These results highlight the importance of specific parental input as a function of children's neonatal status in the development of EFs.

title: How explanations evolve: Social learning and the explore-exploit trade-off
abstract: Explanations are social objects, and when people try to explain something, they usually have at hand the explanations that others have tried before. We present a theory of how people use the explanations they encounter as clues to the broader landscape of possible explanations for the phenomenon to hand, which in turn informs their decisions about how and when to forage further for the explanations they wish to adopt. The challenge of coming up with novel explanations draws people to exploit or imitate appealing ones they have already encountered; this draw increases as less appealing alternatives become more distant (the "strawman" effect). Conversely, when presented with distinct, high-quality explanations, people can synthesize them, recombining the appealing features in new ways. We test and confirm these predictions using a two-stage transmission chain experiment. In Stage One, 101 participants were asked to explain unusual scenarios. In Stage Two, a separate group of 995 participants were asked to explain the same scenarios after reading pairs of explanations drawn from Stage One. We found that participants in Stage Two were more likely to exploit, or imitate, explanations when at least one was high in quality and particularly when it was paired with a weaker alternative. Participants were also more likely to synthesize perspectives from prior explanations when the two explanations were both high-quality and conceptually distinct. In contrast, participants were more likely to explore, or diverge, from prior explanations when the two explanations were both of low quality and distinct. Our work provides new insight into how collective exploration can be promoted, or stalled, by implicit information about what is yet to be discovered.

title: Metarepresentation and the puzzle of desire-attribution
abstract: Among theory-of-mind researchers, it's widely agreed that children acquire the capacity to attribute desires well before they acquire the capacity to attribute beliefs. This suggests that there is something about the concept of desire that makes it less cognitively challenging than the concept of belief, but what could that be? One possibility is that the difference has something to do with the development of the capacity for metarepresentation, but this just raises more questions: according to the standard philosophical model of the propositional attitudes, the concepts of belief and desire share the same basic metarepresentational structure. First, we review three potential solutions to this developmental puzzle and discuss their limitations. Then we propose a novel non-metarepresentational account of young children's concept of desire that grounds the contents of desire attributions in a type of representation that we call modal affordances.

title: How do US children and adults make sense of unequal compensation in division of labor?
abstract: Division of labor is a ubiquitous feature of social life, as it allows people to specialize and reach desired outcomes efficiently. However, it also creates pay disparities, as some roles are compensated more than others. Here we examined how U.S. children (105 6-12-year-olds [52 girls, 52 boys, 1 other; 37 Asian, 51 other, 17 race unknown]) and adults (N = 108 [Mage = 43.39; 70 women, 36 men, 2 other; 91 White, 17 other]) make sense of why some roles receive higher pay. Children, like adults, are more likely to perceive unequal compensation as fair in division of labor compared to cooperative arrangements where all participants perform the same tasks (i.e., "parallel cooperation"). Also, while older children are more likely to see unequal pay as unfair in parallel cooperation, they continue to see unequal compensation as fair in division-of-labor cases. Participant explanations provide a potential explanation: a circular meritocratic logic, in which participants assume that higher pay signals greater difficulty, and then use perceived difficulty to justify those same wage disparities. This tendency does not depend on actual job characteristics, and increases with age in the child sample. We discuss how this may help rationalize lower pay for certain occupations-such as assuming female-coded roles like caregiving are easy simply because they offer lower pay.

title: Heterogeneity in holistic face processing disruptions in developmental prosopagnosia
abstract: Developmental prosopagnosia (DP) is a striking disorder characterised by lifelong deficits in face recognition. Research into the nature of DP has broad implications for understanding interrelated theoretical issues in vision, neural organisation, and development. One long-standing but unresolved question is whether holistic face processing, the integration of individual face features into a unified whole, is compromised in DP. Here, we test a large sample of DPs (N = 113), using the three signature effects of holistic processing: the inversion, composite, and part-whole effects. This approach allows us to characterise the extent and pattern of holistic reductions across multiple effects within the same sample and to assess relationships between them. We found that holistic processing is reduced across all three effects in DP. The magnitude of reductions varied across the different effects; however, follow-up analyses indicated that reductions in the composite effect were slightly less robust. We found little evidence linking these reductions to DP severity, though limited reliability in the holistic measures may constrain these conclusions. While we observed reductions in holistic processing at the group level, few individual DPs met the thresholds for impairment. Our findings suggest that DP is associated with weaker holistic effects, but do not support the notion that impairments in holistic processing are necessary for DP.

title: Early self-regulation in context: Multidimensional organization of neonatal non-nutritive sucking and its association with subclinical maternal depressive traits
abstract: From the very first days of life, infants' affective regulation unfolds within a dyadic co-regulatory system shaped by caregiver responsivity. In contexts of reduced maternal availability, such as maternal depressive states, infants may be required to compensate for diminished interpersonal regulation by increasingly relying on their internal resources. Neonatal non-nutritive sucking (NNS) represents one of the earliest spontaneously available regulatory behaviors, contributing to physiological and behavioral homeostasis from birth. However, it remains unclear whether its spontaneous organization is associated with early relational vulnerability indexed by maternal depressive symptoms. The present study aimed to characterize the spontaneous organization of NNS in a sample of newborns (N = 42) and to examine whether individual differences in NNS are associated with maternal postnatal depressive subclinical traits measured using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS). Results from an exploratory principal component analysis indicated that neonatal sucking behavior was organized along two functional dimensions, reflecting overall sucking effort and behavioral activation, and the temporal organization of sucking bursts. Importantly, higher maternal depressive traits, though subclinical, were selectively associated with increased sucking effort, with infants of mothers reporting higher depressive traits showing more frequent and intense sucking, while no differences emerged for the organizational dimension. Overall, these findings suggest that individual differences in maternal depressive traits within the subclinical range may be associated with neonatal NNS effort, a precocious compensatory mobilization of regulatory resources, potentially serving both to support autonomous regulation and to elicit maternal engagement.

title: Gesture use in autobiographical memory narration: The comparison of blind and sighted early teenagers
abstract: Gestures are an integral component of speech. During autobiographical memory narration, gestures can be linked to the episodic quality of recalled events, facilitating speech production or supporting visuospatial processing. Gestures' role in children's autobiographical memory, particularly in blindness, remains unclear. The present study examined how cue modality (visually known, haptically known, abstract) related to episodic details of autobiographical memories and gesture use in blind and sighted early teenagers, and whether gesture use was associated with the episodic richness of recalled memories. Thirty-three blind and thirty-six sighted early teenagers were asked to recall autobiographical memories using a cue-word methodology. The recalled memories were subsequently coded for episodic and non-episodic details, as well as for representational and non-representational gesture use. Results showed that memory content varied as a function of cue modality in a similar manner across groups, with haptically-known cues eliciting fewer episodic details than visually-known and abstract cues. This cue-modality effect was attenuated when controlling for age, suggesting it may be partly age-driven. Blind teenagers produced more non-episodic details than sighted ones despite comparable levels of episodic content. Sighted teenagers gestured more frequently than blind teenagers, although gesture use did not vary by cue modality. Crucially, gesture frequency was not related to episodic quality of autobiographical memories in either group. These findings suggest that while gestures may support autobiographical retrieval in adults capable of producing extended, coherent narratives, their role may be more limited in sighted and blind teenagers, potentially due to developmental differences in scene construction and narrative ability.

title: Altered dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates in autism spectrum disorder
abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is associated with widespread alterations in functional brain networks, but its transient dynamic brain states and potential transcriptomic correlates remain unclear. We applied Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA) to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 110 individuals with ASD and 110 healthy controls (HCs) from the Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange I (ABIDE I) dataset. Five recurrent phase-locking states were identified, and dynamic brain state metrics were compared between groups. Compared with HCs, individuals with ASD showed reduced fractional occupancy (FO) of State 5, which was predominantly characterized by the visual network with additional involvement of the sensorimotor network. Exploratory analyses within the ASD group revealed nominal negative associations between State 4 FO and ADOS total and social scores. To investigate potential transcriptomic correlates, we derived an ROI-wise ASD-HC State 5 weighted beta map and related it to Allen Human Brain Atlas (AHBA) gene expression data and SFARI ASD risk gene sets. SFARI ASD risk gene sets showed a consistent pattern of negative spatial associations with the ASD-related State 5 imaging phenotype, but these associations did not reach statistical significance after BrainSMASH testing and FDR correction. Exploratory rank-based Gene Ontology (GO) analysis implicated biological functions related to neuronal structure, synaptic function, and the regulation of neuronal excitability. These findings identify alterations in dynamic brain state organization in ASD and provide exploratory transcriptomic clues to their potential biological context.

title: Understanding verbal and numerical probability information and decision making among individuals with and without autism spectrum disorder
abstract: This study examined how individuals with and without autism spectrum disorder (ASD) interpret probabilistic information expressed verbally or numerically, and how such interpretations influence decision-making. Two experiments were conducted: Experiment 1 included 48 participants with ASD and 41 participants without ASD in the final analyses, and Experiment 2 included an independent sample of 49 participants without ASD. Participants translated verbal probability expressions (e.g., likely, doubtful) into numerical estimates and made hypothetical treatment recommendations based on either verbal or numerical probabilities. Compared with non-ASD individuals, participants with ASD showed less differentiated numerical translations across verbal probability expressions, indicating greater similarity in the numerical meanings assigned to different expressions. A hierarchical Bayesian analysis followed by cluster analysis identified three decision-making profiles. Notably, individuals with ASD were more likely to belong to a cluster characterized by stronger sensitivity to the directionality (positive vs. negative framing) of verbal probability expressions and weaker reliance on numerical translation. In contrast, non-ASD individuals were more frequently represented in a cluster that relied primarily on numerical information. These findings suggest that individuals with and without ASD differ in how verbal probability expressions are interpreted and incorporated into decision making, highlighting the importance of considering individual differences in the communication of uncertainty.

title: Neuregulin 2 and tubulin protein levels in children with autism spectrum disorder
abstract:
Background Multiple lines of evidence suggest that neuregulin 2 (NRG2) and tubulin play important roles in the neuron cytoskeleton, neuronal development, synaptic plasticity, and downstream signaling pathways implicated in autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This study aimed to investigate plasma levels of NRG2 and tubulin in ASD and to examine their association with the ASD severity and social impairment. Method Plasma levels of NRG2 and tubulin were measured using a sandwich enzyme immunoassay in 40 children with ASD and 40 age-matched healthy controls. Autism severity and social impairment were evaluated by the childhood autism rating scale (CARS) and Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS) respectively. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was performed to determine the area under the curve (AUC), and Spearman’s correlation coefficients (r) were calculated to examine the relationships between NRG2 and tubulin levels and CARS, SRS, and age using SPSS. Results Significantly decreased plasma levels of NRG2 were observed in children with ASD ( n = 40, 4.27 ± 0.26 ng/ml [mean ± SEM]) compared with healthy controls ( n = 40, 5.44 ± 0.42 ng/ml, [mean ± SEM], p < 0.05). Similarly, plasma tubulin levels were significantly lower in children with ASD ( n = 37, 3.65 ± 0.42 ng /ml) than in healthy controls ( n = 38, 6.05 ± 0.48 ng /ml), [mean ± SEM], p < 0.05). Segregation of children with ASD into ASD level 2 and ASD level 3 autism revealed that both the ASD level 2 ( n = 17, 3.03 ± 0.40 ng /ml, p = 0.001) and ASD level 3 group ( n = 20, 4.18 ± 0.57 ng /ml p = 0.01) had significantly lower tubulin levels ( p < 0.05), compared with control children. NRG2 was significantly positively correlated with SRS scores (r = 0.434, p = 0.005), whereas tubulin exhibited significant diagnostic accuracy (AUC = 0.743, 95% CI [0.146–0.369], p < 0.001). Conclusion Our findings highlight the potential involvement of NRG2 and tubulin in the pathophysiology of ASD, particularly in relation to neuronal development and synaptic function. Their association with social ability of children with ASD and diagnostic sensitivity suggests that they may serve as promising candidate biomarkers. Further large-scale studies are needed to confirm these findings and clarify their roles in ASD pathogenesis.

Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a group of neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by impairments in social communication, as well as restricted and repetitive behaviors and interests, as defined in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders 5 (DSM-5) [ 1 ]. The worldwide prevalence of ASD is estimated to be approximately 1 in 127 individuals [ 2 ]. A study from the United States involving 11 communities in the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring Network reported a prevalence of 1 in 36 children (2.8%) [ 3 ]. In Saudi Arabia, the prevalence of autism varies, however, a recent study reported a prevalence of 2.51% among children aged 2–4 years, with a male to female ratio of 3:1, while other studies have reported lower prevalence rates [ 4 ]. Neuregulins are soluble proteins that function as growth and differentiation factors and are structurally related to the epidermal growth factor (EGF) family. The neuregulin family includes four isoforms, NRG1, NRG2, NRG3 and NRG4, which are involved in the development and homeostasis of the nervous system, heart, and other organs. The interaction of neuregulins with ErbB receptors plays an essential role in several biological processes in the nervous system, including neuronal migration and development, synaptic plasticity, and the regulation of neuromuscular receptor expression [ 5 ]. NRG1 plays a critical role in nervous system development and is highly expressed in the embryonic and fetal brain. In contrast, NRG2 transcript levels increase markedly after birth, suggesting a role in adulthood. NRG2 is persistently expressed in the cerebellum, olfactory bulb and dentate gyrus, highlighting its potential involvement in neurodevelopment disorders such as ASD [ 6 , 7 ]. NRG2 has been shown to regulate N-methyle-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor function through ErbB4 signalling in the postnatal brain and has been associated with cognitive impairment in psychiatric disorders [ 8 ]. Furthermore, NRG2 knockout animal studies have revealed dopamine dysregulation in the dorsal striatum and medial prefrontal cortex, accompanied by behavioral abnormalities resembling those observed in psychiatric disorders [ 9 ]. Tubulin is a globular protein composed of α- and β- tubulin heterodimers that polymerize to form protofilaments, which subsequently assemble into microtubules, the primary components of the cytoskeleton in all eukaryotic cells [ 10 ]. Mutations in α- and β tubulin genes have been associated with a range of neurodevelopmental disorders [ 11 ]. Microtubules are essential for maintaining cytoskeleton structure, supporting synaptic plasticity, and facilitating axonal growth and maintenance. They also serve as intracellular transport tracks for the movement of specific proteins and organelles [ 12 ]. Disruptions in microtubule organization can impair neuronal proliferation, migration and synaptogenesis. Myelination, the process of insulating nerve fibers, is essential for efficient neuronal communication and overall brain function. Abnormal myelination has been reported in individuals with ASD, further supporting the involvement of cytoskeletal and microtubule-related pathways in the pathophysiology of the disorder [ 13 ]. Thus, NRG2 and tubulin are involved in neuronal development, function and signaling pathways that are critical for normal brain function, and their impairment or dysregulation may contribute to the etiology of psychiatric disorders such as autism. Therefore, in this study, we aimed to investigate the plasma levels of NRG2 and tubulin proteins in patients with ASD compared with age-matched healthy control children. Materials and methods Patient selection This case-control study was conducted at the Autism Research and Treatment Centre, Department of Physiology, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Patients were diagnosed with ASD by certified consultant neurologist according to the criteria of the 5th edition of the diagnostic and statistical manual of mental disorders criteria (American Psychiatric Association, 2013). The ASD group comprised 40 male children aged 3–12 years (mean ± SD = 6.82 ± 2.37 years). Patients with neurological disorders (such as palsy or tuberous sclerosis), metabolic disorders (e.g., phenylketonuria or diabetes), or autoimmune diseases were excluded from the study. The control group consisted of 40 age- and sex-matched healthy children, who attended a routine follow-up at the Well Baby Clinic, College of Medicine, King Khalid Hospital and were unrelated to the children with ASD and ranged in age from 3 to 14 years (mean ± SD = 7.97 ± 3.74 years). The control These children had no history of neuropsychiatric disorders, immunological conditions, or chronic diseases that could affect NRG2 or tubulin levels. The control group consisted of 40 age- and sex-matched healthy children who were unrelated to the children with ASD and ranged in age from 3 to 14 years (mean ± SD: 7.97 ± 3.74 years). These children had no history of neuropsychiatric disorders, immunological conditions, or chronic diseases that could affect NRG2 or tubulin levels. The study was approved by the Ethical Committee of the College of Medicine and King Khalid University Hospital (Approval - No. E-10-220). Written informed consent was obtained from the parents or legal guardian of all participants prior to the study. ASD diagnosis/study measurements Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) The diagnosis of ASD was based on clinical examination, neuropsychiatric assessment and clinical history given by the caregivers. Autism severity was assessed by using the Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) which rates children on a scale from 1 to 4 across 15 behavioral domains, as described previously [ 14 ]. According to this scale, children with scores of 30–36 were classified as having ASD level 2 autism, whereas those with scores of 36.5 or higher classified as having ASD level 3 autism. Short Sensory Profile (SSP) Sensory processing skills of children with ASD were assessed using the SSP questionnaire. Scores below 142 indicated severe sensory processing impairment (definite difference from typical performance), scores between 142 and 152 indicated mild-to-moderate impairment (probable difference from typical performance), and scores between 153 and 190 indicated typical sensory performance [ 15 ]. Social Responsiveness Scale (SRS) The social abilities of children with ASD were assessed using a validated instrument that evaluates interpersonal behavior, communication, and stereotypical traits associated with ASD. The instrument includes five subscales: social awareness, social cognition, social communication, social motivation, and autistic mannerisms. SRS scores range from 0 to 195, reflecting varying levels of social impairment in individuals with ASD. Scores between 60 and 75 indicate a mild-to-moderate level of social impairment, whereas scores of 76 or higher suggest severe social impairment and are strongly associated with a clinical diagnosis of ASD [ 16 ]. Blood collection Approximately 3 ml blood was collected from each child with ASD and age-matched healthy control. Samples were incubated at room temperature for 1 h, after which plasma was separated by centrifugation at 1500×g for 10 min, aliquoted and stored at − 80 °C until analysis. Determination of plasma tubulin and NRG2 levels by ELISA Plasma tubulin-β levels were measured using a Human TUBβ (Tubulin Beta) ELISA kit (Cat. No. ELK5140; ELK Biotechnology Limited, Sugar Land, TX, USA), and neuregulin-2 levels were measured using a Human NRG2 ELISA kit (Cat. No. E-EL-H0899; Elabscience Biotechnology, Houston, TX, USA), according to the manufacturers’ instructions. Both assays were based on sandwich-ELISA principles, in which antibodies specific to human tubulin-β or NRG2 were pre-coated onto microtiter plates. The test samples and standards were added to the plates and incubated at 80 min at 37 °C. After washing, biotin-conjugated antibodies specific to human tubulin-β and neuregulin-2 were added and the plates were incubated for 50 min at 37 °C. Subsequently, horseradish peroxidase (HRP) conjugated with avidin was added, followed by incubation for an additional 50 min at 37 °C. The mirotiter plates were washed five times and TMB substrate solution was added at incubated for 20 min at 37 °C. The reaction was stopped, and absorbance was measured at 450 nm ± 10 nm using a microplate reader. Statistical analysis Data were analyzed using a commercially available Social Sciences Software, version 26 (SPSS Inc. Chicago, IL, USA). Results were expressed as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Comparisons between children with ASD and healthy control children were performed using the Mann–Whitney U test. Results Analysis of NRG2 and tubulin levels As shown in Fig. 1 , children with autism had significantly lower plasma levels of NRG2 ( n = 40, 4.27 ± 0.26 ng/ml [mean ± SEM]) compared with healthy controls ( n = 40, 5.44 ± 0.42 ng/ml, [mean ± SEM], p < 0.05). However, no statistically significant differences in NRG2 levels were observed between control subjects and children with ASD level 2 or ASD level 3 autism, p > 0.05, (Fig. 2 ). Plasma tubulin levels were significantly lower in children with ASD ( n = 37, 3.65 ± 0.42 ng /ml [mean ± SEM])) compared with healthy control subjects ( n = 38, 6.05 ± 0.48 ng /ml [mean ± SEM], p < 0.05), as shown in Fig. 3 . When the ASD group was stratified by severity, both children with ASD level 2 ( n = 17; 3.03 ± 0.40 ng/mL; p = 0.001) and ASD level 3 autism ( n = 20; 4.18 ± 0.57 ng/mL; p = 0.01) exhibited significantly lower tubulin levels compared with control children ( p < 0.05), as illustrated in Fig. 4 . Correlation analysis of NRG2 and tubulin with CARS, SRS, SSP and age Spearman’s correlation coefficient (r) was used to evaluate the associations between NRG2 and tubulin, as well as between each of them and CARS, SRS, SSP, and age as measures of ASD severity. Tubulin did not show significant correlations with CARS, SRS, SSP, or age ( p > 0.05; Table 1 ). However, among all parameters, NRG2 showed the only significant positive correlation with SRS, which reflects social impairment associated with ASD ( r = 0.434, p = 0.005; Table 1 ; Fig. 5 ). Tubulin and NRG2 showed a non-significant positive correlation with each other ( p > 0.05; Table 1 ). Data showing the CARS, SRS and SSP for patients with ASD are shown in the Appendix . AUC-ROC analysis of NRG2 and tubulin for ASD Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was performed to evaluate the performance of NRG2 and tubulin in predicting ASD. Among the evaluated markers, tubulin showed significant predictive ability (AUC = 0.743, 95% CI [0.146–0.369], p < 0.001), supporting its role as a predictive marker for ASD, Table 2 ; Fig. 6 . However, NRG2 did not show any predictive ability for ASD ( p > 0.05), Table 2 ; Fig. 7 . Discussion In this study, plasma levels of both NRG2 and tubulin were significantly reduced in children with ASD compared with healthy subjects. NRG2 showed a significant positive correlation with SRS, whereas tubulin did not show any significant correlations with CARS, SRS, or SSP. Similar findings have reported previously, where significantly reduced NRG2 gene expression was observed in individuals with ASD compared with control subjects. Exome sequencing of the NRG2 gene revealed a small deletion in the EGF-like domain at the C-terminus of the NRG2 precursor protein, a region critical for its biological activity [ 17 ]. Reduced gene expression or sequence variation in NRG2 gene suggests a loss-of-function mechanism supports and its association with ASD. Furthermore, linkage and association studies have identified the NRG2 gene locus as being implicated in psychiatric disorders [ 18 , 19 ]. NRG2 belongs to epidermal growth factor family, which regulates cell growth and development through the ErbB family of receptor tyrosine kinases, comprising ErbB1, ErbB2, ErbB3 and ErbB4 [ 20 , 21 ]. The neuregulin-ErbB signaling complex is involved in multiple cellular functions throughout the body, including critical roles in the nervous system [ 22 ]. The genomic region containing the NRG2 locus has been linked to attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in multigenerational extended families and also associated with schizophrenia and bipolar disorder [ 19 , 23 , 24 ]. title: The role of bilateral temporal poles activity mediating the association between anxiety symptoms and sleep problems in children with autism spectrum disorder
abstract:
BACKGROUND: Sleep problems and anxiety symptoms frequently occur in children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). This investigation sought to examine the shared neural mechanisms that underly the co-occurrence of anxiety symptoms and sleep problems in this population.

METHODS: A total of 163 children with ASD were recruited. The anxiety symptoms and sleep problems were assessed through the Child Behavior Checklist and Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire, respectively. Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging(rs-fMRI) was utilized to compute the amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations (ALFF). Mediation analyses were conducted to examine the interrelationships among ALFF, anxiety symptoms, and sleep problems.

RESULTS: Sleep problems scores were positively linked to anxiety scores. ALFF in bilateral temporal poles were positively linked to anxiety scores. Mediation analyses revealed the right superior temporal pole mediated the pathway from sleep problems to anxiety symptoms. The left middle temporal pole exhibited a significant mediating effect in both directions of anxiety-sleep relationship.

CONCLUSION: These findings enhance comprehension of neurobiological processes that underlie the co-occurrence of anxiety symptoms and sleep problems, while identifying promising targets for subsequent clinical therapeutic approaches. As all rs-fMRI scans were performed under sedation, our results cannot be generalized to unsedated children or those scanned with different sedative protocols.

title: The association between adult attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and lifestyle factors: findings from the UK Biobank
abstract:
Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder, with diagnosis persisting in adulthood in up to 55% of cases. The association of ADHD with health-related behaviors in middle-aged and older adults remains relatively underexplored. We examined the relationship between ADHD in later adulthood and nutritional and lifestyle factors. Methods This cross-sectional study included UK Biobank participants aged 40 years and older. Individuals reporting ADHD diagnosis were compared to age- and sex-matched individuals with a ratio of 1:10. Multivariate linear, logistic and multinominal regression models were used to assess the relationship of ADHD diagnosis with lifestyle factors, adjusting for sex, age, education, BMI, sleeplessness, alcohol intake, smoking and physical activity. Interaction with age and sex were additionally tested. Results The sample included 133 individuals with ADHD diagnosis and 1330 in the comparison group (mean age 56.0 ± 7.9 years, 42.8% men). After adjusting for potential confounders, ADHD was significantly associated with higher likelihood of being a former or current smoker (OR [95% CI], 2.2 [1.4, 3.3]; p < .001; 2.2 [1.2, 4]; p = .02 respectively), increased alcohol intake (OR [95% CI] 1.8 [1.1, 3]; p =.01), and higher energy intake (β [SE], 0.7 [0.4]; p < .001). The association between ADHD and smoking was stronger among men compared to women (p-for interaction=0.006). No significant associations were found between ADHD diagnosis and adherence to the Mediterranean diet or physical activity. Conclusion Our findings, which demonstrate associations between adult ADHD diagnosis and health-related behaviors, underscore the need for tailored health promotion strategies to mitigate long-term health risks in this population. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at https://doi.org/10.1186/s12888-026-08501-3 .

Introduction Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is a highly heritable neurodevelopmental disorder associated with significant functional impairments, elevated health risks and societal costs, underscoring the importance of evidence-based interventions and lifestyle considerations [ 1 ]. ADHD’s core features, such as inattention, impulsivity, hyperactivity and executive dysfunction, can interfere with functioning and development [ 2 ], undermine self-regulation and consistency in daily routines [ 3 ]. These influences may explain why individuals with an ADHD diagnosis often struggle with consistent routines and health-promoting behaviors [ 4 , 5 ], specifically influencing dietary habits, physical activity, smoking rates and alcohol use. The Mediterranean diet, high in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, legumes, and healthy fats like olive oil, along with moderate consumption of meat, dairy products, and alcohol intake [ 6 ], is associated with lower risks of cardiovascular disease [ 7 ], metabolic disorders, and cognitive decline in the general population [ 8 , 9 ], with well-documented anti-inflammatory [ 10 , 11 ] and neuroprotective properties [ 12 ]. These features may be particularly relevant for individuals with ADHD, as this diet may support weight regulation, neuronal functioning and cognitive performance [ 13 , 14 ]. Indeed, several studies have shown that individuals with ADHD are less likely to adhere to the Mediterranean diet compared to those without this condition [ 15 – 17 ]. However, most of this evidence derives from studies in children and younger populations, leaving adherence patterns in older adults with ADHD largely unexplored. Beyond unhealthy diet, lower physical activity is also commonly observed among individuals with ADHD [ 18 , 19 ]. In addition, ADHD is strongly associated with increased risk of smoking, with childhood ADHD predicting nicotine dependence in later life and earlier smoking initiation in young adults [ 20 – 22 ]. Similarly, impulsivity, a core ADHD characteristic, is linked to alcohol use disorders, including increased binge drinking and earlier onset of alcohol use [ 23 , 24 ], with young adults with ADHD reporting higher alcohol consumption than controls [ 25 , 26 ]. Because most existing studies concentrate on children and young adults, a critical gap remains in our understanding of how ADHD is associated with health behaviors in later adulthood, limiting the evidence available to inform lifestyle interventions in this population. Yet, although ADHD is one of the most common neurodevelopmental disorders of childhood [ 27 ], symptoms persist into adulthood in up to 55% of cases [ 28 ], and the prevalence among adults is estimated at 1–2.5%. The current study aimed to assess the relationship between ADHD and lifestyle factors in middle-aged and older adults. Considering age and sex differences in ADHD health effects [ 29 , 30 ], we also tested for effect-modification by these factors. The current findings may improve understanding of ADHD associations with nutritional and life-style factors during older adulthood and help address the limited evidence regarding lifestyle interventions for middle-aged and older adults with ADHD. Methods Study design and population This study is a secondary data analysis using the UK Biobank dataset, a large cohort designed to improve chronic diseases prevention, diagnosis, and treatment. The resource includes 502,367 UK participants, aged 40 years and older, recruited between 2006 and 2010. The UK Biobank collects health, environmental, and lifestyle data through questionnaires, physical measurements, and biological samples, offering insights into genetics, behavior, and health outcomes. Participants voluntarily completed a touchscreen questionnaire and underwent an online interview, providing self-reported data on mental health, health behaviors, and lifestyle factors. Quality control by the UK Biobank ensured reliable data for secondary analyses [ 31 ]. The initial sample included 502,367 participants (Fig. 1 ). Of them, 345,036 individuals did not complete a mental health questionnaire. From the remaining 157,331 who did, we identified 133 individuals who reported a diagnosis of ADHD as one of their mental health diagnoses in response to the relevant item in the mental health questionnaire. From the remaining 157,201 participants who did not report an ADHD diagnosis, 43,422 were excluded for not completing the diet questionnaire and 3,185 for implausible or extreme values in energy intake and BMI, defined as more than three standard deviations from the mean of the z-score value. Among the remaining 110,594 individuals with no report of ADHD, we randomly selected 1,330 participants at a 1:10 ratio to maximize statistical efficiency and precision of estimates, given the limited number of cases and the abundance of eligible controls [ 32 ]. Comparison group was matched to ADHD participants based on age and sex using the matchit function from the MatchIt package in R (version 4.5.0). ADHD ascertainment ADHD diagnosis was identified using a self-reported question from the UK Biobank mental health questionnaire (Field ID 20544): “Have you been diagnosed with one or more of the following mental health problems by a professional, even if you don’t have it currently? (tick all that apply).” ADHD was included as one of the mentioned disorders [ 33 ]. A binary variable was created indicating ADHD diagnosis presence or absence. Study outcomes Dietary patterns were assessed using the UK Biobank touchscreen questionnaire [ 34 ] and the validated Oxford WebQ 24-hour recall questionnaire, which asked participants to choose the number of portions consumed from various food groups and items on the previous day [ 35 ]. For participants who completed more than one dietary recall assessment, mean energy intake was calculated across all available questionnaires. Mediterranean Diet Score was calculated using the I-MEDAS (Israel-Mediterranean Diet Adherence Screener) scale [ 36 ], including items such as frequency of olive oil use, consumption of fruits, vegetables, legumes, whole grains, fish, red meat, and sweetened beverages. Higher scores indicate greater adherence to the Mediterranean dietary pattern. Information on intake scores by ADHD status is provided in Supplemental Table 1 . The I-MEDAS was selected because it represents an expanded adaptation of the original MEDAS screener [ 37 ], retaining its core Mediterranean diet components while incorporating additional indicators of overall diet quality, including whole-grain consumption and intake of sweet and savory pastries and salty snacks. These additional components are particularly relevant in ADHD, which has been associated with poorer diet quality, higher intake of processed foods, and greater energy intake. Physical activity levels were assessed using the validated short International Physical Activity Questionnaire (IPAQ) [ 38 ], which assesses frequency, intensity, and duration of walking, as well as moderate and vigorous physical activity. “Moderate” activity requires moderate effort, (e.g., walking upstairs, gym, jogging, energetic dancing, aerobics), while “vigorous” activity requires vigorous effort (e.g., running, cycling uphill, carrying heavy furniture upstairs, martial arts, competitive sports or intensive exercise). Total physical activity was quantified by weighting time spent in activities by energy expenditure, producing MET minutes per week. Based on this assessment, the Physical Activity variable in this study indicates whether an individual met the 2017 UK Physical Activity Guidelines, defined as engaging in at least 150 minutes of walking or moderate activity per week or 75 minutes of vigorous activity per week. A categorical measure was chosen for physical activity considering the older ages of the study participants who are less frequently engaged in vigorous activity. Smoking status was assessed using the UK Biobank touchscreen questionnaire, categorized as “never,” “previous” or “current” smoking. Alcohol consumption frequency was extracted from the same questionnaire and defined as frequency of alcoholic drinking per day/week or month. Alcohol consumption was categorized as either “Daily or almost daily”, or “less”, in accordance with the Mediterranean diet guidelines. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated from participants’ self-reported height and weight. The estimated intake of energy was calculated by the UK Biobank from standard food composition tables, based on responses to the 24-hour recall diet questionnaire. Study covariates Age, sex, and education were self-reported and included as potential confounders, as they represent well-established demographic and socioeconomic factors associated with both ADHD status and the lifestyle outcomes examined. Previous research has demonstrated sex and age differences in ADHD prevalence and symptom expression [ 39 , 40 ], as well as associations between socioeconomic position, including educational attainment, and ADHD diagnosis [ 41 ]. These factors are also strongly associated with lifestyle behaviors including smoking, alcohol consumption, dietary patterns, and physical activity [ 42 , 43 ]. Sleep disorders, assessed via the UK Biobank touchscreen questionnaire, were considered a potential confounder, as they are associated with both ADHD and dietary patterns [ 44 – 46 ]. Similarly, physical activity levels were considered a potential confounder in the relationship between ADHD diagnosis and dietary patterns, as they may influence dietary decisions, alcohol consumption and smoking status [ 47 – 49 ]. Physical activity was treated as an outcome when examining its direct association with ADHD but included as a covariate in models assessing other lifestyle factors (e.g., diet, smoking, alcohol consumption) to account for its interrelation with these behaviors and to better isolate the specific association of ADHD with each outcome. Statistical analysis Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the characteristics of the study variables. Categorical variables were presented as frequencies and percentages, and continuous variables as mean and standard deviation (mean ± SD). Chi-square and Independent samples t-tests were used to compare categorical and continuous variables, respectively, between ADHD groups. Multivariable linear, logistic and multinominal regression models were used to examine the associations between ADHD diagnosis and the study outcomes, adjusting for potential confounders. The basic model included age and sex (the matching variables) and education. Model 2 further adjusted for BMI and model 3 additionally included smoking status, alcohol intake frequency, sleep disorders and adherence to physical activity guidelines. Because alcohol consumption constitutes one component of the I-MEDAS score and was also analyzed as an independent outcome, the association between ADHD and Mediterranean diet adherence was examined without adjusting for alcohol intake frequency. Model 1 included only demographic covariates to estimate the unadjusted association. Model 2 added BMI, a central health indicator known to be related to both ADHD and lifestyle behaviors. Model 3 further incorporated behavioral factors, providing a comprehensive adjustment for interrelated lifestyle characteristics. Total energy consumption was root transformed due to significant skewness exhibition. Interaction terms between ADHD diagnosis and age as well as ADHD diagnosis and sex, were included in the basic model to test whether each of these variables modify the association between ADHD diagnosis and the study outcomes. For significant interactions, a stratified analysis was done with age, sex, and education as covariates. All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS (version 27.0.1). A p -value of below 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. To account for multiple comparisons across the primary outcomes, a Bonferroni correction was performed. For interaction terms, a significance threshold of 0.10 was applied, consistent with common practice, given the lower statistical power of tests for effect modification. As an additional sensitivity analysis we repeated the primary analyses after excluding participants with a history of cardiovascular disease, diabetes, or depression ( n = 503), as these chronic conditions may independently influence lifestyle behaviors and potentially confound the observed associations [ 50 – 52 ]. To assess the robustness of the null findings to potential underdiagnosis of ADHD, we conducted a sensitivity analysis using a probabilistic Monte Carlo quantitative bias analysis, assuming non-differential exposure misclassification [ 53 ]. title: Effects of Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation on Core Symptoms and Sleep Disturbances in Children With Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Meta-Analysis of Randomized Controlled Trials
abstract:
ABSTRACT Objective This meta‐analysis was designed to determine whether transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) confers measurable benefits for selected behavioral features of autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and for sleep problems in pediatric ASD populations. Methods A comprehensive literature retrieval was conducted across eight electronic databases—PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Embase, CNKI, CBM, VIP, and Wanfang—covering the period from each database's inception through June 1, 2026. Eligible studies were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that evaluated the therapeutic efficacy of transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) in patients with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The methodological quality of the included trials was appraised using the Cochrane Risk of Bias assessment instrument. Quantitative synthesis was performed with RevMan 5.4 and Stata 17.0, following the PRISMA statement for systematic reviews and meta‐analyses. Results Ultimately, seven studies qualified for inclusion in this systematic review. Pooled analyses showed that tDCS was associated with lower ATEC scores (mean difference [MD] = −8.81, 95% confidence interval [CI]: −12.06 to −5.56, p < 0.00001), ABC scores (MD = −12.08, 95% CI: −21.75 to −2.41, p = 0.01), and CSHQ scores (MD = −4.95, 95% CI: −8.66 to −1.24, p = 0.009). However, no statistically significant difference was observed for CARS scores (MD = −1.12, 95% CI: −4.15 to 1.91, p = 0.47). Conclusion tDCS, most commonly delivered at 1 mA over the DLPFC, was associated with improvements in some ASD‐related behavioral outcomes; preliminary evidence also suggested a potential benefit for sleep disturbances, although this finding was based on only two low‐certainty studies and warrants cautious interpretation.

1 Introduction Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) represents a neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by core impairments encompassing persistent deficits in social communication and reciprocal social interaction, alongside constrained or stereotyped patterns of behavior and interests. Nevertheless, these manifestations often remain undetected until environmental or social expectations surpass the individual's adaptive capacity, and ASD‐related symptoms generally lead to substantial functional impairment spanning several domains. According to surveillance estimates from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) via the Autism and Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network, roughly 1 in 31 children at 8 years of age (3.2%) are diagnosed with ASD. At present, the prevalence of ASD among boys (49.2 per 1,000) is 3.4 times that observed among girls (14.3 per 1,000) (Shaw et al. 2025 ). Such an upward trend in prevalence could signify not merely an actual growth in ASD incidence but may equally be attributable to refinements in diagnostic criteria or advances in assessment instruments (Sharma et al. 2018 ). The etiology of ASD is multifactorial, with genetic and environmental determinants each contributing critically to the pathogenesis of the disorder (Sharma et al. 2018 ). Pathological studies on ASD have found differences in brain development, structure, and connectivity in individuals with the condition. The mechanism of action is complex, and effective clinical treatments are still lacking. Recent studies have shown promising results in treating ASD using non‐invasive brain stimulation techniques (Khaleghi et al. 2020 ), with one of the main techniques being tDCS. This method applies a current through electrodes placed on the scalp (Fernández‐Corazza et al. 2020 ). During tDCS, a low‐intensity electrical current is applied via electrodes positioned on the scalp, which modifies neuronal membrane potentials and consequently changes spontaneous firing rates (Sandrini et al. 2020 ). In a two‐electrode configuration, one electrode functions as the anode while the other acts as the cathode. Anodal polarization enhances neuronal excitability through depolarization, whereas cathodal polarization reduces excitability via hyperpolarization. This approach is capable of modulating the excitability of distinct cortical regions, and its influence on neuronal excitability may persist for minutes to hours following extended stimulation (Dalong et al. 2020 ; Li et al. 2019 ). Typically, a single tDCS session lasts no more than 20 min, employing a current strength of 1–2 mA. Under such parameters, tDCS has demonstrated a favorable safety profile and good tolerability (Zewdie et al. 2020 ). This form of brain stimulation has been tested as a therapeutic option in various psychiatric disorders, and tDCS appears to have positive effects on depression and certain symptoms of schizophrenia (Borrione et al. 2022 ; Narita et al. 2020 ), particularly in areas such as inhibitory control and working memory (Salehinejad et al. 2019 ). Increasing evidence suggests that social, cognitive, and sensory dysfunctions in ASD are associated with abnormalities in distributed networks rather than isolated brain regions. Therefore, tDCS may produce favorable effects due to its ability to modulate functional connectivity in the brain. Nevertheless, although tDCS has attracted increasing attention in autism research, its effects on sleep problems remain poorly characterized. Sleep disturbances are very common in children with autism and can have a big impact on their quality of life. A lot of people have sleep problems, and this makes them act in a worse way and makes them find it harder to think. Some studies have looked at how tDCS can help with the main symptoms of ASD, but there is not much evidence that it can improve sleep problems in children with ASD. Against this backdrop, the present meta‐analysis seeks to fill this gap by systematically assessing the efficacy of tDCS for alleviating ASD symptoms, with particular emphasis on its influence on sleep disturbances within this population. This will help clinicians and researchers understand better how tDCS could be used to treat not only core behavioral symptoms but also sleep problems, which are a clinical challenge that hasn't been fully addressed yet. Although some reviews have explored this area, there is a lack of objective, evidence‐based conclusions (Osório and Brunoni 2019 ). This means that a meta‐analysis is needed to evaluate the efficacy of tDCS in treating ASD. 2 Materials and Methods This systematic review and meta‐analysis was prospectively registered with the PROSPERO database (registration no. CRD42024588423). Its design and reporting conformed rigorously to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, thereby guaranteeing transparency and comprehensiveness. 2.1 Inclusion Criteria for Studies 2.1.1 Study Design Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) investigating tDCS in pediatric ASD populations and published in either Chinese or English were eligible. 2.1.2 Participants Individuals with a definitive ASD diagnosis established according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, Fifth Edition (DSM‐5) (American Psychiatric Association 2013 ) or the Chinese Classification of Mental Disorders, Third Edition (CCMD‐3). 2.1.3 Intervention While the control arm received sham stimulation or standard rehabilitation, the experimental arm received tDCS in addition to routine care. 2.1.4 Outcome Measures Core ASD symptoms—including social interaction, language ability, perception/cognition, and health/behavior—were evaluated using the Autism Treatment Evaluation Checklist (ATEC), where higher scores denote greater symptom severity and lower scores indicate milder manifestations. The Autism Behavior Checklist (ABC) serves as a preliminary instrument for assessing social interaction, communication, stereotyped behaviors, and interests in children with ASD. The Childhood Autism Rating Scale (CARS) is employed to facilitate the diagnosis and evaluation of ASD in children and to track therapeutic response. The Children's Sleep Habits Questionnaire (CSHQ) was designed primarily to determine the presence, characteristics, and severity of sleep problems in children. For inclusion, studies needed to report pre‐ and post‐intervention means and standard deviations (SD) for these scales in both the tDCS and sham groups. 2.2 Exclusion Criteria for Studies Empirical studies such as reviews, conference proceedings, and anecdotal reports. Cohort, case‐control, and cross‐sectional study designs were excluded. Likewise, articles published in languages other than English or Chinese were not considered. 2.3 Literature Search A total of eight electronic databases—PubMed, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, Embase, CNKI, CBM, VIP, and Wanfang—were searched, encompassing all records available from their inception through June 1, 2026. To maximize the identification of pertinent studies, a customized search strategy integrating medical subject headings (MeSH) with free‐text terms was employed for each database. In PubMed, the search combined MeSH terms such as “Autism Spectrum Disorder,” “Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation,” and terms for randomized controlled trials (e.g., “Randomized Controlled Trial,” “Placebo Controlled Trial”), along with corresponding free‐text keywords like “autism,” “tDCS,” and “RCT.” In Embase, Emtree terms aligned with autism and brain stimulation were used in combination with free‐text terms and filters for clinical trials. For Chinese databases (CNKI, CBM, VIP, Wanfang), equivalent subject terms and keywords were mapped from Chinese terminology to capture local literature comprehensively. The exact English search strategy was as follows: #1: “Autism Spectrum Disorder” OR “Autistic Spectrum Disorder” OR “Autism” OR “Disorder, Autistic Spectrum” #2: “Transcranial Direct Current Stimulation” OR “Noninvasive Brain Stimulation” OR “Transcranial Electrical Stimulation” OR “Transcranial Direct Current” OR “tDCS” OR “NIBS” #3: “Randomized Controlled Trial” OR “Controlled Clinical Trial” OR “Randomized” OR “Placebo” OR “RCT” OR “RCTs” #4: #1 AND #2 AND #3 Study selection and data extraction were performed independently by MingchenWang and Meimei Yang using a standardized form. Any disagreements concerning study eligibility or data interpretation were initially addressed through discussion between the two reviewers. When a consensus remained unattainable, Mingchen Wang was consulted as the third reviewer to render the final decision. This process ensured that study selection and data extraction were rigorous and minimized bias. 2.4 Outcome Measures Two researchers independently screened the studies against the predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. The screening process began with an assessment of titles and abstracts, followed by a full‐text review. Any disagreements that arose were settled through discussion. The following variables were extracted: (1) first author and publication year; (2) demographic information (number of patients, country, and age); (3) means and standard deviations (SD) for the following scale scores: (I) ABC, ATEC, CARS, and CSHQ; and (II) tDCS parameters (intensity, location, and treatment duration). Summary data from these RCTs were independently extracted by two researchers. 2.5 Quality Assessment of Literature The Cochrane Handbook version 5.1.0 (Higgins et al. 2019 ) served as the basis for appraising methodological quality, as it provides overarching recommendations regarding the reporting of RCTs. This earlier version of the Cochrane risk‐of‐bias tool was selected, rather than the current RoB 2 tool, because RoB 2 requires domain‐level signaling questions that were not consistently reported across the included trials; we acknowledge this as a methodological limitation and address its implications for the certainty of evidence in the discussion. For any quantitative synthesis that incorporated two or more studies, publication bias was evaluated based on the p ‐value derived from Egger's test. In accordance with the quality assessment criteria specified in the handbook, risk was classified into three categories: unclear, low, and high risk. Four authors were responsible for assessing the quality of the literature, and cross‐checking was performed to ensure accuracy, resulting in the final risk classification. 2.6 Statistical Analysis Meta‐analytic calculations were performed using RevMan 5.4 and Stata 17.0. Continuous data were summarized as the mean difference (MD) or standardized mean difference (SMD), with 95% confidence intervals computed for each estimate. Heterogeneity across studies was quantified using the I 2 value together with the p ‐value. The selection between fixed‐ and random‐effects models depended on the heterogeneity parameters: when I 2 < 50% and p > 0.1, a fixed‐effects model was selected; when I 2 ≥ 50% and P ≤ 0.1, a random‐effects model was chosen. Substantial heterogeneity was defined by I 2 ≥ 50% combined with P ≤ 0.1, and under such circumstances a random‐effects model was utilized. Statistical significance was determined at p < 0.05, with P ≥ 0.05 indicating a non‐significant result. A Z‐test was employed to determine the overall effect of tDCS, and bilateral P ‐values were derived. The significance thresholds were established a priori: p < 0.05 for the overall effect and p < 0.10 for tests of heterogeneity (χ 2 and subgroup interactions).
